item.title: 高分辨率世界生成不必再造一个精修网络：ScaleWorld 让每个尺度「精修自己的预测」 ｜ ScaleWorld: High-Resolution World Generation through Shared Prediction and Refinement
item.description:
一句话：直接生成高分辨率视频，算力与显存都吃不消。

要点：

  • 需求与代价：高分辨率生成让视频世界模型能渲染细粒度的场景结构与纹理，但**直接生成高分辨率视频会带来巨大的计算与显存开销**
  • ScaleWorld 是一个**因果视频模型**，把「低分辨率世界预测」与「高分辨率精修」**统一在同一个共享主干**里
  • 关键点是不再需要单独的精修网络：它**精修自己的预测**，从而在不引入额外模型的条件下产出高分辨率世界视频

为什么值得看：引擎里 LOD 的常识是「同一个模型多尺度出结果」，而世界模型往往被做成「低分模型 + 高分精修模型」两套。把两者合成一个共享主干，省的是模型数量与显存，而不是画质。

中文摘要：高分辨率生成让视频世界模型能够渲染细粒度的场景结构与纹理，但直接生成高分辨率视频会带来可观的计算与显存开销。ScaleWorld 提出一个因果视频模型，把低分辨率的「世界预测」与高分辨率的「精修」统一在同一个共享主干中：低分辨率阶段负责预测世界的演化，高分辨率阶段则精修它自己的预测结果，因此不需要额外训练一个独立的精修网络。对需要在不同分辨率与算力档位下部署同一世界模型的团队，这种「一份主干、多尺度自精修」的做法比维护两套模型更接近引擎里 LOD 的思路。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-20

本期推送：2026-11-22

ScaleWorld: High-Resolution World Generation through Shared Prediction and Refinement

Abstract

High-resolution generation enables video world models to render fine-grained scene structures and textures, but directly generating high-resolution video incurs substantial computational and memory costs. We present ScaleWorld, a causal video model that unifies low-resolution world prediction and high-resolution refinement within a single shared backbone. By refining its own predictions, ScaleWorld produces high-resolution world videos without requiring a separate refinement model. For each video chunk, the shared backbone first completes a low-resolution prediction and then performs one-step high-resolution refinement conditioned on that prediction. To support efficient streaming generation, we maintain separate causal states with a long low-resolution history for prediction and a short high-resolution history for refinement. To address task interference during distillation, we separate specialist optimization from capability consolidation and introduce task-asymmetric on-policy distillation (TA-OPD). This procedure transfers prediction and refinement behaviors from specialized teachers into a shared student through local velocity matching under their respective sampling and history policies. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ScaleWorld achieves high-quality world generation with improved computational and memory efficiency.

11footnotetext: Equal contribution.

1 Introduction

Video world models generate evolving visual environments conditioned on observations and control inputs [20, 3, 18]. High-resolution generation enables these models to depict fine-grained scene structures and textures as the environment evolves. Causal video diffusion supports incremental generation [27, 9], but directly generating high-resolution video incurs substantial computational and memory costs. Increasing spatial resolution raises both denoising computation and temporal-state storage, making high-resolution output costly to sustain in streaming world generation.

Coarse-to-fine pipelines address this cost by predicting at low resolution and refining the result with a dedicated model [8, 32]. This reduces the spatial cost of world prediction, but deploying separate predictors and refiners still requires storing two sets of model weights. Prediction and refinement share visual priors for structure, appearance, and motion, motivating a shared backbone. Cross-resolution reuse has been explored by Self-Cascade, Pyramid Flow, and HiStream [4, 11, 19]. Our focus is the coexistence of independently usable world prediction and conditional streaming refinement within one causal model. We therefore ask: can a world model learn high-resolution refinement while retaining native prediction?

We present ScaleWorld, a shared causal model for streaming world prediction and streaming high-resolution refinement. Both roles follow a chunk-wise autoregressive paradigm: the model first completes a low-resolution (LR) prediction, then uses the same backbone to perform one-step high-resolution (HR) refinement conditioned on that prediction and its own refinement history. No future LR chunks are required, so each completed prediction can be refined without waiting for a full video. The native LR output remains independently usable, and HR outputs do not feed back into prediction history. This design must accommodate the roles’ distinct temporal requirements while consolidating both capabilities in shared parameters.

To support efficient inference, we share model weights while maintaining separate causal states. World prediction retains a longer clean history at low resolution to infer scene evolution. Refinement already receives the current LR structure, content, and motion, and uses a shorter HR history to support the continuity of synthesized detail. It further retains key–value (KV) states from the denoising forward pass as noisy-forward history, avoiding an additional HR model evaluation for history construction. These asymmetric histories limit the cost of refinement while preserving longer temporal context for world prediction.

Sharing visual representations does not ensure that prediction and refinement can be effectively distilled together. In our joint distillation experiments, we observe conflicting gradients between the two tasks, and better reconstruction during refinement can accompany reduced temporal stability in world prediction (Appendix C.1). We therefore separate specialist optimization from capability consolidation. Starting from a jointly trained and causally adapted model, we first optimize prediction and refinement specialists under their respective sampling and history policies. Building on on-policy distillation [14, 31], we introduce task-asymmetric on-policy distillation (TA-OPD) to consolidate the frozen specialists into a shared student. TA-OPD matches expert velocities at student-visited denoising queries for prediction, and at matched conditional noise queries with network-specific recurrent histories for refinement, respecting the roles’ different execution policies.

We evaluate ScaleWorld on camera-controlled world generation, examining native prediction retention, refinement of fixed generated inputs, and complete HR generation. The shared model retains competitive native prediction performance and achieves HR generation quality comparable to a separate specialist cascade. Matched deployments of the same unified checkpoint show that sharing weights reduces peak GPU memory while preserving throughput. Noisy-forward history accelerates refinement over clean recommit by avoiding an extra HR forward pass.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    A shared causal world model for streaming prediction and streaming HR refinement, refining each completed LR prediction with the same backbone while retaining an independently usable native prediction path.

  • •

    A training and inference framework combining TA-OPD and asymmetric causal histories to meet the distinct optimization and temporal requirements of both roles.

  • •

    Empirical evidence of competitive prediction and HR generation quality, with controlled deployment measurements of memory savings from weight sharing and timing comparisons of refinement-history construction.

    • 2 Related Work

    Controllable world generation. Video diffusion models learn rich appearance and motion priors [6, 21]. Genie [1] learns action-controllable environments from unlabeled videos, while GameNGen [22] simulates interactive gameplay through action-conditioned frame prediction. Beyond games, GAIA-1 [7] generates driving scenarios conditioned on video, text, and actions. Cosmos [17] provides pretrained diffusion and autoregressive video world foundation models for physical AI.

    For efficient streaming generation, CausVid [27] and Self Forcing [9] combine few-step generation with autoregressive execution. Causal Forcing [33] uses autoregressive teacher trajectories for initialization before distribution matching distillation. WorldPlay [20], LingBot-World 2.0 [3], and Matrix-Game 3.5 [18] advance long-horizon controlled world generation. SANA-WM [32] combines camera-controlled generation with a separate long-video refiner. Our work focuses on high-resolution generation within a shared world-model backbone, with streaming execution for both prediction and refinement.

    Shared coarse-to-fine generation. Self-Cascade [4] reuses a pretrained low-resolution diffusion model for higher-resolution adaptation. Pyramid Flow [11] jointly learns resolution stages within a unified flow, while PyramidalWan [13] adapts pretrained video models to pyramidal generation. HiStream [19] performs early denoising at low resolution and later denoising at high resolution with dual-resolution caches. It also downsamples the final high-resolution output to refresh the low-resolution history cache. In ScaleWorld, each prediction chunk completes its native output before conditional refinement. The two roles maintain separate causal states, and refined outputs do not feed back into prediction.

    Other forms of parameter reuse include LongCat-Video [16], which trains a refinement expert through LoRA adaptation of its base model, and HiFI [10], which shares one model across frame interpolation and spatial upsampling. Our study examines parameter sharing between world prediction and conditional refinement under distinct sampling budgets and causal-memory policies.

    Generative video refinement. VEnhancer [5] improves generated videos through joint spatial and temporal enhancement. SeedVR [25] studies diffusion-based video restoration, while SeedVR2 [24] enables one-step restoration through adversarial post-training. FlashVSR [35] targets one-step streaming super-resolution. Ultra Flash [8] combines an autoregressive low-resolution generator with a dedicated causal refiner, using latent upsampling, single-step distillation, and preference optimization on generated contexts. Building on advances in streaming refinement, ScaleWorld consolidates refinement and native world prediction within one shared backbone.

    Distillation and capability composition. Distribution matching distillation (DMD) [26] transfers a diffusion model’s generative behavior to a one-step student. Self Forcing [9] addresses the exposure bias of autoregressive video generation through student-rollout training. DiffusionOPD [14] consolidates specialist capabilities on student trajectories, while DanceOPD [31] composes capabilities through routed velocity-field matching. For autoregressive video, OPSD-V [15] supervises student-visited denoising states using a teacher with cleaner, data-assisted temporal context. TA-OPD consolidates prediction and refinement specialists into a shared causal model through local velocity matching under role-specific sampling and history policies.

    3 Method

    Figure 2 summarizes ScaleWorld. We first define the shared streaming interface, then specify the two causal states, explain specialist training and consolidation, and analyze streaming execution and resource costs.

    3.1 Shared Streaming Prediction and Refinement

    We implement world prediction (WM) and high-resolution refinement (Ref) as two chunk-wise causal samplers with a shared velocity network v_θ. Our implementation conditions prediction on an initial observation I, text c, and camera controls a; refinement is learned through video super-resolution. For chunk k, the model first completes a low-resolution (LR) latent ẑₖ^L and then generates its high-resolution (HR) counterpart:

    ẑₖ^L=S_θ^WM(εₖ^L;I,c,a_≤k,Mₖ₋₁^WM),(1)
    ẑₖ^H=S_θ^Ref(εₖ^H;c,U(ẑₖ^L),Mₖ₋₁^Ref).(2)

    Here U spatially upsamples the LR latent, εₖ^L and εₖ^H collect the samplers’ random draws, and Mₖ₋₁^WM and Mₖ₋₁^Ref contain their separate histories before chunk k. Both roles are causal across chunks: refinement uses the completed current LR chunk and preceding context, without accessing future LR chunks. The LR output remains independently usable, and HR outputs never enter prediction history.

    For fixed parameters, supplied camera controls, and independent sampling streams, the sequence distribution factorizes as

    \beginsplitp_θ(z^L,z^H|I,c,a)=&p_θ^WM(z^L|I,c,a) &·p_θ^Ref(z^H|z^L,c).\endsplit

    		(3)

    Internal random variables and recurrent states are marginalized; refinement operates causally across chunks (Eq. 2).

    Shared visual interface. Both roles share a causal video backbone and its output head. The upsampled LR latent is concatenated with the noisy target before patch embedding. WM sets these condition channels to zero and uses image anchoring, text, and camera poses injected through Unified Camera Positional Encoding (UCPE) [29]. Ref supplies the LR latent and text, with no direct camera input or clean HR anchor. The expanded projection retains the original weights and zero-initializes the new condition weights, preserving the WM function at initialization (Appendix A.6).

    Role-specific sampling. For m∈{WM,Ref}, let cₘ collect the corresponding conditions. Under the flow parameterization zₜ=(1-σₜ)z₀+σₜε, the network predicts

    ẑ₀=zₜ-σₜv_θ(zₜ,t;cₘ,Mᵐ).

    		(4)

    WM uses a sequence of denoising queries, re-noising each clean prediction at the next noise level:

    z_k,j+1^θ,WM=(1-σⱼ₊₁)ẑ_k,j^θ,WM+σⱼ₊₁ε_k,j+1.

    		(5)

    Here j indexes queries, and the last clean prediction becomes the completed LR chunk. Ref uses one conditional noise query to produce its HR counterpart. Table 1 summarizes the two roles; their state updates are defined next.

    3.2 Asymmetric Causal Memory

    We design an asymmetric causal memory around the different information available to the two roles. WM predicts unobserved scene evolution from preceding context, whereas Ref receives the current scene structure and motion through its LR condition. We therefore couple a long clean LR history for prediction with a short noisy-forward HR history for refinement. The design is asymmetric in both temporal span and history construction. Window capacities are implementation choices specified in Appendix A.2.

    Clean KV for world prediction. WM re-encodes each completed LR chunk at zero noise to obtain clean KV features K_k,clean^WM for subsequent prediction. With Aₘ denoting the append-and-window operation for role m,

    Mₖ^WM=A_WM(Mₖ₋₁^WM,K_k,clean^WM).

    		(6)

    Clean recommit adds one LR evaluation after denoising.

    Noisy-forward KV reuse for refinement. Applying clean recommit to Ref would require a second HR model evaluation solely to construct history after its one-step generation. To avoid this cost, we reuse the KV features K_k,fwd^Ref computed within the refinement forward that generates the current HR chunk:

    Mₖ^Ref=A_Ref(Mₖ₋₁^Ref,K_k,fwd^Ref).

    		(7)

    These features are computed from the noisy HR input together with the current LR condition and preceding refinement context. They are retained from that forward pass, rather than obtained by re-encoding the completed HR output ẑₖ^H. Subsequent chunks attend to this memory within the short refinement window. Thus, each HR denoising evaluation serves two purposes: generating the current output and providing temporal features for later chunks. The resulting memory construction removes the additional HR clean-recommit evaluation while keeping prediction history and its update rule unchanged.

    Learning with noisy-forward memory. The refinement specialist learns with this recurrent memory. TA-OPD preserves the same KV construction when consolidating refinement into the shared student, and streaming inference follows that rule. This exposes the model during training to the type of history it will reuse at inference. Section 4.3 reports a controlled ablation of refinement-history construction; Appendix C.3 gives the protocol.

    For window advancement, both roles reindex temporal RoPE to local positions and transform cached keys without another model evaluation. Training and inference share this rule; Appendix A.3 details RoPE and retained anchors.

    3.3 Task-Asymmetric On-Policy Distillation

    We introduce task-asymmetric on-policy distillation (TA-OPD) to consolidate separately optimized prediction and refinement behaviors into one shared model. This separation is motivated by the conflicting gradient directions and imbalanced gradient magnitudes observed when jointly optimizing the specialist objectives (Appendix C.1). Building on on-policy distillation [14, 31], TA-OPD matches specialist velocities at the student’s current queries under each task’s sampling and memory policies.

    Specialist preparation. Joint bidirectional training first establishes both task interfaces, followed by causal adaptation and consistency distillation. From this shared foundation, we optimize a prediction specialist φ_WM and a refinement specialist φ_Ref through distribution matching distillation (DMD) [26], using their respective sampling and causal-memory policies. The refinement specialist additionally uses an auxiliary reconstruction objective, whereas the subsequent TA-OPD stage uses only local velocity matching. Both specialists are then frozen, and the shared student θ is initialized from the prediction specialist.

    Task-asymmetric supervision. For WM, the specialist supervises every student-visited denoising query in each content block. After each chunk, teacher and student separately encode the same completed student LR prediction at zero noise to build their own clean KV states. Supervision follows the student’s trajectory and generated history, with each network constructing its own features.

    For Ref, teacher and student process the same conditional HR noise query using their own recurrent histories and retain their own noisy-forward KV. Both networks recursively process preceding chunks to construct their own histories, while only the final block contributes to the velocity-matching loss. LR conditions during consolidation are obtained from degraded real videos, and the single-step HR noise input is sampled independently of the student. Student dependence in refinement therefore enters through its recurrent feature states. WM additionally follows a student-generated denoising trajectory. Within each task, teacher and student match the current noisy latent, timestep, conditions, window capacity, and RoPE rule, while their KV states remain network-specific.

    Local velocity matching. For chunk k and query j, let z_k,j^θ,m be the student’s current noisy latent and tⱼᵐ its timestep. For ψ∈{θ,φₘ}, define

    q_ψ,k,jᵐ=v_ψ(sg[z_k,j^θ,m],tⱼᵐ;c_m,k,sg[M_ψ,k,jᵐ]).

    		(8)

    Here c_m,k collects the chunk’s conditions, M_ψ,k,jᵐ is network ψ’s state before the query, and sg stops gradients through earlier sampling and history construction. Let d_θᵐ denote the joint distribution of queries and network states generated by the above procedure, with τ one realization. The consolidation objective is

    \beginsplitL_con&=∑ₘpₘ 𝔼_τ∼d_θᵐ[Lₘ(τ)], Lₘ(τ)&=(1)/(|Bₘ|)∑_k∈Bₘ∑ⱼ₌₁^Jₘwⱼᵐ ℓ_k,jᵐ, ℓ_k,jᵐ&=MSE(q_θ,k,jᵐ,sg[q_φₘ,k,jᵐ]).\endsplit

    		(9)

    Here Bₘ is the set of supervised blocks, Jₘ is the number of denoising queries (J_Ref=1), and wⱼᵐ=1/Jₘ. MSE is averaged over latent elements to avoid scaling the loss directly with spatial resolution. The coefficient pₘ denotes the frequency of task-m updates, rather than an additional per-update loss multiplier. The sampling schedules and task-update frequencies are specified in Appendix A.

    Although d_θᵐ changes as the student evolves, each update treats the sampled queries and cached histories as fixed. Gradients pass only through the current student velocity prediction, not through the rollout, state construction, or the parameter dependence of d_θᵐ. TA-OPD adds no reconstruction or perceptual-reward terms. Rollout lengths, supervised-block selection, and specialist-training settings are specified in Appendix A.

    3.4 Streaming Inference

    At inference, the shared model alternates between prediction and refinement. Each completed LR chunk updates the clean prediction memory and conditions its HR counterpart; the refinement forward simultaneously produces the HR output and the noisy-forward KV for subsequent chunks. This process uses only the available LR prefix and follows the same causal-memory rules as training. With fixed parameters, independent sampling streams, and unchanged prediction settings, enabling refinement leaves the native LR sample path unchanged.

    Memory and computation. The asymmetric memory allocates long-term context at low resolution while restricting the more expensive HR history to a shorter window. Let n_L,n_H denote spatial tokens per latent frame and w,s the prediction and refinement window capacities, including the current chunk and any retained anchor. For the same backbone, cache precision, and prediction-window capacity w, the self-attention KV-payload ratio relative to direct-HR prediction is

    (M_KVᶜᵃˢᶜᵃᵈᵉ)/(M_KV^direct-HR)=(n_Lw+n_Hs)/(n_Hw)=(n_L)/(n_H)+s/w.

    		(10)

    With s fixed, each additional prediction-window slot costs only n_L/n_H as much KV storage as a direct-HR slot. This ratio covers only KV storage; total GPU memory also includes weights and other allocations (Appendix D.2).

    Parameter sharing removes the duplicate backbone weights required by separate prediction and refinement specialists, while both causal memories are retained. Noisy-forward KV reuse additionally saves computation by removing the extra HR clean-recommit forward pass.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    We build ScaleWorld on Wan2.2 TI2V-5B, with world prediction at 480×832 and streaming refinement at 960×1664.

    We evaluate native world prediction and final high-resolution generation on WBench [28], reporting overall and per-dimension scores. All methods receive the same observations, camera commands, and temporal intervals, while retaining their supported inference settings. Native prediction baselines include HY-World 1.5 [20], LingBot-World 2.0 (fast) [3], and Matrix-Game 3.5 [18]. For high-resolution generation, we compare against WorldPlay [20], LingBot-World 2.0 [3], and Matrix-Game 3.5 [18] paired with Ultra Flash [8] or FlashVSR [35].

    We evaluate refinement separately using the same fixed set of decoded LR videos generated by our world model. We report MUSIQ [12] and CLIP-IQA+ [23] for perceptual quality, LR-consistency PSNR for preservation of the input content, and motion-compensated residuals (MC L1 and MC HF L1) for temporal variation. Appendices A and B detail training, evaluation protocols, and metrics.

    4.2 Generation Quality and Capability Retention

    Shared versus separate generation. Table 2(a) compares the unified model with a cascade of separately optimized specialists. The noisy-forward shared model achieves comparable overall HR quality, with stronger setting and interaction adherence and slightly lower visual quality. These results suggest that prediction and refinement can coexist in one backbone; the matched deployment comparison below isolates the resource savings from sharing its weights.

    Capability retention. The unified model remains close to its WM specialist on native WBench performance and achieves the highest visual-quality score among the evaluated native models (Table 2(b)). The modest decrease in consistency shows that retention is not uniform across dimensions. For refinement, the shared noisy-forward model remains close to its independent specialist on MUSIQ under the same decoded-LR protocol (Table 12). Figure 3 compares native camera-controlled outputs across models.

    Complete HR systems. Our unified prediction–refinement pipeline achieves the highest overall WBench score (81.60) among all evaluated systems, including native world models and cascaded high-resolution baselines (Tables 2 and 3). These scores reflect both prediction and refinement. We therefore compare refiners on fixed LR inputs below to control for upstream differences.

    Refinement of fixed predictions. On the same generated LR inputs, our refiner improves perceptual quality, LR consistency, and motion-compensated residuals over Ultra Flash under the full-frame protocol (Table 4). FlashVSR’s elevated MC L1 and MC HF L1 residuals suggest temporal fluctuations consistent with inter-frame flicker, although its center-crop protocol limits direct numerical comparison. Our outputs exhibit smoother frame-to-frame transitions and greater temporal continuity. Figure 4 shows qualitative comparisons.

    Figure 5 illustrates our unified prediction–refinement pipeline on camera-controlled rollouts. The HR outputs preserve the scene layout of the LR predictions while producing sharper structural boundaries and richer local textures, as highlighted by the matched crops.

    4.3 Training and Efficiency Analysis

    Distillation strategies. We compare mixed DMD, CD + mixed DMD, and TA-OPD from identical initialization (Table 5). TA-OPD achieves the highest overall native prediction score and setting adherence. In contrast, mixed DMD and CD + mixed DMD suffer from cross-task gradient interference during joint distillation (Table 6), limiting their overall performance.

    Task interference in mixed distillation. WM and Ref gradients shift from weak global alignment to opposing directions across the backbone during mixed distillation (Table 6). These measurements show conflicting update directions in the sampled training states and motivate separate specialist optimization before consolidation. Appendix C.1 details the diagnostic protocol and output analysis.

    Noisy-forward refinement history. Table 7 compares clean-recommit and noisy-forward histories with all other training and evaluation settings fixed. Reusing KV from the generation forward eliminates the additional HR pass used for clean recommit, yielding a 2× generator speedup before VAE decoding. End-to-end throughput improves by 26.9%, including WM prediction, refinement, history construction, and decoding (Table 12). Noisy-forward history also improves MUSIQ and LR consistency on fixed inputs, with a small increase in MC L1. It thus reduces computation while improving perceptual quality, with a measured trade-off in temporal residuals. Appendix C.3 gives the full settings.

    Shared-backbone deployment. Table 8 compares one- and two-copy deployments of the same unified checkpoint under matched inference settings (Appendix D). Weight sharing halves resident backbone storage and reduces peak GPU memory by 21.1% while preserving end-to-end throughput. KV allocation remains unchanged because both role-specific causal states are retained; the memory savings therefore come from removing duplicate weights.

    Parameter sharing and asymmetric memory address different costs: the former reduces resident weights, while the latter stores the longer prediction history at low resolution. The direct-HR comparison in Eq. 10 concerns KV payload and is distinct from the measured deployment savings.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented ScaleWorld, a shared causal model for camera-controlled prediction and high-resolution refinement. Its asymmetric temporal contexts allocate long history to low-resolution prediction, while specialist training and TA-OPD integrate the two capabilities. Experiments show comparable overall generation quality to a separate specialist cascade, retained native prediction capability, and lower resident deployment memory. The resulting model produces high-resolution worlds incrementally with one backbone. Limitations are discussed in Appendix E.

    （参考文献见原文。）


    Supplementary Material

    Appendix A Implementation Details

    A.1 Shared Visual Interface

    The reference backbone is Wan2.2 TI2V-5B. Its VAE uses 48 latent channels with spatial stride 16, and the transformer uses 2×2 spatial patches. For Ref, a 48-channel interpolated LR latent is concatenated with the noisy target before patch embedding. The added projection weights are initialized to zero when expanding a pretrained input layer. WM uses zero-valued LR channels and its image/camera conditioning; Ref uses a zero image-anchor mask and no camera condition. The shared transformer and output head serve both roles.

    Pixel-space degradation uses blur, bicubic downsampling, and noise while retaining consecutive frames. Latent conditioning uses nearest-neighbor spatial interpolation in the reference recipe. These operations are distinct: bicubic describes the LR video construction, not the latent upsampler. Additional latent-condition noise/dropout and a learned latent upsampler are disabled during reference consolidation. No refinement-specific spatial Swin partition is enabled.

    A.2 Sampling and Temporal State

    Table 10 describes the noisy-forward Ref consolidation variant used as the reference for the Method. Here Ref denotes high-resolution refinement. The shared shift parameter is 5.0; nominal timestep indices are warped by the common scheduler. Teacher and student use matching flow/noise parameterizations. The four-step WM transitions re-noise clean student predictions, whereas one-step Ref has no additional within-chunk query.

    For clean WM commitment, both networks separately process the same completed student chunk at context timestep zero. For Ref, each network retains its own noisy-forward entries; the specialist is also run on unsupervised history blocks. No student KV tensors are copied into a specialist. All preceding states and transitions are detached, so the local velocity loss does not backpropagate through earlier chunks. All six WM content blocks receive supervision at all four queries. For Ref, a two-to-four-block rollout provides noisy-forward history, and only the final block contributes the regression loss.

    A.3 Temporal RoPE Reindexing

    Both WM and Ref use local temporal positions within their respective attention windows. Reindexing addresses positional extrapolation when inference exceeds the finite temporal spans used for training. Let pᵢ and p̃ᵢ be the old and new temporal positions of a retained token, and let R(p) denote the temporal RoPE rotation. If Kᵢ already includes the rotation at pᵢ, its updated key is

    K̃ᵢ=R(p̃ᵢ)R(pᵢ)⁻¹Kᵢ.

    		(11)

    The corresponding value is retained unchanged. This updates positional encoding without recomputing the hidden features of the retained history. Spatial RoPE coordinates are unaffected.

    For Ref with an eight-latent window and four-latent chunks, the most recent history chunk occupies positions 0–3 and the incoming chunk occupies 4–7 once the window is full. On each subsequent shift, the retained keys are reindexed to 0–3 before the new chunk is processed. For WM, a retained image anchor occupies the initial position, and the remaining window contains the most recent content history and current chunk. The anchor keeps its designated position while the moving history is reindexed. The indexing convention is shared between specialist rollouts, student and teacher histories during TA-OPD, and streaming inference. Reindexing aligns the range of temporal positions; it does not make long generated histories identical to training data.

    A.4 Frame Alignment and Startup

    For the causal Wan VAE, F latent frames correspond to 4(F-1)+1 pixel frames. The first latent frame corresponds to the initial observation, while subsequent four-latent content blocks each produce 16 pixel frames. WM starts from a one-latent observation anchor. Refinement processes this anchor before the subsequent content blocks; standalone refinement training uses uniform four-latent blocks. Noisy-forward refinement retains the KV entries from its generation pass, whereas clean-recommit refinement adds an HR history forward.

    A.5 Optimization and Specialist Training

    WM training uses camera-annotated navigation video; refinement additionally uses natural HR video with synthetic spatial degradation.

    The causal specialists are trained with DMD after shared-model preparation. In that stage, the real and learned fake score models provide distribution-matching guidance to a causal generator; the resulting generator becomes a TA-OPD teacher. The reference refinement specialist learns with noisy-forward history and window-local RoPE positions during its DMD rollouts. Its training includes an auxiliary reconstruction objective, whereas the subsequent TA-OPD stage uses only local velocity regression. Specialist preparation and TA-OPD therefore have distinct objectives while preserving the corresponding generation context policies.

    The reference optimizer follows a deterministic WM, WM, Ref update cycle with learning rate 2×10⁻⁶, effective batch size 16, gradient clipping 0.5, and EMA decay 0.99. Consolidation uses local flow MSE without an extra reconstruction or reward term. Both specialists inherit the jointly trained backbone before task-specific DMD training.

    A.6 Function-Preserving Input Expansion

    We establish the functional equivalence of the original WM and its zero-conditioned input expansion with the original parameters fixed. Let x contain all original patch-embedding input channels and let r denote the appended LR condition. For a flattened input patch, the original affine projection is P_W,b(x)=Wx+b; the expanded projection is

    P̃_W,A,b(x,r)=Wx+Ar+b,

    		(12)

    where A contains only the added condition-channel weights. This notation also represents the implemented 3D convolution, whose kernel is linear in the input channels. The expansion copies W and b and initializes A to zero.

    Proposition (zero-condition equivalence).

    Suppose the added condition enters only through Eq. 12, with no joint normalization over the original and added channels before projection. Keep all original weights, conditioning paths, token geometry, and downstream computations unchanged. For identical timesteps, WM conditions, and causal states, setting r=0 makes the expanded model’s prediction equal to that of the original model, for any finite A, in exact arithmetic. With A=0, the same equality holds for any finite r, provided all other inputs and execution settings remain unchanged.

    Proof.

    By linearity,

    P̃_W,A,b(x,0)=Wx+A0+b=P_W,b(x).

    		(13)

    Thus both networks receive identical patch embeddings. Since all remaining operations, parameters, and conditions agree, their predictions and corresponding cache updates agree. Starting from equal causal states, induction over denoising queries and clean-history commitments extends the equality to the WM rollout when the sampler, random draws, and state-management policies are identical. The A=0 case follows from 0r=0. □

    Gradient implication.

    For a WM loss whose dependence on A is only through this projection, zero conditioning gives

    ∇_AL_WM=∑ₚ(∂L_WM)/(∂hₚ)rₚ^⊤=0,

    		(14)

    where p indexes projected patches and hₚ is their embedding. This is a statement about the loss gradient, not the optimizer update: stored momentum or weight decay can still change A.

    Numerical precision.

    The equalities above hold in exact arithmetic. Floating-point implementations may differ across kernels; numerical validation should use matched executions, a declared tolerance, and isolated WM random streams.

    Appendix B Evaluation Details

    B.1 World-Generation Evaluation

    WBench evaluator.

    All WBench results reported in this paper are evaluated with Doubao as the multimodal judge. We use the same evaluator, prompt templates, output parsing, dimension definitions, and aggregation procedure for every method. The reported Average is the arithmetic mean of the five unrounded WBench dimension scores.

    Matched prediction paths.

    The native WM and self-cascade should use identical WM random draws, conditions, and mutable runtime settings. Separate per-role random streams prevent refinement sampling from changing later WM noise. This execution check is distinct from comparing the trained unified model against the WM specialist.

    B.2 Refinement Inputs

    Controlled refinement interface.

    For fixed-input comparisons, the refinement role can receive an encoded external LR video through the same condition channels. When comparing pixel-input refiners, all methods receive the same decoded LR video, which our model re-encodes for conditioning. Native latent handoff is evaluated separately as part of the complete self-cascade.

    Generated and paired inputs.

    For generated LR, we evaluate refinement without assuming a unique HR target. For held-out real-video pairs, PSNR, SSIM, temporal PSNR, and perceptual distances provide reconstruction diagnostics [30, 2]. Bicubic upsampling provides a reference for refinement, alongside content and temporal analysis.

    B.3 Measured Fixed-Input Refinement Protocol

    The two refinement variants in Table 4 use identical training and evaluation settings and differ only in refinement-history construction. Both use EMA weights, with the same initialization, training data, objectives, training-update budget, and history-window capacity. Clean-recommit KV re-encodes completed HR chunks at context timestep zero, whereas noisy-forward KV retains the entries from the conditional noisy generation forward.

    Table 4 uses the same frozen LR videos generated by our world model, with matched case IDs, frame counts, and 24 FPS timestamps. The videos contain 193, 289, 385, 481, or 577 frames; all decoded frames are retained. MUSIQ and CLIP-IQA+ are computed at frames 0,8,16,… using pyiqa 0.1.16 (default MUSIQ weights and the CLIP-IQA+ RN50 learned-prompt model). We average sampled image-quality scores within each video and then weight videos equally.

    LR-consistency PSNR uses OpenCV AREA downsampling of floating-point RGB outputs and the mean squared error over all pixels, channels, and frames of one video, with peak value 1. For MC L1, we estimate forward and backward Farnebäck flow from the corresponding LR view, with maximum side length 640. The backward flow warps the preceding HR grayscale frame to the current frame; forward–backward consistency and image bounds define a shared validity mask for all methods within a protocol. The residual excludes a four-pixel HR border. MC HF L1 uses grayscale minus a Gaussian blur with standard deviation one HR pixel. These are LR-guided motion-compensated diagnostics, not official WBench consistency scores.

    The full-frame Bicubic baseline uses OpenCV INTER_CUBIC. The FlashVSR baseline follows its PIL Bicubic resize-then-crop implementation; resizing and cropping are performed in memory without re-encoding the output videos. Both of our variants and Ultra Flash retain the full frame. External chunk layouts are not used to infer chunk-boundary measurements.

    Interpretation of temporal metrics.

    Motion-aware temporal residuals are interpreted together with motion magnitude and detail, since static or blurred output can exhibit low temporal error. For WBench, official scores retain their original preprocessing; additional common-resolution and native-crop analyses are identified separately.

    B.4 Evaluation Accounting and Computational Costs

    Evaluation units.

    Multiple turns or sampling seeds from one case do not count as independent scenes.

    Cost accounting.

    We separate denoising, cache construction, interface conversion, and VAE decoding. Peak memory includes both role caches and any resident modules or preallocated output buffers. Finite cache windows bound history storage, not necessarily the memory required when retaining a complete output video.

    Appendix C Additional Experimental Analysis

    C.1 Gradient and Output Diagnostics of Mixed DMD

    We examine historical mixed-DMD runs to characterize task interference. At each diagnostic step, WM and Ref generator gradients are computed separately at the same model parameters, without an optimizer update between the two probes. Dot products and squared norms are aggregated across FSDP shards to obtain global and per-block cosine similarities. The native probes use each task’s sampling policy; their batches and random draws need not be identical across training steps.

    Table 6 follows a run initialized from consistency-distillation step 1200, with WM:Ref updates at 3:1, Ref high-noise DMD weight 0.5, and wavelet-reconstruction weight 0.25. The reported cosines compare the two DMD gradients only. Negative alignment persists at the sampled steps 600–800 and extends to all 30 transformer blocks at step 800. In a separate two-block Ref run with reconstruction weight 0.25 and no high-noise reweighting, the step-200 cosine is -0.1734 between WM DMD and Ref reconstruction, and -0.1037 between WM DMD and the total Ref objective. The latter Ref gradient has approximately 3.29 times the WM gradient norm.

    Output diagnostics also show competing quality trends. In a WM:Ref=1:1 run, mean Ref PSNR over 32 validation cases increases from 26.446 to 27.444 dB between steps 0 and 400. Over 32 WM cases with matched sample IDs, frame indices, and noise seeds, the median prediction-to-GT luminance-jump ratio rises from 1.815 to 2.515, and the corresponding color-jump ratio rises from 1.538 to 2.237. These ratios measure adjacent-frame changes in global luminance and color, not comprehensive world consistency. Together, these diagnostics reveal cross-task gradient interference during mixed distillation and competing quality trends between prediction and refinement, supporting separate specialist optimization before capability consolidation.

    C.2 Reference Specialist Configuration

    Specialist teachers for consolidation. Table 11 summarizes the current student trained with prediction and refinement specialists. Task-specific SFT supplies score-model supervision for specialist DMD, whose few-step generators then serve as frozen TA-OPD teachers. Each teacher constructs its own temporal state under the corresponding sampling and history policy. The table reports the resulting student’s native WM and fixed-input refinement scores.

    C.3 Refinement-History Ablation

    Controlled ablation of refinement KV construction. Table 7 compares clean-recommit KV with the noisy-forward KV used in Figures  and 2. Both variants use TA-OPD and keep WM history clean. We reuse the fixed-input quality measurements in Table 4, obtained on identical frozen LR videos. All other training and evaluation settings are held fixed, isolating the effect of refinement-history construction. Clean recommit adds one HR forward per content chunk to construct history; noisy-forward KV retains entries from the denoising forward. We report detail, temporal error, and generator time and FPS to measure the quality–cost trade-off. Generator time includes HR generation and history construction before VAE decoding. Clean-recommit and noisy-forward take 0.60 and 0.30 s per 16-frame content chunk, respectively. Dividing 16 by these times gives 26.7 and 53.3 generator FPS, yielding a 2× generator speedup and a 50% reduction in generator time.

    C.4 Additional System Metrics

    Table 12 summarizes system-level WBench scores, fixed-input refinement quality, and end-to-end generation throughput. Deployment costs are reported in Table 8.

    Appendix D Efficiency and Memory Analysis

    D.1 Model Storage and Deployment Configuration

    Table 8 compares separate specialists with one or two resident copies of the unified model under matched hardware, precision, output size, and batch size. The two-copy control uses identical U weights and inference settings to the shared-copy run, isolating duplicated weight storage from model quality. The parameter count in Table 8 includes all resident DiT copies per rank. Backbone parameters, actual resident weight memory, allocated self-attention KV memory, and full-pipeline peak memory are reported separately. Peak memory also includes the VAE, text encoder, other caches, activations, temporary buffers, and retained outputs; it is not the sum of separately measured peaks.

    Measurement protocol.

    All deployments use four GPUs, BF16, batch size one, four-step 480×832 prediction, and one-step 960×1664 refinement. End-to-end FPS is 16 divided by the median latency of eight 16-frame chunks after six warm-up chunks. The measured latency includes WM prediction, refinement, history construction, and four-GPU halo-8 MG decoding. First-chunk latency uses warm kernels and empty streaming caches. Peak memory is the maximum allocated across GPUs with the backbone, VAE, text encoder, and caches resident.

    D.2 KV Storage across Resolutions

    Prediction and refinement need not retain equally long temporal windows at the same spatial resolution. Let n_L and n_H denote the spatial tokens per latent frame, and let w and s be the allocated WM and Ref window capacities in latent frames, including current-chunk and sink slots. For a dense self-attention cache with L layers, batch size B, KV width d_KV per layer, and b bytes per element, one set of key–value states requires 2LBd_KVb bytes per stored token. The factor two counts keys and values. We assume identical backbones and cache precision, without cache sharding, quantization, or token compression.

    Writing κ=2LBd_KVb, the two-role self-cascade and a direct-HR WM with the same prediction-window capacity have

    M_cascade^KV=κ(n_Lw+n_Hs),(15)
    M_direct^KV=κn_Hw.(16)

    For ρ=n_H/n_L, their ratio is

    (M_cascade^KV)/(M_direct^KV)=1/ρ+s/w.

    		(17)

    Thus the self-cascade uses less KV storage whenever s<(1-1/ρ)w. For fixed s, each additional WM window slot costs only 1/ρ as much KV storage as a direct-HR slot. These are storage identities; they do not assume equal prediction quality at the two resolutions.

    Reference configuration.

    For 480×832 prediction and 960×1664 refinement, Table 9 gives n_L=390, n_H=1560, and ρ=4. With w=25 and s=8, Eq. 17 is 0.57, corresponding to a 43% reduction in self-attention KV payload.

    Measured deployment memory.

    Measured deployment costs follow Table 8: weight and KV allocations are reported per GPU, while peak memory is the maximum allocated memory across the four GPUs. The analytical ratio above describes KV payload, independently of these measured deployment costs.

    The reduction in Eq. 17 comes from retaining the prediction context at low resolution with a shorter HR refinement window, and also applies to a separate-model cascade with the same cache geometry. Sharing weights additionally avoids storing a second backbone. Whether the shorter HR window preserves sufficient detail consistency is evaluated through refinement and temporal results.

    Appendix E Limitations

    Our formulation targets camera-controlled visual prediction, not an explicit physical state simulator. High-resolution refinement may introduce unsupported structures or alter appearance even when it does not feed back into the native prediction recurrence. Although refinement training incorporates synthetic degradations designed to mimic generation artifacts [8, 34], these degradations may not fully capture the errors in world-model predictions. A residual gap between training conditions and generated LR inputs may therefore remain, potentially limiting refinement robustness during self-cascading. Capability retention and temporal robustness must therefore be interpreted within the evaluated controls, domains, and horizons.

一句话：直接生成高分辨率视频，算力与显存都吃不消。

要点：

  • 需求与代价：高分辨率生成让视频世界模型能渲染细粒度的场景结构与纹理，但**直接生成高分辨率视频会带来巨大的计算与显存开销**
  • ScaleWorld 是一个**因果视频模型**，把「低分辨率世界预测」与「高分辨率精修」**统一在同一个共享主干**里
  • 关键点是不再需要单独的精修网络：它**精修自己的预测**，从而在不引入额外模型的条件下产出高分辨率世界视频

为什么值得看：引擎里 LOD 的常识是「同一个模型多尺度出结果」，而世界模型往往被做成「低分模型 + 高分精修模型」两套。把两者合成一个共享主干，省的是模型数量与显存，而不是画质。

中文摘要：高分辨率生成让视频世界模型能够渲染细粒度的场景结构与纹理，但直接生成高分辨率视频会带来可观的计算与显存开销。ScaleWorld 提出一个因果视频模型，把低分辨率的「世界预测」与高分辨率的「精修」统一在同一个共享主干中：低分辨率阶段负责预测世界的演化，高分辨率阶段则精修它自己的预测结果，因此不需要额外训练一个独立的精修网络。对需要在不同分辨率与算力档位下部署同一世界模型的团队，这种「一份主干、多尺度自精修」的做法比维护两套模型更接近引擎里 LOD 的思路。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-20

本期推送：2026-11-22

ScaleWorld: High-Resolution World Generation through Shared Prediction and Refinement

Abstract

High-resolution generation enables video world models to render fine-grained scene structures and textures, but directly generating high-resolution video incurs substantial computational and memory costs. We present ScaleWorld, a causal video model that unifies low-resolution world prediction and high-resolution refinement within a single shared backbone. By refining its own predictions, ScaleWorld produces high-resolution world videos without requiring a separate refinement model. For each video chunk, the shared backbone first completes a low-resolution prediction and then performs one-step high-resolution refinement conditioned on that prediction. To support efficient streaming generation, we maintain separate causal states with a long low-resolution history for prediction and a short high-resolution history for refinement. To address task interference during distillation, we separate specialist optimization from capability consolidation and introduce task-asymmetric on-policy distillation (TA-OPD). This procedure transfers prediction and refinement behaviors from specialized teachers into a shared student through local velocity matching under their respective sampling and history policies. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ScaleWorld achieves high-quality world generation with improved computational and memory efficiency.

11footnotetext: Equal contribution.

1 Introduction

Video world models generate evolving visual environments conditioned on observations and control inputs [20, 3, 18]. High-resolution generation enables these models to depict fine-grained scene structures and textures as the environment evolves. Causal video diffusion supports incremental generation [27, 9], but directly generating high-resolution video incurs substantial computational and memory costs. Increasing spatial resolution raises both denoising computation and temporal-state storage, making high-resolution output costly to sustain in streaming world generation.

Coarse-to-fine pipelines address this cost by predicting at low resolution and refining the result with a dedicated model [8, 32]. This reduces the spatial cost of world prediction, but deploying separate predictors and refiners still requires storing two sets of model weights. Prediction and refinement share visual priors for structure, appearance, and motion, motivating a shared backbone. Cross-resolution reuse has been explored by Self-Cascade, Pyramid Flow, and HiStream [4, 11, 19]. Our focus is the coexistence of independently usable world prediction and conditional streaming refinement within one causal model. We therefore ask: can a world model learn high-resolution refinement while retaining native prediction?

We present ScaleWorld, a shared causal model for streaming world prediction and streaming high-resolution refinement. Both roles follow a chunk-wise autoregressive paradigm: the model first completes a low-resolution (LR) prediction, then uses the same backbone to perform one-step high-resolution (HR) refinement conditioned on that prediction and its own refinement history. No future LR chunks are required, so each completed prediction can be refined without waiting for a full video. The native LR output remains independently usable, and HR outputs do not feed back into prediction history. This design must accommodate the roles’ distinct temporal requirements while consolidating both capabilities in shared parameters.

To support efficient inference, we share model weights while maintaining separate causal states. World prediction retains a longer clean history at low resolution to infer scene evolution. Refinement already receives the current LR structure, content, and motion, and uses a shorter HR history to support the continuity of synthesized detail. It further retains key–value (KV) states from the denoising forward pass as noisy-forward history, avoiding an additional HR model evaluation for history construction. These asymmetric histories limit the cost of refinement while preserving longer temporal context for world prediction.

Sharing visual representations does not ensure that prediction and refinement can be effectively distilled together. In our joint distillation experiments, we observe conflicting gradients between the two tasks, and better reconstruction during refinement can accompany reduced temporal stability in world prediction (Appendix C.1). We therefore separate specialist optimization from capability consolidation. Starting from a jointly trained and causally adapted model, we first optimize prediction and refinement specialists under their respective sampling and history policies. Building on on-policy distillation [14, 31], we introduce task-asymmetric on-policy distillation (TA-OPD) to consolidate the frozen specialists into a shared student. TA-OPD matches expert velocities at student-visited denoising queries for prediction, and at matched conditional noise queries with network-specific recurrent histories for refinement, respecting the roles’ different execution policies.

We evaluate ScaleWorld on camera-controlled world generation, examining native prediction retention, refinement of fixed generated inputs, and complete HR generation. The shared model retains competitive native prediction performance and achieves HR generation quality comparable to a separate specialist cascade. Matched deployments of the same unified checkpoint show that sharing weights reduces peak GPU memory while preserving throughput. Noisy-forward history accelerates refinement over clean recommit by avoiding an extra HR forward pass.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    A shared causal world model for streaming prediction and streaming HR refinement, refining each completed LR prediction with the same backbone while retaining an independently usable native prediction path.

  • •

    A training and inference framework combining TA-OPD and asymmetric causal histories to meet the distinct optimization and temporal requirements of both roles.

  • •

    Empirical evidence of competitive prediction and HR generation quality, with controlled deployment measurements of memory savings from weight sharing and timing comparisons of refinement-history construction.

    • 2 Related Work

    Controllable world generation. Video diffusion models learn rich appearance and motion priors [6, 21]. Genie [1] learns action-controllable environments from unlabeled videos, while GameNGen [22] simulates interactive gameplay through action-conditioned frame prediction. Beyond games, GAIA-1 [7] generates driving scenarios conditioned on video, text, and actions. Cosmos [17] provides pretrained diffusion and autoregressive video world foundation models for physical AI.

    For efficient streaming generation, CausVid [27] and Self Forcing [9] combine few-step generation with autoregressive execution. Causal Forcing [33] uses autoregressive teacher trajectories for initialization before distribution matching distillation. WorldPlay [20], LingBot-World 2.0 [3], and Matrix-Game 3.5 [18] advance long-horizon controlled world generation. SANA-WM [32] combines camera-controlled generation with a separate long-video refiner. Our work focuses on high-resolution generation within a shared world-model backbone, with streaming execution for both prediction and refinement.

    Shared coarse-to-fine generation. Self-Cascade [4] reuses a pretrained low-resolution diffusion model for higher-resolution adaptation. Pyramid Flow [11] jointly learns resolution stages within a unified flow, while PyramidalWan [13] adapts pretrained video models to pyramidal generation. HiStream [19] performs early denoising at low resolution and later denoising at high resolution with dual-resolution caches. It also downsamples the final high-resolution output to refresh the low-resolution history cache. In ScaleWorld, each prediction chunk completes its native output before conditional refinement. The two roles maintain separate causal states, and refined outputs do not feed back into prediction.

    Other forms of parameter reuse include LongCat-Video [16], which trains a refinement expert through LoRA adaptation of its base model, and HiFI [10], which shares one model across frame interpolation and spatial upsampling. Our study examines parameter sharing between world prediction and conditional refinement under distinct sampling budgets and causal-memory policies.

    Generative video refinement. VEnhancer [5] improves generated videos through joint spatial and temporal enhancement. SeedVR [25] studies diffusion-based video restoration, while SeedVR2 [24] enables one-step restoration through adversarial post-training. FlashVSR [35] targets one-step streaming super-resolution. Ultra Flash [8] combines an autoregressive low-resolution generator with a dedicated causal refiner, using latent upsampling, single-step distillation, and preference optimization on generated contexts. Building on advances in streaming refinement, ScaleWorld consolidates refinement and native world prediction within one shared backbone.

    Distillation and capability composition. Distribution matching distillation (DMD) [26] transfers a diffusion model’s generative behavior to a one-step student. Self Forcing [9] addresses the exposure bias of autoregressive video generation through student-rollout training. DiffusionOPD [14] consolidates specialist capabilities on student trajectories, while DanceOPD [31] composes capabilities through routed velocity-field matching. For autoregressive video, OPSD-V [15] supervises student-visited denoising states using a teacher with cleaner, data-assisted temporal context. TA-OPD consolidates prediction and refinement specialists into a shared causal model through local velocity matching under role-specific sampling and history policies.

    3 Method

    Figure 2 summarizes ScaleWorld. We first define the shared streaming interface, then specify the two causal states, explain specialist training and consolidation, and analyze streaming execution and resource costs.

    3.1 Shared Streaming Prediction and Refinement

    We implement world prediction (WM) and high-resolution refinement (Ref) as two chunk-wise causal samplers with a shared velocity network v_θ. Our implementation conditions prediction on an initial observation I, text c, and camera controls a; refinement is learned through video super-resolution. For chunk k, the model first completes a low-resolution (LR) latent ẑₖ^L and then generates its high-resolution (HR) counterpart:

    ẑₖ^L=S_θ^WM(εₖ^L;I,c,a_≤k,Mₖ₋₁^WM),(1)
    ẑₖ^H=S_θ^Ref(εₖ^H;c,U(ẑₖ^L),Mₖ₋₁^Ref).(2)

    Here U spatially upsamples the LR latent, εₖ^L and εₖ^H collect the samplers’ random draws, and Mₖ₋₁^WM and Mₖ₋₁^Ref contain their separate histories before chunk k. Both roles are causal across chunks: refinement uses the completed current LR chunk and preceding context, without accessing future LR chunks. The LR output remains independently usable, and HR outputs never enter prediction history.

    For fixed parameters, supplied camera controls, and independent sampling streams, the sequence distribution factorizes as

    \beginsplitp_θ(z^L,z^H|I,c,a)=&p_θ^WM(z^L|I,c,a) &·p_θ^Ref(z^H|z^L,c).\endsplit

    		(3)

    Internal random variables and recurrent states are marginalized; refinement operates causally across chunks (Eq. 2).

    Shared visual interface. Both roles share a causal video backbone and its output head. The upsampled LR latent is concatenated with the noisy target before patch embedding. WM sets these condition channels to zero and uses image anchoring, text, and camera poses injected through Unified Camera Positional Encoding (UCPE) [29]. Ref supplies the LR latent and text, with no direct camera input or clean HR anchor. The expanded projection retains the original weights and zero-initializes the new condition weights, preserving the WM function at initialization (Appendix A.6).

    Role-specific sampling. For m∈{WM,Ref}, let cₘ collect the corresponding conditions. Under the flow parameterization zₜ=(1-σₜ)z₀+σₜε, the network predicts

    ẑ₀=zₜ-σₜv_θ(zₜ,t;cₘ,Mᵐ).

    		(4)

    WM uses a sequence of denoising queries, re-noising each clean prediction at the next noise level:

    z_k,j+1^θ,WM=(1-σⱼ₊₁)ẑ_k,j^θ,WM+σⱼ₊₁ε_k,j+1.

    		(5)

    Here j indexes queries, and the last clean prediction becomes the completed LR chunk. Ref uses one conditional noise query to produce its HR counterpart. Table 1 summarizes the two roles; their state updates are defined next.

    3.2 Asymmetric Causal Memory

    We design an asymmetric causal memory around the different information available to the two roles. WM predicts unobserved scene evolution from preceding context, whereas Ref receives the current scene structure and motion through its LR condition. We therefore couple a long clean LR history for prediction with a short noisy-forward HR history for refinement. The design is asymmetric in both temporal span and history construction. Window capacities are implementation choices specified in Appendix A.2.

    Clean KV for world prediction. WM re-encodes each completed LR chunk at zero noise to obtain clean KV features K_k,clean^WM for subsequent prediction. With Aₘ denoting the append-and-window operation for role m,

    Mₖ^WM=A_WM(Mₖ₋₁^WM,K_k,clean^WM).

    		(6)

    Clean recommit adds one LR evaluation after denoising.

    Noisy-forward KV reuse for refinement. Applying clean recommit to Ref would require a second HR model evaluation solely to construct history after its one-step generation. To avoid this cost, we reuse the KV features K_k,fwd^Ref computed within the refinement forward that generates the current HR chunk:

    Mₖ^Ref=A_Ref(Mₖ₋₁^Ref,K_k,fwd^Ref).

    		(7)

    These features are computed from the noisy HR input together with the current LR condition and preceding refinement context. They are retained from that forward pass, rather than obtained by re-encoding the completed HR output ẑₖ^H. Subsequent chunks attend to this memory within the short refinement window. Thus, each HR denoising evaluation serves two purposes: generating the current output and providing temporal features for later chunks. The resulting memory construction removes the additional HR clean-recommit evaluation while keeping prediction history and its update rule unchanged.

    Learning with noisy-forward memory. The refinement specialist learns with this recurrent memory. TA-OPD preserves the same KV construction when consolidating refinement into the shared student, and streaming inference follows that rule. This exposes the model during training to the type of history it will reuse at inference. Section 4.3 reports a controlled ablation of refinement-history construction; Appendix C.3 gives the protocol.

    For window advancement, both roles reindex temporal RoPE to local positions and transform cached keys without another model evaluation. Training and inference share this rule; Appendix A.3 details RoPE and retained anchors.

    3.3 Task-Asymmetric On-Policy Distillation

    We introduce task-asymmetric on-policy distillation (TA-OPD) to consolidate separately optimized prediction and refinement behaviors into one shared model. This separation is motivated by the conflicting gradient directions and imbalanced gradient magnitudes observed when jointly optimizing the specialist objectives (Appendix C.1). Building on on-policy distillation [14, 31], TA-OPD matches specialist velocities at the student’s current queries under each task’s sampling and memory policies.

    Specialist preparation. Joint bidirectional training first establishes both task interfaces, followed by causal adaptation and consistency distillation. From this shared foundation, we optimize a prediction specialist φ_WM and a refinement specialist φ_Ref through distribution matching distillation (DMD) [26], using their respective sampling and causal-memory policies. The refinement specialist additionally uses an auxiliary reconstruction objective, whereas the subsequent TA-OPD stage uses only local velocity matching. Both specialists are then frozen, and the shared student θ is initialized from the prediction specialist.

    Task-asymmetric supervision. For WM, the specialist supervises every student-visited denoising query in each content block. After each chunk, teacher and student separately encode the same completed student LR prediction at zero noise to build their own clean KV states. Supervision follows the student’s trajectory and generated history, with each network constructing its own features.

    For Ref, teacher and student process the same conditional HR noise query using their own recurrent histories and retain their own noisy-forward KV. Both networks recursively process preceding chunks to construct their own histories, while only the final block contributes to the velocity-matching loss. LR conditions during consolidation are obtained from degraded real videos, and the single-step HR noise input is sampled independently of the student. Student dependence in refinement therefore enters through its recurrent feature states. WM additionally follows a student-generated denoising trajectory. Within each task, teacher and student match the current noisy latent, timestep, conditions, window capacity, and RoPE rule, while their KV states remain network-specific.

    Local velocity matching. For chunk k and query j, let z_k,j^θ,m be the student’s current noisy latent and tⱼᵐ its timestep. For ψ∈{θ,φₘ}, define

    q_ψ,k,jᵐ=v_ψ(sg[z_k,j^θ,m],tⱼᵐ;c_m,k,sg[M_ψ,k,jᵐ]).

    		(8)

    Here c_m,k collects the chunk’s conditions, M_ψ,k,jᵐ is network ψ’s state before the query, and sg stops gradients through earlier sampling and history construction. Let d_θᵐ denote the joint distribution of queries and network states generated by the above procedure, with τ one realization. The consolidation objective is

    \beginsplitL_con&=∑ₘpₘ 𝔼_τ∼d_θᵐ[Lₘ(τ)], Lₘ(τ)&=(1)/(|Bₘ|)∑_k∈Bₘ∑ⱼ₌₁^Jₘwⱼᵐ ℓ_k,jᵐ, ℓ_k,jᵐ&=MSE(q_θ,k,jᵐ,sg[q_φₘ,k,jᵐ]).\endsplit

    		(9)

    Here Bₘ is the set of supervised blocks, Jₘ is the number of denoising queries (J_Ref=1), and wⱼᵐ=1/Jₘ. MSE is averaged over latent elements to avoid scaling the loss directly with spatial resolution. The coefficient pₘ denotes the frequency of task-m updates, rather than an additional per-update loss multiplier. The sampling schedules and task-update frequencies are specified in Appendix A.

    Although d_θᵐ changes as the student evolves, each update treats the sampled queries and cached histories as fixed. Gradients pass only through the current student velocity prediction, not through the rollout, state construction, or the parameter dependence of d_θᵐ. TA-OPD adds no reconstruction or perceptual-reward terms. Rollout lengths, supervised-block selection, and specialist-training settings are specified in Appendix A.

    3.4 Streaming Inference

    At inference, the shared model alternates between prediction and refinement. Each completed LR chunk updates the clean prediction memory and conditions its HR counterpart; the refinement forward simultaneously produces the HR output and the noisy-forward KV for subsequent chunks. This process uses only the available LR prefix and follows the same causal-memory rules as training. With fixed parameters, independent sampling streams, and unchanged prediction settings, enabling refinement leaves the native LR sample path unchanged.

    Memory and computation. The asymmetric memory allocates long-term context at low resolution while restricting the more expensive HR history to a shorter window. Let n_L,n_H denote spatial tokens per latent frame and w,s the prediction and refinement window capacities, including the current chunk and any retained anchor. For the same backbone, cache precision, and prediction-window capacity w, the self-attention KV-payload ratio relative to direct-HR prediction is

    (M_KVᶜᵃˢᶜᵃᵈᵉ)/(M_KV^direct-HR)=(n_Lw+n_Hs)/(n_Hw)=(n_L)/(n_H)+s/w.

    		(10)

    With s fixed, each additional prediction-window slot costs only n_L/n_H as much KV storage as a direct-HR slot. This ratio covers only KV storage; total GPU memory also includes weights and other allocations (Appendix D.2).

    Parameter sharing removes the duplicate backbone weights required by separate prediction and refinement specialists, while both causal memories are retained. Noisy-forward KV reuse additionally saves computation by removing the extra HR clean-recommit forward pass.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    We build ScaleWorld on Wan2.2 TI2V-5B, with world prediction at 480×832 and streaming refinement at 960×1664.

    We evaluate native world prediction and final high-resolution generation on WBench [28], reporting overall and per-dimension scores. All methods receive the same observations, camera commands, and temporal intervals, while retaining their supported inference settings. Native prediction baselines include HY-World 1.5 [20], LingBot-World 2.0 (fast) [3], and Matrix-Game 3.5 [18]. For high-resolution generation, we compare against WorldPlay [20], LingBot-World 2.0 [3], and Matrix-Game 3.5 [18] paired with Ultra Flash [8] or FlashVSR [35].

    We evaluate refinement separately using the same fixed set of decoded LR videos generated by our world model. We report MUSIQ [12] and CLIP-IQA+ [23] for perceptual quality, LR-consistency PSNR for preservation of the input content, and motion-compensated residuals (MC L1 and MC HF L1) for temporal variation. Appendices A and B detail training, evaluation protocols, and metrics.

    4.2 Generation Quality and Capability Retention

    Shared versus separate generation. Table 2(a) compares the unified model with a cascade of separately optimized specialists. The noisy-forward shared model achieves comparable overall HR quality, with stronger setting and interaction adherence and slightly lower visual quality. These results suggest that prediction and refinement can coexist in one backbone; the matched deployment comparison below isolates the resource savings from sharing its weights.

    Capability retention. The unified model remains close to its WM specialist on native WBench performance and achieves the highest visual-quality score among the evaluated native models (Table 2(b)). The modest decrease in consistency shows that retention is not uniform across dimensions. For refinement, the shared noisy-forward model remains close to its independent specialist on MUSIQ under the same decoded-LR protocol (Table 12). Figure 3 compares native camera-controlled outputs across models.

    Complete HR systems. Our unified prediction–refinement pipeline achieves the highest overall WBench score (81.60) among all evaluated systems, including native world models and cascaded high-resolution baselines (Tables 2 and 3). These scores reflect both prediction and refinement. We therefore compare refiners on fixed LR inputs below to control for upstream differences.

    Refinement of fixed predictions. On the same generated LR inputs, our refiner improves perceptual quality, LR consistency, and motion-compensated residuals over Ultra Flash under the full-frame protocol (Table 4). FlashVSR’s elevated MC L1 and MC HF L1 residuals suggest temporal fluctuations consistent with inter-frame flicker, although its center-crop protocol limits direct numerical comparison. Our outputs exhibit smoother frame-to-frame transitions and greater temporal continuity. Figure 4 shows qualitative comparisons.

    Figure 5 illustrates our unified prediction–refinement pipeline on camera-controlled rollouts. The HR outputs preserve the scene layout of the LR predictions while producing sharper structural boundaries and richer local textures, as highlighted by the matched crops.

    4.3 Training and Efficiency Analysis

    Distillation strategies. We compare mixed DMD, CD + mixed DMD, and TA-OPD from identical initialization (Table 5). TA-OPD achieves the highest overall native prediction score and setting adherence. In contrast, mixed DMD and CD + mixed DMD suffer from cross-task gradient interference during joint distillation (Table 6), limiting their overall performance.

    Task interference in mixed distillation. WM and Ref gradients shift from weak global alignment to opposing directions across the backbone during mixed distillation (Table 6). These measurements show conflicting update directions in the sampled training states and motivate separate specialist optimization before consolidation. Appendix C.1 details the diagnostic protocol and output analysis.

    Noisy-forward refinement history. Table 7 compares clean-recommit and noisy-forward histories with all other training and evaluation settings fixed. Reusing KV from the generation forward eliminates the additional HR pass used for clean recommit, yielding a 2× generator speedup before VAE decoding. End-to-end throughput improves by 26.9%, including WM prediction, refinement, history construction, and decoding (Table 12). Noisy-forward history also improves MUSIQ and LR consistency on fixed inputs, with a small increase in MC L1. It thus reduces computation while improving perceptual quality, with a measured trade-off in temporal residuals. Appendix C.3 gives the full settings.

    Shared-backbone deployment. Table 8 compares one- and two-copy deployments of the same unified checkpoint under matched inference settings (Appendix D). Weight sharing halves resident backbone storage and reduces peak GPU memory by 21.1% while preserving end-to-end throughput. KV allocation remains unchanged because both role-specific causal states are retained; the memory savings therefore come from removing duplicate weights.

    Parameter sharing and asymmetric memory address different costs: the former reduces resident weights, while the latter stores the longer prediction history at low resolution. The direct-HR comparison in Eq. 10 concerns KV payload and is distinct from the measured deployment savings.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented ScaleWorld, a shared causal model for camera-controlled prediction and high-resolution refinement. Its asymmetric temporal contexts allocate long history to low-resolution prediction, while specialist training and TA-OPD integrate the two capabilities. Experiments show comparable overall generation quality to a separate specialist cascade, retained native prediction capability, and lower resident deployment memory. The resulting model produces high-resolution worlds incrementally with one backbone. Limitations are discussed in Appendix E.

    （参考文献见原文。）


    Supplementary Material

    Appendix A Implementation Details

    A.1 Shared Visual Interface

    The reference backbone is Wan2.2 TI2V-5B. Its VAE uses 48 latent channels with spatial stride 16, and the transformer uses 2×2 spatial patches. For Ref, a 48-channel interpolated LR latent is concatenated with the noisy target before patch embedding. The added projection weights are initialized to zero when expanding a pretrained input layer. WM uses zero-valued LR channels and its image/camera conditioning; Ref uses a zero image-anchor mask and no camera condition. The shared transformer and output head serve both roles.

    Pixel-space degradation uses blur, bicubic downsampling, and noise while retaining consecutive frames. Latent conditioning uses nearest-neighbor spatial interpolation in the reference recipe. These operations are distinct: bicubic describes the LR video construction, not the latent upsampler. Additional latent-condition noise/dropout and a learned latent upsampler are disabled during reference consolidation. No refinement-specific spatial Swin partition is enabled.

    A.2 Sampling and Temporal State

    Table 10 describes the noisy-forward Ref consolidation variant used as the reference for the Method. Here Ref denotes high-resolution refinement. The shared shift parameter is 5.0; nominal timestep indices are warped by the common scheduler. Teacher and student use matching flow/noise parameterizations. The four-step WM transitions re-noise clean student predictions, whereas one-step Ref has no additional within-chunk query.

    For clean WM commitment, both networks separately process the same completed student chunk at context timestep zero. For Ref, each network retains its own noisy-forward entries; the specialist is also run on unsupervised history blocks. No student KV tensors are copied into a specialist. All preceding states and transitions are detached, so the local velocity loss does not backpropagate through earlier chunks. All six WM content blocks receive supervision at all four queries. For Ref, a two-to-four-block rollout provides noisy-forward history, and only the final block contributes the regression loss.

    A.3 Temporal RoPE Reindexing

    Both WM and Ref use local temporal positions within their respective attention windows. Reindexing addresses positional extrapolation when inference exceeds the finite temporal spans used for training. Let pᵢ and p̃ᵢ be the old and new temporal positions of a retained token, and let R(p) denote the temporal RoPE rotation. If Kᵢ already includes the rotation at pᵢ, its updated key is

    K̃ᵢ=R(p̃ᵢ)R(pᵢ)⁻¹Kᵢ.

    		(11)

    The corresponding value is retained unchanged. This updates positional encoding without recomputing the hidden features of the retained history. Spatial RoPE coordinates are unaffected.

    For Ref with an eight-latent window and four-latent chunks, the most recent history chunk occupies positions 0–3 and the incoming chunk occupies 4–7 once the window is full. On each subsequent shift, the retained keys are reindexed to 0–3 before the new chunk is processed. For WM, a retained image anchor occupies the initial position, and the remaining window contains the most recent content history and current chunk. The anchor keeps its designated position while the moving history is reindexed. The indexing convention is shared between specialist rollouts, student and teacher histories during TA-OPD, and streaming inference. Reindexing aligns the range of temporal positions; it does not make long generated histories identical to training data.

    A.4 Frame Alignment and Startup

    For the causal Wan VAE, F latent frames correspond to 4(F-1)+1 pixel frames. The first latent frame corresponds to the initial observation, while subsequent four-latent content blocks each produce 16 pixel frames. WM starts from a one-latent observation anchor. Refinement processes this anchor before the subsequent content blocks; standalone refinement training uses uniform four-latent blocks. Noisy-forward refinement retains the KV entries from its generation pass, whereas clean-recommit refinement adds an HR history forward.

    A.5 Optimization and Specialist Training

    WM training uses camera-annotated navigation video; refinement additionally uses natural HR video with synthetic spatial degradation.

    The causal specialists are trained with DMD after shared-model preparation. In that stage, the real and learned fake score models provide distribution-matching guidance to a causal generator; the resulting generator becomes a TA-OPD teacher. The reference refinement specialist learns with noisy-forward history and window-local RoPE positions during its DMD rollouts. Its training includes an auxiliary reconstruction objective, whereas the subsequent TA-OPD stage uses only local velocity regression.
