Specialist preparation and TA-OPD therefore have distinct objectives while preserving the corresponding generation context policies.

    The reference optimizer follows a deterministic WM, WM, Ref update cycle with learning rate 2×10⁻⁶, effective batch size 16, gradient clipping 0.5, and EMA decay 0.99. Consolidation uses local flow MSE without an extra reconstruction or reward term. Both specialists inherit the jointly trained backbone before task-specific DMD training.

    A.6 Function-Preserving Input Expansion

    We establish the functional equivalence of the original WM and its zero-conditioned input expansion with the original parameters fixed. Let x contain all original patch-embedding input channels and let r denote the appended LR condition. For a flattened input patch, the original affine projection is P_W,b(x)=Wx+b; the expanded projection is

    P̃_W,A,b(x,r)=Wx+Ar+b,

    		(12)

    where A contains only the added condition-channel weights. This notation also represents the implemented 3D convolution, whose kernel is linear in the input channels. The expansion copies W and b and initializes A to zero.

    Proposition (zero-condition equivalence).

    Suppose the added condition enters only through Eq. 12, with no joint normalization over the original and added channels before projection. Keep all original weights, conditioning paths, token geometry, and downstream computations unchanged. For identical timesteps, WM conditions, and causal states, setting r=0 makes the expanded model’s prediction equal to that of the original model, for any finite A, in exact arithmetic. With A=0, the same equality holds for any finite r, provided all other inputs and execution settings remain unchanged.

    Proof.

    By linearity,

    P̃_W,A,b(x,0)=Wx+A0+b=P_W,b(x).

    		(13)

    Thus both networks receive identical patch embeddings. Since all remaining operations, parameters, and conditions agree, their predictions and corresponding cache updates agree. Starting from equal causal states, induction over denoising queries and clean-history commitments extends the equality to the WM rollout when the sampler, random draws, and state-management policies are identical. The A=0 case follows from 0r=0. □

    Gradient implication.

    For a WM loss whose dependence on A is only through this projection, zero conditioning gives

    ∇_AL_WM=∑ₚ(∂L_WM)/(∂hₚ)rₚ^⊤=0,

    		(14)

    where p indexes projected patches and hₚ is their embedding. This is a statement about the loss gradient, not the optimizer update: stored momentum or weight decay can still change A.

    Numerical precision.

    The equalities above hold in exact arithmetic. Floating-point implementations may differ across kernels; numerical validation should use matched executions, a declared tolerance, and isolated WM random streams.

    Appendix B Evaluation Details

    B.1 World-Generation Evaluation

    WBench evaluator.

    All WBench results reported in this paper are evaluated with Doubao as the multimodal judge. We use the same evaluator, prompt templates, output parsing, dimension definitions, and aggregation procedure for every method. The reported Average is the arithmetic mean of the five unrounded WBench dimension scores.

    Matched prediction paths.

    The native WM and self-cascade should use identical WM random draws, conditions, and mutable runtime settings. Separate per-role random streams prevent refinement sampling from changing later WM noise. This execution check is distinct from comparing the trained unified model against the WM specialist.

    B.2 Refinement Inputs

    Controlled refinement interface.

    For fixed-input comparisons, the refinement role can receive an encoded external LR video through the same condition channels. When comparing pixel-input refiners, all methods receive the same decoded LR video, which our model re-encodes for conditioning. Native latent handoff is evaluated separately as part of the complete self-cascade.

    Generated and paired inputs.

    For generated LR, we evaluate refinement without assuming a unique HR target. For held-out real-video pairs, PSNR, SSIM, temporal PSNR, and perceptual distances provide reconstruction diagnostics [30, 2]. Bicubic upsampling provides a reference for refinement, alongside content and temporal analysis.

    B.3 Measured Fixed-Input Refinement Protocol

    The two refinement variants in Table 4 use identical training and evaluation settings and differ only in refinement-history construction. Both use EMA weights, with the same initialization, training data, objectives, training-update budget, and history-window capacity. Clean-recommit KV re-encodes completed HR chunks at context timestep zero, whereas noisy-forward KV retains the entries from the conditional noisy generation forward.

    Table 4 uses the same frozen LR videos generated by our world model, with matched case IDs, frame counts, and 24 FPS timestamps. The videos contain 193, 289, 385, 481, or 577 frames; all decoded frames are retained. MUSIQ and CLIP-IQA+ are computed at frames 0,8,16,… using pyiqa 0.1.16 (default MUSIQ weights and the CLIP-IQA+ RN50 learned-prompt model). We average sampled image-quality scores within each video and then weight videos equally.

    LR-consistency PSNR uses OpenCV AREA downsampling of floating-point RGB outputs and the mean squared error over all pixels, channels, and frames of one video, with peak value 1. For MC L1, we estimate forward and backward Farnebäck flow from the corresponding LR view, with maximum side length 640. The backward flow warps the preceding HR grayscale frame to the current frame; forward–backward consistency and image bounds define a shared validity mask for all methods within a protocol. The residual excludes a four-pixel HR border. MC HF L1 uses grayscale minus a Gaussian blur with standard deviation one HR pixel. These are LR-guided motion-compensated diagnostics, not official WBench consistency scores.

    The full-frame Bicubic baseline uses OpenCV INTER_CUBIC. The FlashVSR baseline follows its PIL Bicubic resize-then-crop implementation; resizing and cropping are performed in memory without re-encoding the output videos. Both of our variants and Ultra Flash retain the full frame. External chunk layouts are not used to infer chunk-boundary measurements.

    Interpretation of temporal metrics.

    Motion-aware temporal residuals are interpreted together with motion magnitude and detail, since static or blurred output can exhibit low temporal error. For WBench, official scores retain their original preprocessing; additional common-resolution and native-crop analyses are identified separately.

    B.4 Evaluation Accounting and Computational Costs

    Evaluation units.

    Multiple turns or sampling seeds from one case do not count as independent scenes.

    Cost accounting.

    We separate denoising, cache construction, interface conversion, and VAE decoding. Peak memory includes both role caches and any resident modules or preallocated output buffers. Finite cache windows bound history storage, not necessarily the memory required when retaining a complete output video.

    Appendix C Additional Experimental Analysis

    C.1 Gradient and Output Diagnostics of Mixed DMD

    We examine historical mixed-DMD runs to characterize task interference. At each diagnostic step, WM and Ref generator gradients are computed separately at the same model parameters, without an optimizer update between the two probes. Dot products and squared norms are aggregated across FSDP shards to obtain global and per-block cosine similarities. The native probes use each task’s sampling policy; their batches and random draws need not be identical across training steps.

    Table 6 follows a run initialized from consistency-distillation step 1200, with WM:Ref updates at 3:1, Ref high-noise DMD weight 0.5, and wavelet-reconstruction weight 0.25. The reported cosines compare the two DMD gradients only. Negative alignment persists at the sampled steps 600–800 and extends to all 30 transformer blocks at step 800. In a separate two-block Ref run with reconstruction weight 0.25 and no high-noise reweighting, the step-200 cosine is -0.1734 between WM DMD and Ref reconstruction, and -0.1037 between WM DMD and the total Ref objective. The latter Ref gradient has approximately 3.29 times the WM gradient norm.

    Output diagnostics also show competing quality trends. In a WM:Ref=1:1 run, mean Ref PSNR over 32 validation cases increases from 26.446 to 27.444 dB between steps 0 and 400. Over 32 WM cases with matched sample IDs, frame indices, and noise seeds, the median prediction-to-GT luminance-jump ratio rises from 1.815 to 2.515, and the corresponding color-jump ratio rises from 1.538 to 2.237. These ratios measure adjacent-frame changes in global luminance and color, not comprehensive world consistency. Together, these diagnostics reveal cross-task gradient interference during mixed distillation and competing quality trends between prediction and refinement, supporting separate specialist optimization before capability consolidation.

    C.2 Reference Specialist Configuration

    Specialist teachers for consolidation. Table 11 summarizes the current student trained with prediction and refinement specialists. Task-specific SFT supplies score-model supervision for specialist DMD, whose few-step generators then serve as frozen TA-OPD teachers. Each teacher constructs its own temporal state under the corresponding sampling and history policy. The table reports the resulting student’s native WM and fixed-input refinement scores.

    C.3 Refinement-History Ablation

    Controlled ablation of refinement KV construction. Table 7 compares clean-recommit KV with the noisy-forward KV used in Figures  and 2. Both variants use TA-OPD and keep WM history clean. We reuse the fixed-input quality measurements in Table 4, obtained on identical frozen LR videos. All other training and evaluation settings are held fixed, isolating the effect of refinement-history construction. Clean recommit adds one HR forward per content chunk to construct history; noisy-forward KV retains entries from the denoising forward. We report detail, temporal error, and generator time and FPS to measure the quality–cost trade-off. Generator time includes HR generation and history construction before VAE decoding. Clean-recommit and noisy-forward take 0.60 and 0.30 s per 16-frame content chunk, respectively. Dividing 16 by these times gives 26.7 and 53.3 generator FPS, yielding a 2× generator speedup and a 50% reduction in generator time.

    C.4 Additional System Metrics

    Table 12 summarizes system-level WBench scores, fixed-input refinement quality, and end-to-end generation throughput. Deployment costs are reported in Table 8.

    Appendix D Efficiency and Memory Analysis

    D.1 Model Storage and Deployment Configuration

    Table 8 compares separate specialists with one or two resident copies of the unified model under matched hardware, precision, output size, and batch size. The two-copy control uses identical U weights and inference settings to the shared-copy run, isolating duplicated weight storage from model quality. The parameter count in Table 8 includes all resident DiT copies per rank. Backbone parameters, actual resident weight memory, allocated self-attention KV memory, and full-pipeline peak memory are reported separately. Peak memory also includes the VAE, text encoder, other caches, activations, temporary buffers, and retained outputs; it is not the sum of separately measured peaks.

    Measurement protocol.

    All deployments use four GPUs, BF16, batch size one, four-step 480×832 prediction, and one-step 960×1664 refinement. End-to-end FPS is 16 divided by the median latency of eight 16-frame chunks after six warm-up chunks. The measured latency includes WM prediction, refinement, history construction, and four-GPU halo-8 MG decoding. First-chunk latency uses warm kernels and empty streaming caches. Peak memory is the maximum allocated across GPUs with the backbone, VAE, text encoder, and caches resident.

    D.2 KV Storage across Resolutions

    Prediction and refinement need not retain equally long temporal windows at the same spatial resolution. Let n_L and n_H denote the spatial tokens per latent frame, and let w and s be the allocated WM and Ref window capacities in latent frames, including current-chunk and sink slots. For a dense self-attention cache with L layers, batch size B, KV width d_KV per layer, and b bytes per element, one set of key–value states requires 2LBd_KVb bytes per stored token. The factor two counts keys and values. We assume identical backbones and cache precision, without cache sharding, quantization, or token compression.

    Writing κ=2LBd_KVb, the two-role self-cascade and a direct-HR WM with the same prediction-window capacity have

    M_cascade^KV=κ(n_Lw+n_Hs),(15)
    M_direct^KV=κn_Hw.(16)

    For ρ=n_H/n_L, their ratio is

    (M_cascade^KV)/(M_direct^KV)=1/ρ+s/w.

    		(17)

    Thus the self-cascade uses less KV storage whenever s<(1-1/ρ)w. For fixed s, each additional WM window slot costs only 1/ρ as much KV storage as a direct-HR slot. These are storage identities; they do not assume equal prediction quality at the two resolutions.

    Reference configuration.

    For 480×832 prediction and 960×1664 refinement, Table 9 gives n_L=390, n_H=1560, and ρ=4. With w=25 and s=8, Eq. 17 is 0.57, corresponding to a 43% reduction in self-attention KV payload.

    Measured deployment memory.

    Measured deployment costs follow Table 8: weight and KV allocations are reported per GPU, while peak memory is the maximum allocated memory across the four GPUs. The analytical ratio above describes KV payload, independently of these measured deployment costs.

    The reduction in Eq. 17 comes from retaining the prediction context at low resolution with a shorter HR refinement window, and also applies to a separate-model cascade with the same cache geometry. Sharing weights additionally avoids storing a second backbone. Whether the shorter HR window preserves sufficient detail consistency is evaluated through refinement and temporal results.

    Appendix E Limitations

    Our formulation targets camera-controlled visual prediction, not an explicit physical state simulator. High-resolution refinement may introduce unsupported structures or alter appearance even when it does not feed back into the native prediction recurrence. Although refinement training incorporates synthetic degradations designed to mimic generation artifacts [8, 34], these degradations may not fully capture the errors in world-model predictions. A residual gap between training conditions and generated LR inputs may therefore remain, potentially limiting refinement robustness during self-cascading. Capability retention and temporal robustness must therefore be interpreted within the evaluated controls, domains, and horizons.

item.title: 大模型画得好、小模型跑得快：SpecWM 把「验证」变成「精修」，不再靠外部打分器判断 ｜ SpecWM: Turning Verification into Refinement for Streaming World Models
item.description:
一句话：现有推测式方法的验证只覆盖外部打分器的维度，而且只打分、不纠错。

要点：

  • 组合思路：视频世界模型里，**大模型质量高、小模型推理快**；推测式方法用「快速草稿 + 选择性重生成」来兼得
  • 两个缺陷：验证环节只覆盖**外部打分器**的评估维度，而且额外引入解码与打分成本；更关键的是，**这些分数不提供任何修正**，只能决定要不要丢弃重来
  • SpecWM 因此把「验证」直接改造成「精修」——让验证过程本身产出改进，而不是产出一个阈值

为什么值得看：「草稿—验证」是实时生成最常用的加速范式，但只打分不纠错等于扔掉了一半信息。把验证变成精修，意味着同一份计算既做判断又做改进——这对延迟预算紧的流式系统是直接收益。

中文摘要：视频世界模型近来在交互式生成上进展明显：大模型给出更高质量，小模型提供更快推理。已有的推测式（speculative）方法试图兼得两者优势——先快速生成草稿，再依据对已解码帧的奖励做选择性重生成。但作者指出两个缺陷：验证只覆盖外部打分器的评估维度，还会额外增加解码与打分开销；更重要的是，这些分数不提供任何修正，只能用来决定是否重做。SpecWM 因此把验证改造成精修：让「检查」这一步本身产出对结果的改进，而不只是产出一个通过/不通过的判断。对受延迟约束的流式世界模型，这相当于让同一笔计算同时承担判断与改进两个职责。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-20

本期推送：2026-11-22

SpecWM: Turning Verification into Refinement for Streaming World Models

Abstract

Recently, video world models have advanced interactive generation, with large models offering higher quality and smaller models enabling faster inference. Existing speculative methods combine their strengths through fast draft generation and selective target regeneration guided by rewards on decoded frames. However, verification covers only the external scorer’s evaluation dimensions and adds decoding and scoring costs. Moreover, these scores provide no correction, requiring costly target regeneration for rejected drafts. To address these limitations, we propose Speculative World Model (SpecWM), a unified, training-free inference framework for streaming world models. It verifies draft chunks using the target’s latent velocity field. Verification also yields a reusable correction; two thresholds select Accept, Refine, or Reject. Specifically, one-step refinement reuses it to improve perceptual quality, while three-step refinement strengthens camera following and trajectory consistency. These findings motivate transition-aware refinement. On WBench Navigation, SpecWM improves visual quality at 1.63× speedup over the target and raises NavScore from the draft’s 75.99 to 85.63, achieving the best quality-speed-control trade-off. Additionally, our LongSpecBench shows sustained quality and control over long, multi-turn rollouts, while experiments on Hy-Nomas validate SpecWM across backbones and denoising budgets.

1 Introduction

Streaming world models enable users to explore generated environments that evolve in response to their actions [11, 17]. Such interaction requires high visual quality, accurate control following, and rapid responses to changing inputs. However, larger models offer stronger quality and control at substantial computational cost, whereas smaller models generate faster at the expense of visual quality and accuracy in following the controls (Fig. 1, right).

Existing reward-based speculative methods combine these strengths through fast draft generation and selective target regeneration. Rewards computed on decoded draft frames determine which chunks to accept and which to regenerate with the target. Setting up this verifier requires choosing a reward model, aggregating frame scores, and calibrating an acceptance threshold [16]. However, verification is limited to the attributes captured by the external scorer [44]. Decoding and scoring also add runtime costs per chunk. Moreover, these scores provide no direct refinement signal to improve the draft itself (Fig. 1, left). Consequently, every rejected draft requires computationally expensive regeneration by the target through its full sampling process, reducing the savings from fast draft generation. How can verification itself provide a reusable correction to improve the trade-off among speed, visual quality, and control in speculative generation for streaming world models?

We propose Speculative World Model (SpecWM), a unified, training-free inference framework that turns verification into refinement for streaming autoregressive (AR) world models. SpecWM replaces decoded-frame reward scoring with a single final-stage evaluation of the target’s latent velocity field v. This evaluation yields a clean prediction under the same history and controls. Its difference from the draft provides a verification score. Moreover, the same prediction supplies a reusable correction. Based on this score, SpecWM uses two thresholds to select Accept, Refine, or Reject to allocate target computation across chunks.

One-step refinement directly reuses the prediction from verification, without further target denoising. Three-step refinement starts at a higher noise level and runs three consecutive target denoising steps. With verification fixed, our uniform-refinement experiments reveal complementary effects (Table 1). One-step refinement improves imaging quality and perceptual preference over the draft, with limited improvement in navigation control. Three-step refinement strengthens camera following and trajectory consistency, but lowers perceptual preference and aesthetics relative to one step; imaging quality remains similar. Image diffusion studies link early denoising to coarse structure and later steps to fine detail [48]. Our results suggest a similar distinction: final-stage correction improves appearance, while earlier intervention allows greater trajectory revision.

These findings motivate transition-aware refinement. For chunks routed to Refine, SpecWM uses three steps at a control change, two in the next chunk, and one thereafter. This schedule improves control near transitions while favoring perceptual quality and speed during continued motion. Throughout this schedule, verification remains fixed at one final-stage probe per draft chunk. Additionally, the draft generates the next chunk while the target verifies the current one, thereby reducing latency.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    SpecWM. We propose a unified, training-free framework that turns verification into refinement. With transition-aware refinement, SpecWM achieves a 1.63× generation-loop speedup over Target-only on WBench Navigation [51], improving imaging quality and perceptual preference while maintaining target-level navigation control.

  • •

    LongSpecBench. We construct a benchmark of long, multi-turn rollouts with revisits to jointly evaluate generation quality, speed, and sustained controllability. SpecWM leads the evaluated methods in world-model quality (WMQ) and quality-efficiency score (QES).

  • •

    Beyond model scale. SpecWM extends from model-scale to denoising-budget differences on Hy-Nomas [7], where draft and target share the same weights. It outperforms Draft-only and SDVG-style across four human-evaluated dimensions, achieving near-target preference at a 1.33× generation-loop speedup over Target-only.

    • 2 Related Work

    Autoregressive video generation and world models. Diffusion models [14], latent representations [37], and transformers [36] underpin video synthesis [15, 1, 6, 47, 12]. Building on this foundation, camera and motion conditioning enable controllable generation [13, 43], while flexible temporal conditioning incorporates generation history [4, 41]. For streaming generation, causal distillation reduces latency [50, 52], and training on self-generated histories addresses the training-inference mismatch [18]. Longer rollouts further require managing accumulated errors through long-video tuning, cache refreshes, and rolling denoising [46, 26]. These developments support interactive world models that respond to user actions [2, 11, 17, 7]. Evaluation likewise extends from video quality in VBench [19] to multi-turn interaction in WBench [51]. SpecWM addresses computation allocation during streaming inference to balance visual quality, speed, and control.

    Caching and efficient inference. Efficient samplers [40, 28], distillation [38, 49], and consistency models [42] reduce denoising steps. Beyond reducing steps, caching exploits redundancy in features, attention, and guidance [30, 29]. Adaptive reuse responds to estimated output changes or chunk-level variation [25, 31]. For world models, selective token recomputation [10] and history-guided caching with residual correction [35] address reuse across evolving content. System optimizations combine caching with sparse attention, quantization, and kernel fusion [21]. These approaches lower the cost of running a generator by reusing internal computations or reducing sampling steps. SpecWM instead allocates computation according to the draft chunk’s discrepancy from the target. Accept, Refine, and Reject provide different levels of target intervention. This allocation applies to pairings with different model scales or denoising budgets, including shared-weight configurations.

    Speculative verification and refinement. Speculative decoding combines draft proposals with target verification [20, 5]; feature prediction and multiple decoding heads improve proposal generation [22, 3]. DSpark uses confidence and serving load to schedule token verification [8]. In video generation, SDVG uses ImageReward [44] on decoded draft frames to select acceptance or target regeneration [16]. However, this verifier incurs decoding and scoring costs, and its coverage depends on the external scorer. Moreover, the scores guide selection without supplying a direct correction. Separately, other methods allocate computation within one generator: Speculative Forcing freezes converged tokens [9], while Surprise Forcing skips steps according to chunk difficulty [39]. SpecWM instead verifies draft chunks using the target’s latent velocity prediction. The resulting clean estimate can correct the draft, adding refinement between acceptance and full regeneration.

    3 Preliminaries

    Controlled autoregressive generation. Let zᵢ denote chunk i’s clean latent, Hᵢ=(z₀,…,zᵢ₋₁) the committed history, aᵢ the camera controls, and c the initial-image and text conditions. For N chunks, the generator samples

    zᵢ∼G(·|Hᵢ,aᵢ,c), i=0,…,N-1.

    		(1)

    The selected output is appended to the history. For speculative generation, we pair frozen generators G_D and G_T with different model scales or denoising budgets. They share a latent representation, chunk length, and control interface, and condition on the same history and inputs.

    Velocity-based denoising. Following flow matching and rectified flow [24, 27], we use a linear interpolation between a clean latent z and noise ε. At noise level σ, the noisy latent is x_σ=(1-σ)z+σε. The model predicts a latent velocity field v, from which we obtain the clean estimate

    z̃=x_σ-σv(x_σ,σ;Hᵢ,aᵢ,c).

    		(2)

    For the LingBot implementation [11], we use four native denoising stages k∈{0,1,2,3}, with decreasing noise levels 1≥σ₀>σ₁>σ₂>σ₃>0. At intermediate stages k<3, the clean estimate is re-noised to σₖ₊₁ for the next update. At the final stage, it is returned.

    4 SpecWM

    SpecWM turns target verification into reusable refinement (Fig. 2, main panel). A final-stage velocity prediction yields a clean candidate, whose discrepancy from the draft provides a verification score. Two thresholds then select Accept, Refine, or Reject to allocate target computation. For chunks routed to Refine, control transitions determine the correction entry point. With separate models, draft generation overlaps target verification to reduce latency. Both roles then use the selected output as shared context.

    4.1 Verification and Reusable Refinement

    We describe SpecWM using LingBot’s four-stage sampler. Draft predictions are aligned with target noise levels. For shared-weight pairing, we instead subdivide the draft’s final update along the target grid (Sec. 5.5).

    Draft proposal and alignment. The draft generates ẑᵢ=G_D(Hᵢ,aᵢ,c;ξᵢ^D), where ξᵢ^D denotes its sampling randomness, and retains the clean prediction from each denoising stage. Draft and target can have different noise schedules. We therefore interpolate the draft’s clean predictions by noise level to obtain z̄^D_i,k at target level σₖᵀ. To form target inputs, we re-noise these estimates using Ξᵢᵀ=(ηᵢᵀ,εᵀ_i,0:2), which contains the target’s initial noise and three re-noising draws. The resulting aligned states are given by

    x^D_i,0=ηᵢᵀ, x^D_i,4=ẑᵢ,
    x^D_i,k=(1-σₖᵀ)z̄^D_i,k+σₖᵀεᵀ_i,k-1, k=1,2,3.(3)

    These states provide the input for verification and the starting points for longer corrections. Interpolation and random-state details are given in the supplementary material.

    One probe, two outputs. Using the aligned final-stage state, we evaluate the target at k=3 to obtain

    uᵀ_i,4=x^D_i,3-σ₃ᵀv_T(x^D_i,3,σ₃ᵀ;Hᵢ,aᵢ,c).

    		(4)

    We then compare this clean prediction with the draft output:

    eᵢ=(∥ẑᵢ-uᵀ_i,4∥₁)/(∥uᵀ_i,4∥₁+ε), ε=10⁻⁶.

    		(5)

    The norms cover valid latent elements. The score eᵢ guides routing, while the prediction uᵀ_i,4 can be committed as a one-step correction without further target denoising. Thus, verification directly provides a refinement candidate. Keeping this probe fixed gives all refinement lengths the same scoring rule. Its low cost and observed score variation across chunks motivate the final-stage choice (Sec. 5.3).

    4.2 Threshold-Based Computation Allocation

    Given the discrepancy score eᵢ, two thresholds τ<τᵣ determine how the target intervenes. Let rᵢ^(ℓᵢ) denote a corrected chunk obtained with ℓᵢ target denoising steps, as defined in Sec. 4.3. The selected output is

    zᵢ=\begincasesẑᵢ,&eᵢ<τ (Accept), rᵢ^(ℓᵢ),&τ≤eᵢ<τᵣ (Refine), G_T(Hᵢ,aᵢ,c;Ξᵢᵀ),&eᵢ≥τᵣ (Reject).\endcases

    		(6)

    Accept retains the draft when the discrepancy is small. Refine corrects intermediate discrepancies, reusing the probe candidate for the shortest correction or running a longer target chain. Reject runs the target’s full sampler to regenerate the chunk. Thus, the thresholds choose the action, while the transition schedule selects where refinement begins.

    Burst fallback.  Repeated rejections incur draft and probe costs before each full regeneration. To avoid these recurring costs, SpecWM switches to target-only generation after m=2 consecutive Reject decisions. It generates the next n=4 chunks directly with the target, up to the end of the rollout. Fallback skips draft proposals and verification probes; target outputs are committed directly. Both models append these outputs to their histories before normal routing resumes with the rejection counter reset. We denote these target-only chunks by T in the routing statistics, separately from chunks regenerated after a Reject decision.

    4.3 Transition-Aware Refinement

    Once a chunk is routed to Refine, the remaining choice is its correction length. Our uniform-refinement study reveals complementary effects (Table 1). One-step correction improves perceptual quality over the draft. Three-step correction improves camera following and trajectory consistency, but lowers perceptual preference and aesthetics relative to one step. We therefore allocate longer corrections near control transitions and shorter corrections during continued motion, with verification fixed.

    Refinement entry point. Control transitions determine how far back along the denoising trajectory correction begins. For LingBot, this gives ℓᵢ=3 steps at a transition, two in the next chunk, and one thereafter. The initial chunk is treated as a transition. The schedule follows chunk positions, regardless of earlier routing decisions. Controls or navigation-turn metadata identify transitions, as detailed in the supplementary material.

    Executing the correction. For ℓᵢ=1, we directly reuse rᵢ⁽¹⁾=uᵀ_i,4. For longer corrections, ℓᵢ∈{2,3}, we start from the aligned state q_4-ℓᵢ=x^D_i,4-ℓᵢ and run consecutive target updates for k=4-ℓᵢ,…,3:

    z̃ₖ=qₖ-σₖᵀv_T(qₖ,σₖᵀ;Hᵢ,aᵢ,c),
    qₖ₊₁=\begincases(1-σₖ₊₁ᵀ)z̃ₖ+σₖ₊₁ᵀεᵀ_i,k,&k<3, z̃ₖ,&k=3.\endcases(7)

    The final state q₄ becomes rᵢ^(ℓᵢ). Each update uses the preceding target output under the fixed history. The initial probe selects the route, and the resulting correction is committed once; the score is not recomputed during refinement. Fixed-length variants replace the schedule with a constant ℓᵢ across all chunks routed to Refine.

    A longer correction starts at a higher noise level and lets the target revise more of the denoising trajectory, paralleling the role of entry noise in diffusion editing [34]. Across backbones, the policy therefore selects a correction interval on the native noise grid, which in turn determines the number of target updates (Sec. 5.5).

    4.4 Overlapped Speculative Execution

    During target verification of chunk i, the draft generates chunk i+1 under the tentative history Hᵢ∥ẑᵢ (Fig. 3). This LingBot pipeline therefore reduces latency while still verifying one candidate at a time (K=1).

    Retain or re-propose. Accept preserves this history, so the next proposal can be retained. Refine or Reject replaces ẑᵢ with zᵢ, making the next proposal’s history outdated. The draft then restores its state from before proposing chunk i, appends zᵢ, and re-proposes chunk i+1. The target also appends zᵢ. Fallback chunks update both histories.

    To maintain consistent histories, both LingBot models commit the selected latent through clean-context forward passes into separate key-value (KV) caches. Temporary state is restored after probing or correction, before the selected output is committed. With shared weights, Hy-Nomas instead executes both roles sequentially using one cache with native history noise, updated only after output selection. The supplementary material details both implementations and their cache updates.

    Denoising cost and runtime.  For LingBot, Accept and one-step Refine each use one target probe. Two- and three-step Refine add ℓᵢ target denoising calls after that probe. Reject runs the complete four-step target sampler; fallback runs it without a probe. These counts describe target denoising work; draft generation and cache updates add separate costs. Because overlap depends on retaining the next proposal, we measure the full generation loop, including cache updates, restoration, re-proposal, and communication. We therefore report speedup alongside A/F/R/T shares to relate measured runtime to routing decisions.

    5 Experiments

    We evaluate SpecWM on WBench Navigation and ablate refinement, routing, and execution. LongSpecBench then tests sustained control and scene consistency over long rollouts, while Hy-Nomas examines shared-weight pairing through different denoising budgets.

    5.1 Experimental Setup

    Models and generation. We use the distilled LingBot-World 2.0 causal-fast models [11] for WBench and LongSpecBench: a 1.3B draft and a 14B target with native four-stage sampling. WBench videos contain 253 frames at 16 fps (about 16 seconds), generated in 16 chunks of four latent frames. Resolution follows the input aspect ratio with a maximum pixel area of 480×832. We use a context window of 18 latent frames and six sink frames. Methods share inputs, seeds, and GPU type. Sequence parallelism uses four GPUs per model: four for single-model baselines and eight for draft-target overlap.

    Benchmarks. Main comparisons and ablations use the full 158-case WBench Navigation split [51] with shared scenes and controls. Each metric uses its applicable cases and valid outputs. LongSpecBench and Hy-Nomas-Bench are detailed in Secs. 5.4 and 5.5.

    Metrics. Table 1 groups metrics into visual quality, consistency, and camera control. HPSv3 [32] follows WBench normalization; Spatial measures consistency upon returning to the initial viewpoint [51]. NavScore averages navigation accuracy and trajectory consistency, each computed over valid cases using estimated camera poses. Quality and control scores are multiplied by 100; Speedup and probe discrepancies retain their original scales.

    Generation speedup. Speedup is the reciprocal of the mean per-case runtime ratio to Target-only. Across all three benchmarks, timing covers the full generation loop, including state updates, communication, and any rollback, decoding, or scoring required by routing. Model loading and final output decoding are excluded.

    Compared methods. Target-only and Draft-only provide quality and speed references. Accept-all probes and retains every draft, while Refine-all corrects every chunk. SDVG-style adapts decoded-frame reward routing [16] to the same model pair. LingBot-based SpecWM uses fixed refinement lengths (1/2/3-step) or the 3→2→1 schedule. These variants share the score, thresholds, fallback, and overlap to isolate refinement length.

    Policy settings. All latent-probe variants on LingBot use final-stage verification. For WBench, Accept-all discrepancies on 20 calibration cases set τ=0.2381 and τᵣ=0.2704 at the 70th and 90th percentiles, fixed throughout evaluation. The full policy uses 3→2→1 refinement, burst fallback (m,n)=(2,4), and overlap with K=1.

    5.2 Main Results on WBench

    Quality-speed-control trade-off. SpecWM achieves the best overall quality-speed-control trade-off among the evaluated methods (Table 1, Fig. 4). At 1.63× speedup over Target-only, it retains comparable NavScore (85.63 versus 85.49) and improves HPSv3 from 74.57 to 77.66. It also gains 9.64 NavScore points over Draft-only. Our selective target intervention thus recovers target-level control with lower latency and higher perceptual preference.

    Effects of refinement length. Longer refinement favors control over perceptual preference. Increasing Refine-all from one to three steps raises NavScore from 75.92 to 85.17, but lowers HPSv3 from 77.80 to 74.26 and speedup from 1.78× to 1.10×. Imaging quality remains similar. These complementary effects motivate allocating correction length around transitions. By selecting where and how long to refine, SpecWM therefore approaches both one-step perceptual preference and target-level control, while maintaining lower latency than uniform three-step correction.

    Refinement reduces regeneration. Equal acceptance rates need not yield equal efficiency. Both SDVG-style and SpecWM accept 68% of chunks, but SpecWM refines 13%, leaving 19% for full target generation, including fallback, versus 32% for SDVG-style. Refinement therefore reduces the share requiring a full target run. Together with latent verification and overlapped execution, SpecWM raises speedup from 1.42× to 1.63× while improving visual quality and control. Fig. 5 illustrates its preservation of scene structure and response to changing controls in both cases.

    5.3 Ablation Studies and Analysis

    Table 2 isolates refinement, routing, and execution under the same final-stage verification.

    Probe selection.  In a five-chunk pilot from one video, final-stage discrepancies span 0.1738–0.2698, a max/min ratio of 1.55 versus 1.22 and 1.30 at the first two stages. Separate optimized timings give 1.5 s for one stage versus 4.4 s for four-stage verification. The observed score variation, lower cost, and reusable candidate together motivate our choice of the final-stage probe.

    Refinement schedule. The full schedule raises NavScore from fixed one-step refinement’s 76.39 to 85.63. Removing the intermediate two-step correction lowers it to 81.49 and spatial consistency from 80.83 to 76.90, for only a small speedup increase (1.63× to 1.67×). Thus, continued correction supports control and consistency after transitions.

    Score-guided routing. Removing Refine lowers speedup to 1.21× and NavScore to 82.18; removing Reject raises speedup to 2.07× but lowers NavScore to 80.46. Thus, refinement reduces reliance on full regeneration, while retaining regeneration improves control. Moreover, random routing with matched shares gives 0.95× speedup and NavScore 75.98. Effective allocation depends on which chunks receive each action, not only on overall route shares.

    Fallback and overlapped execution.  Removing fallback or overlap lowers speedup from 1.63× to 1.45× or 1.29×, respectively. Fallback skips repeated draft and probe costs during consecutive target generation, while overlap prepares the next draft during verification (Fig. 3). These gains persist with state restoration and re-proposal costs included, linking computation savings to lower generation latency.

    5.4 LongSpecBench: Long-Horizon Evaluation

    Benchmark design. We construct LongSpecBench to test sustained control and scene persistence over long rollouts with repeated turns and revisits. Its 100 initial scenes come from WBench [51] (30), WorldMark [45] (30), and TrajectoryBench [33] (40). The first 20 cases set τ=0.2395 and τᵣ=0.2716 using the same 70th/90th-percentile rule; the remaining 80 form the evaluation split. Each rollout contains ten to twelve action turns and revisits over 509 frames at 16 fps (about 32 seconds, 32 chunks), with the same input-dependent resolution as WBench.

    Evaluation dimensions. Seven metrics measure visual quality (Imaging, Aesth.), temporal and revisit consistency (Long-T., Revisit), and control through motion direction (Dir.), response to changes (Resp.), and camera following (Cam.). Cam. scores trajectory following on [0,100] using poses estimated by MegaSaM [23].

    Composite evaluation metrics. World-model quality is WMQ=0.30Q+0.35C+0.35U, where Q, C, and U average the visual-quality, consistency, and control groups. For Speedup S, efficiency is E=100S/(1+S), giving the quality-efficiency score QES=100(WMQ/100)^0.80(E/100)^0.20. Both composites use the method-level scores in Table 3, with equal weights within groups and rounding to two decimals only after calculation.

    Long-horizon results. SpecWM preserves near-target revisit consistency (76.56 versus 76.77) at 1.67× speedup, while leading all three control metrics (Table 3). It closes most of the draft’s revisit gap, from 66.40 to 76.56. These results extend the shorter-rollout findings: selective correction sustains control and scene persistence through repeated turns and returns. Its leading WMQ (72.41) and QES (70.32) summarize this quality-efficiency trade-off.

    5.5 Pairing by Denoising Budget

    Shared-weight pairing. We evaluate Hy-Nomas [7] with the same distilled 8B weights, using four sampling steps for the draft and eight for the target. A fixed terminal probe provides a score and correction, while transition-aware refinement selects correction intervals on the native grid. Pairwise human evaluation uses the official 280-case Hy-Nomas-Bench; other settings follow native defaults. Sampling and evaluation details appear in the supplementary material.

    Human preference and efficiency. SpecWM achieves near-target human preference at 1.33× generation-loop speedup (Fig. 6). Against Target-only, ties dominate each dimension, with comparable win and loss rates. SpecWM also records positive win-loss margins against Draft-only and SDVG-style across all four dimensions. Compared with SDVG-style, higher preference in camera control and spatial memory accompanies faster generation. Together, relative preference scores and speedups summarize SpecWM’s balance between human preference and efficiency.

    Across backbones and sampling budgets. Together with LingBot, these results validate SpecWM across backbones and pairing strategies. Specifically, LingBot uses different model scales, whereas Hy-Nomas varies the sampling budget within one network. Finer denoising steps provide corrections without increasing model capacity. SpecWM accelerates generation even with identical model weights. Native sampling budgets offer another way to form draft-target pairs without training a separate draft model.

    6 Conclusion

    We present SpecWM, a unified, training-free inference framework that turns verification into refinement for streaming world models. The target’s latent velocity prediction supplies both a verification signal and a reusable correction, reducing reliance on costly regeneration. Our experiments reveal complementary benefits of short and long refinements for perceptual quality and trajectory control. Transition-aware refinement combines these benefits, achieving the best overall quality-speed-control trade-off among the evaluated methods on WBench Navigation and our LongSpecBench. Hy-Nomas further demonstrates effective pairing through different denoising budgets with shared weights. Together, these findings support verification-guided refinement across model-scale and sampling-budget differences. Future work will extend draft-target pairing through cross-model latent alignment.

    LLM Usage Statement

    We used OpenAI GPT to refine our writing, related-work discussions, experimental analyses, figures, and data preparation. We also used it to generate research code for implementation and experiments. We take full responsibility for the accuracy and integrity of all submitted content.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：现有推测式方法的验证只覆盖外部打分器的维度，而且只打分、不纠错。

要点：

  • 组合思路：视频世界模型里，**大模型质量高、小模型推理快**；推测式方法用「快速草稿 + 选择性重生成」来兼得
  • 两个缺陷：验证环节只覆盖**外部打分器**的评估维度，而且额外引入解码与打分成本；更关键的是，**这些分数不提供任何修正**，只能决定要不要丢弃重来
  • SpecWM 因此把「验证」直接改造成「精修」——让验证过程本身产出改进，而不是产出一个阈值

为什么值得看：「草稿—验证」是实时生成最常用的加速范式，但只打分不纠错等于扔掉了一半信息。把验证变成精修，意味着同一份计算既做判断又做改进——这对延迟预算紧的流式系统是直接收益。

中文摘要：视频世界模型近来在交互式生成上进展明显：大模型给出更高质量，小模型提供更快推理。已有的推测式（speculative）方法试图兼得两者优势——先快速生成草稿，再依据对已解码帧的奖励做选择性重生成。但作者指出两个缺陷：验证只覆盖外部打分器的评估维度，还会额外增加解码与打分开销；更重要的是，这些分数不提供任何修正，只能用来决定是否重做。SpecWM 因此把验证改造成精修：让「检查」这一步本身产出对结果的改进，而不只是产出一个通过/不通过的判断。对受延迟约束的流式世界模型，这相当于让同一笔计算同时承担判断与改进两个职责。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-20

本期推送：2026-11-22

SpecWM: Turning Verification into Refinement for Streaming World Models

Abstract

Recently, video world models have advanced interactive generation, with large models offering higher quality and smaller models enabling faster inference. Existing speculative methods combine their strengths through fast draft generation and selective target regeneration guided by rewards on decoded frames. However, verification covers only the external scorer’s evaluation dimensions and adds decoding and scoring costs. Moreover, these scores provide no correction, requiring costly target regeneration for rejected drafts. To address these limitations, we propose Speculative World Model (SpecWM), a unified, training-free inference framework for streaming world models. It verifies draft chunks using the target’s latent velocity field. Verification also yields a reusable correction; two thresholds select Accept, Refine, or Reject. Specifically, one-step refinement reuses it to improve perceptual quality, while three-step refinement strengthens camera following and trajectory consistency. These findings motivate transition-aware refinement. On WBench Navigation, SpecWM improves visual quality at 1.63× speedup over the target and raises NavScore from the draft’s 75.99 to 85.63, achieving the best quality-speed-control trade-off. Additionally, our LongSpecBench shows sustained quality and control over long, multi-turn rollouts, while experiments on Hy-Nomas validate SpecWM across backbones and denoising budgets.

1 Introduction

Streaming world models enable users to explore generated environments that evolve in response to their actions [11, 17]. Such interaction requires high visual quality, accurate control following, and rapid responses to changing inputs. However, larger models offer stronger quality and control at substantial computational cost, whereas smaller models generate faster at the expense of visual quality and accuracy in following the controls (Fig. 1, right).

Existing reward-based speculative methods combine these strengths through fast draft generation and selective target regeneration. Rewards computed on decoded draft frames determine which chunks to accept and which to regenerate with the target. Setting up this verifier requires choosing a reward model, aggregating frame scores, and calibrating an acceptance threshold [16]. However, verification is limited to the attributes captured by the external scorer [44]. Decoding and scoring also add runtime costs per chunk. Moreover, these scores provide no direct refinement signal to improve the draft itself (Fig. 1, left). Consequently, every rejected draft requires computationally expensive regeneration by the target through its full sampling process, reducing the savings from fast draft generation. How can verification itself provide a reusable correction to improve the trade-off among speed, visual quality, and control in speculative generation for streaming world models?

We propose Speculative World Model (SpecWM), a unified, training-free inference framework that turns verification into refinement for streaming autoregressive (AR) world models. SpecWM replaces decoded-frame reward scoring with a single final-stage evaluation of the target’s latent velocity field v. This evaluation yields a clean prediction under the same history and controls. Its difference from the draft provides a verification score. Moreover, the same prediction supplies a reusable correction. Based on this score, SpecWM uses two thresholds to select Accept, Refine, or Reject to allocate target computation across chunks.

One-step refinement directly reuses the prediction from verification, without further target denoising. Three-step refinement starts at a higher noise level and runs three consecutive target denoising steps. With verification fixed, our uniform-refinement experiments reveal complementary effects (Table 1). One-step refinement improves imaging quality and perceptual preference over the draft, with limited improvement in navigation control. Three-step refinement strengthens camera following and trajectory consistency, but lowers perceptual preference and aesthetics relative to one step; imaging quality remains similar. Image diffusion studies link early denoising to coarse structure and later steps to fine detail [48]. Our results suggest a similar distinction: final-stage correction improves appearance, while earlier intervention allows greater trajectory revision.

These findings motivate transition-aware refinement. For chunks routed to Refine, SpecWM uses three steps at a control change, two in the next chunk, and one thereafter. This schedule improves control near transitions while favoring perceptual quality and speed during continued motion. Throughout this schedule, verification remains fixed at one final-stage probe per draft chunk. Additionally, the draft generates the next chunk while the target verifies the current one, thereby reducing latency.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    SpecWM. We propose a unified, training-free framework that turns verification into refinement. With transition-aware refinement, SpecWM achieves a 1.63× generation-loop speedup over Target-only on WBench Navigation [51], improving imaging quality and perceptual preference while maintaining target-level navigation control.

  • •

    LongSpecBench. We construct a benchmark of long, multi-turn rollouts with revisits to jointly evaluate generation quality, speed, and sustained controllability. SpecWM leads the evaluated methods in world-model quality (WMQ) and quality-efficiency score (QES).

  • •

    Beyond model scale. SpecWM extends from model-scale to denoising-budget differences on Hy-Nomas [7], where draft and target share the same weights. It outperforms Draft-only and SDVG-style across four human-evaluated dimensions, achieving near-target preference at a 1.33× generation-loop speedup over Target-only.

    • 2 Related Work

    Autoregressive video generation and world models. Diffusion models [14], latent representations [37], and transformers [36] underpin video synthesis [15, 1, 6, 47, 12]. Building on this foundation, camera and motion conditioning enable controllable generation [13, 43], while flexible temporal conditioning incorporates generation history [4, 41]. For streaming generation, causal distillation reduces latency [50, 52], and training on self-generated histories addresses the training-inference mismatch [18]. Longer rollouts further require managing accumulated errors through long-video tuning, cache refreshes, and rolling denoising [46, 26]. These developments support interactive world models that respond to user actions [2, 11, 17, 7]. Evaluation likewise extends from video quality in VBench [19] to multi-turn interaction in WBench [51]. SpecWM addresses computation allocation during streaming inference to balance visual quality, speed, and control.

    Caching and efficient inference. Efficient samplers [40, 28], distillation [38, 49], and consistency models [42] reduce denoising steps. Beyond reducing steps, caching exploits redundancy in features, attention, and guidance [30, 29]. Adaptive reuse responds to estimated output changes or chunk-level variation [25, 31]. For world models, selective token recomputation [10] and history-guided caching with residual correction [35] address reuse across evolving content. System optimizations combine caching with sparse attention, quantization, and kernel fusion [21]. These approaches lower the cost of running a generator by reusing internal computations or reducing sampling steps. SpecWM instead allocates computation according to the draft chunk’s discrepancy from the target. Accept, Refine, and Reject provide different levels of target intervention. This allocation applies to pairings with different model scales or denoising budgets, including shared-weight configurations.

    Speculative verification and refinement. Speculative decoding combines draft proposals with target verification [20, 5]; feature prediction and multiple decoding heads improve proposal generation [22, 3]. DSpark uses confidence and serving load to schedule token verification [8]. In video generation, SDVG uses ImageReward [44] on decoded draft frames to select acceptance or target regeneration [16]. However, this verifier incurs decoding and scoring costs, and its coverage depends on the external scorer. Moreover, the scores guide selection without supplying a direct correction. Separately, other methods allocate computation within one generator: Speculative Forcing freezes converged tokens [9], while Surprise Forcing skips steps according to chunk difficulty [39]. SpecWM instead verifies draft chunks using the target’s latent velocity prediction. The resulting clean estimate can correct the draft, adding refinement between acceptance and full regeneration.

    3 Preliminaries

    Controlled autoregressive generation. Let zᵢ denote chunk i’s clean latent, Hᵢ=(z₀,…,zᵢ₋₁) the committed history, aᵢ the camera controls, and c the initial-image and text conditions. For N chunks, the generator samples

    zᵢ∼G(·|Hᵢ,aᵢ,c), i=0,…,N-1.

    		(1)

    The selected output is appended to the history. For speculative generation, we pair frozen generators G_D and G_T with different model scales or denoising budgets. They share a latent representation, chunk length, and control interface, and condition on the same history and inputs.

    Velocity-based denoising. Following flow matching and rectified flow [24, 27], we use a linear interpolation between a clean latent z and noise ε. At noise level σ, the noisy latent is x_σ=(1-σ)z+σε. The model predicts a latent velocity field v, from which we obtain the clean estimate

    z̃=x_σ-σv(x_σ,σ;Hᵢ,aᵢ,c).

    		(2)

    For the LingBot implementation [11], we use four native denoising stages k∈{0,1,2,3}, with decreasing noise levels 1≥σ₀>σ₁>σ₂>σ₃>0. At intermediate stages k<3, the clean estimate is re-noised to σₖ₊₁ for the next update. At the final stage, it is returned.

    4 SpecWM

    SpecWM turns target verification into reusable refinement (Fig. 2, main panel). A final-stage velocity prediction yields a clean candidate, whose discrepancy from the draft provides a verification score. Two thresholds then select Accept, Refine, or Reject to allocate target computation. For chunks routed to Refine, control transitions determine the correction entry point. With separate models, draft generation overlaps target verification to reduce latency. Both roles then use the selected output as shared context.

    4.1 Verification and Reusable Refinement

    We describe SpecWM using LingBot’s four-stage sampler. Draft predictions are aligned with target noise levels. For shared-weight pairing, we instead subdivide the draft’s final update along the target grid (Sec. 5.5).

    Draft proposal and alignment. The draft generates ẑᵢ=G_D(Hᵢ,aᵢ,c;ξᵢ^D), where ξᵢ^D denotes its sampling randomness, and retains the clean prediction from each denoising stage. Draft and target can have different noise schedules. We therefore interpolate the draft’s clean predictions by noise level to obtain z̄^D_i,k at target level σₖᵀ. To form target inputs, we re-noise these estimates using Ξᵢᵀ=(ηᵢᵀ,εᵀ_i,0:2), which contains the target’s initial noise and three re-noising draws. The resulting aligned states are given by

    x^D_i,0=ηᵢᵀ, x^D_i,4=ẑᵢ,
    x^D_i,k=(1-σₖᵀ)z̄^D_i,k+σₖᵀεᵀ_i,k-1, k=1,2,3.(3)

    These states provide the input for verification and the starting points for longer corrections. Interpolation and random-state details are given in the supplementary material.

    One probe, two outputs. Using the aligned final-stage state, we evaluate the target at k=3 to obtain

    uᵀ_i,4=x^D_i,3-σ₃ᵀv_T(x^D_i,3,σ₃ᵀ;Hᵢ,aᵢ,c).

    		(4)

    We then compare this clean prediction with the draft output:

    eᵢ=(∥ẑᵢ-uᵀ_i,4∥₁)/(∥uᵀ_i,4∥₁+ε), ε=10⁻⁶.

    		(5)

    The norms cover valid latent elements. The score eᵢ guides routing, while the prediction uᵀ_i,4 can be committed as a one-step correction without further target denoising. Thus, verification directly provides a refinement candidate. Keeping this probe fixed gives all refinement lengths the same scoring rule. Its low cost and observed score variation across chunks motivate the final-stage choice (Sec. 5.3).

    4.2 Threshold-Based Computation Allocation

    Given the discrepancy score eᵢ, two thresholds τ<τᵣ determine how the target intervenes. Let rᵢ^(ℓᵢ) denote a corrected chunk obtained with ℓᵢ target denoising steps, as defined in Sec. 4.3. The selected output is

    zᵢ=\begincasesẑᵢ,&eᵢ<τ (Accept), rᵢ^(ℓᵢ),&τ≤eᵢ<τᵣ (Refine), G_T(Hᵢ,aᵢ,c;Ξᵢᵀ),&eᵢ≥τᵣ (Reject).\endcases

    		(6)

    Accept retains the draft when the discrepancy is small. Refine corrects intermediate discrepancies, reusing the probe candidate for the shortest correction or running a longer target chain. Reject runs the target’s full sampler to regenerate the chunk. Thus, the thresholds choose the action, while the transition schedule selects where refinement begins.

    Burst fallback.  Repeated rejections incur draft and probe costs before each full regeneration. To avoid these recurring costs, SpecWM switches to target-only generation after m=2 consecutive Reject decisions. It generates the next n=4 chunks directly with the target, up to the end of the rollout. Fallback skips draft proposals and verification probes; target outputs are committed directly. Both models append these outputs to their histories before normal routing resumes with the rejection counter reset. We denote these target-only chunks by T in the routing statistics, separately from chunks regenerated after a Reject decision.

    4.3 Transition-Aware Refinement

    Once a chunk is routed to Refine, the remaining choice is its correction length. Our uniform-refinement study reveals complementary effects (Table 1). One-step correction improves perceptual quality over the draft. Three-step correction improves camera following and trajectory consistency, but lowers perceptual preference and aesthetics relative to one step. We therefore allocate longer corrections near control transitions and shorter corrections during continued motion, with verification fixed.

    Refinement entry point. Control transitions determine how far back along the denoising trajectory correction begins. For LingBot, this gives ℓᵢ=3 steps at a transition, two in the next chunk, and one thereafter. The initial chunk is treated as a transition. The schedule follows chunk positions, regardless of earlier routing decisions. Controls or navigation-turn metadata identify transitions, as detailed in the supplementary material.

    Executing the correction. For ℓᵢ=1, we directly reuse rᵢ⁽¹⁾=uᵀ_i,4. For longer corrections, ℓᵢ∈{2,3}, we start from the aligned state q_4-ℓᵢ=x^D_i,4-ℓᵢ and run consecutive target updates for k=4-ℓᵢ,…,3:

    z̃ₖ=qₖ-σₖᵀv_T(qₖ,σₖᵀ;Hᵢ,aᵢ,c),
    qₖ₊₁=\begincases(1-σₖ₊₁ᵀ)z̃ₖ+σₖ₊₁ᵀεᵀ_i,k,&k<3, z̃ₖ,&k=3.\endcases(7)

    The final state q₄ becomes rᵢ^(ℓᵢ). Each update uses the preceding target output under the fixed history. The initial probe selects the route, and the resulting correction is committed once; the score is not recomputed during refinement. Fixed-length variants replace the schedule with a constant ℓᵢ across all chunks routed to Refine.

    A longer correction starts at a higher noise level and lets the target revise more of the denoising trajectory, paralleling the role of entry noise in diffusion editing [34]. Across backbones, the policy therefore selects a correction interval on the native noise grid, which in turn determines the number of target updates (Sec. 5.5).

    4.4 Overlapped Speculative Execution

    During target verification of chunk i, the draft generates chunk i+1 under the tentative history Hᵢ∥ẑᵢ (Fig. 3). This LingBot pipeline therefore reduces latency while still verifying one candidate at a time (K=1).

    Retain or re-propose. Accept preserves this history, so the next proposal can be retained. Refine or Reject replaces ẑᵢ with zᵢ, making the next proposal’s history outdated. The draft then restores its state from before proposing chunk i, appends zᵢ, and re-proposes chunk i+1. The target also appends zᵢ. Fallback chunks update both histories.

    To maintain consistent histories, both LingBot models commit the selected latent through clean-context forward passes into separate key-value (KV) caches. Temporary state is restored after probing or correction, before the selected output is committed. With shared weights, Hy-Nomas instead executes both roles sequentially using one cache with native history noise, updated only after output selection. The supplementary material details both implementations and their cache updates.

    Denoising cost and runtime.  For LingBot, Accept and one-step Refine each use one target probe. Two- and three-step Refine add ℓᵢ target denoising calls after that probe. Reject runs the complete four-step target sampler; fallback runs it without a probe. These counts describe target denoising work; draft generation and cache updates add separate costs. Because overlap depends on retaining the next proposal, we measure the full generation loop, including cache updates, restoration, re-proposal, and communication. We therefore report speedup alongside A/F/R/T shares to relate measured runtime to routing decisions.

    5 Experiments

    We evaluate SpecWM on WBench Navigation and ablate refinement, routing, and execution. LongSpecBench then tests sustained control and scene consistency over long rollouts, while Hy-Nomas examines shared-weight pairing through different denoising budgets.

    5.1 Experimental Setup

    Models and generation. We use the distilled LingBot-World 2.0 causal-fast models [11] for WBench and LongSpecBench: a 1.3B draft and a 14B target with native four-stage sampling. WBench videos contain 253 frames at 16 fps (about 16 seconds), generated in 16 chunks of four latent frames. Resolution follows the input aspect ratio with a maximum pixel area of 480×832. We use a context window of 18 latent frames and six sink frames. Methods share inputs, seeds, and GPU type. Sequence parallelism uses four GPUs per model: four for single-model baselines and eight for draft-target overlap.

    Benchmarks. Main comparisons and ablations use the full 158-case WBench Navigation split [51] with shared scenes and controls. Each metric uses its applicable cases and valid outputs. LongSpecBench and Hy-Nomas-Bench are detailed in Secs. 5.4 and 5.5.

    Metrics. Table 1 groups metrics into visual quality, consistency, and camera control. HPSv3 [32] follows WBench normalization; Spatial measures consistency upon returning to the initial viewpoint [51]. NavScore averages navigation accuracy and trajectory consistency, each computed over valid cases using estimated camera poses. Quality and control scores are multiplied by 100; Speedup and probe discrepancies retain their original scales.

    Generation speedup. Speedup is the reciprocal of the mean per-case runtime ratio to Target-only. Across all three benchmarks, timing covers the full generation loop, including state updates, communication, and any rollback, decoding, or scoring required by routing. Model loading and final output decoding are excluded.

    Compared methods. Target-only and Draft-only provide quality and speed references. Accept-all probes and retains every draft, while Refine-all corrects every chunk. SDVG-style adapts decoded-frame reward routing [16] to the same model pair. LingBot-based SpecWM uses fixed refinement lengths (1/2/3-step) or the 3→2→1 schedule. These variants share the score, thresholds, fallback, and overlap to isolate refinement length.

    Policy settings. All latent-probe variants on LingBot use final-stage verification. For WBench, Accept-all discrepancies on 20 calibration cases set τ=0.2381 and τᵣ=0.2704 at the 70th and 90th percentiles, fixed throughout evaluation. The full policy uses 3→2→1 refinement, burst fallback (m,n)=(2,4), and overlap with K=1.

    5.2 Main Results on WBench

    Quality-speed-control trade-off. SpecWM achieves the best overall quality-speed-control trade-off among the evaluated methods (Table 1, Fig. 4). At 1.63× speedup over Target-only, it retains comparable NavScore (85.63 versus 85.49) and improves HPSv3 from 74.57 to 77.66. It also gains 9.64 NavScore points over Draft-only. Our selective target intervention thus recovers target-level control with lower latency and higher perceptual preference.

    Effects of refinement length. Longer refinement favors control over perceptual preference. Increasing Refine-all from one to three steps raises NavScore from 75.92 to 85.17, but lowers HPSv3 from 77.80 to 74.26 and speedup from 1.78× to 1.10×. Imaging quality remains similar. These complementary effects motivate allocating correction length around transitions. By selecting where and how long to refine, SpecWM therefore approaches both one-step perceptual preference and target-level control, while maintaining lower latency than uniform three-step correction.

    Refinement reduces regeneration. Equal acceptance rates need not yield equal efficiency. Both SDVG-style and SpecWM accept 68% of chunks, but SpecWM refines 13%, leaving 19% for full target generation, including fallback, versus 32% for SDVG-style. Refinement therefore reduces the share requiring a full target run. Together with latent verification and overlapped execution, SpecWM raises speedup from 1.42× to 1.63× while improving visual quality and control. Fig. 5 illustrates its preservation of scene structure and response to changing controls in both cases.

    5.3 Ablation Studies and Analysis

    Table 2 isolates refinement, routing, and execution under the same final-stage verification.

    Probe selection.  In a five-chunk pilot from one video, final-stage discrepancies span 0.1738–0.2698, a max/min ratio of 1.55 versus 1.22 and 1.30 at the first two stages. Separate optimized timings give 1.5 s for one stage versus 4.4 s for four-stage verification. The observed score variation, lower cost, and reusable candidate together motivate our choice of the final-stage probe.

    Refinement schedule. The full schedule raises NavScore from fixed one-step refinement’s 76.39 to 85.63. Removing the intermediate two-step correction lowers it to 81.49 and spatial consistency from 80.83 to 76.90, for only a small speedup increase (1.63× to 1.67×). Thus, continued correction supports control and consistency after transitions.

    Score-guided routing. Removing Refine lowers speedup to 1.21× and NavScore to 82.18; removing Reject raises speedup to 2.07× but lowers NavScore to 80.46. Thus, refinement reduces reliance on full regeneration, while retaining regeneration improves control. Moreover, random routing with matched shares gives 0.95× speedup and NavScore 75.98. Effective allocation depends on which chunks receive each action, not only on overall route shares.

    Fallback and overlapped execution.  Removing fallback or overlap lowers speedup from 1.63× to 1.45× or 1.29×, respectively. Fallback skips repeated draft and probe costs during consecutive target generation, while overlap prepares the next draft during verification (Fig. 3). These gains persist with state restoration and re-proposal costs included, linking computation savings to lower generation latency.

    5.4 LongSpecBench: Long-Horizon Evaluation

    Benchmark design. We construct LongSpecBench to test sustained control and scene persistence over long rollouts with repeated turns and revisits. Its 100 initial scenes come from WBench [51] (30), WorldMark [45] (30), and TrajectoryBench [33] (40). The first 20 cases set τ=0.2395 and τᵣ=0.2716 using the same 70th/90th-percentile rule; the remaining 80 form the evaluation split. Each rollout contains ten to twelve action turns and revisits over 509 frames at 16 fps (about 32 seconds, 32 chunks), with the same input-dependent resolution as WBench.

    Evaluation dimensions. Seven metrics measure visual quality (Imaging, Aesth.), temporal and revisit consistency (Long-T., Revisit), and control through motion direction (Dir.), response to changes (Resp.), and camera following (Cam.). Cam. scores trajectory following on [0,100] using poses estimated by MegaSaM [23].

    Composite evaluation metrics. World-model quality is WMQ=0.30Q+0.35C+0.35U, where Q, C, and U average the visual-quality, consistency, and control groups. For Speedup S, efficiency is E=100S/(1+S), giving the quality-efficiency score QES=100(WMQ/100)^0.80(E/100)^0.20. Both composites use the method-level scores in Table 3, with equal weights within groups and rounding to two decimals only after calculation.

    Long-horizon results. SpecWM preserves near-target revisit consistency (76.56 versus 76.77) at 1.67× speedup, while leading all three control metrics (Table 3). It closes most of the draft’s revisit gap, from 66.40 to 76.56. These results extend the shorter-rollout findings: selective correction sustains control and scene persistence through repeated turns and returns. Its leading WMQ (72.41) and QES (70.32) summarize this quality-efficiency trade-off.

    5.5 Pairing by Denoising Budget

    Shared-weight pairing. We evaluate Hy-Nomas [7] with the same distilled 8B weights, using four sampling steps for the draft and eight for the target. A fixed terminal probe provides a score and correction, while transition-aware refinement selects correction intervals on the native grid. Pairwise human evaluation uses the official 280-case Hy-Nomas-Bench; other settings follow native defaults. Sampling and evaluation details appear in the supplementary material.

    Human preference and efficiency. SpecWM achieves near-target human preference at 1.33× generation-loop speedup (Fig. 6). Against Target-only, ties dominate each dimension, with comparable win and loss rates. SpecWM also records positive win-loss margins against Draft-only and SDVG-style across all four dimensions. Compared with SDVG-style, higher preference in camera control and spatial memory accompanies faster generation. Together, relative preference scores and speedups summarize SpecWM’s balance between human preference and efficiency.

    Across backbones and sampling budgets. Together with LingBot, these results validate SpecWM across backbones and pairing strategies. Specifically, LingBot uses different model scales, whereas Hy-Nomas varies the sampling budget within one network. Finer denoising steps provide corrections without increasing model capacity. SpecWM accelerates generation even with identical model weights. Native sampling budgets offer another way to form draft-target pairs without training a separate draft model.

    6 Conclusion

    We present SpecWM, a unified, training-free inference framework that turns verification into refinement for streaming world models. The target’s latent velocity prediction supplies both a verification signal and a reusable correction, reducing reliance on costly regeneration. Our experiments reveal complementary benefits of short and long refinements for perceptual quality and trajectory control. Transition-aware refinement combines these benefits, achieving the best overall quality-speed-control trade-off among the evaluated methods on WBench Navigation and our LongSpecBench. Hy-Nomas further demonstrates effective pairing through different denoising budgets with shared weights. Together, these findings support verification-guided refinement across model-scale and sampling-budget differences. Future work will extend draft-target pairing through cross-model latent alignment.

    LLM Usage Statement

    We used OpenAI GPT to refine our writing, related-work discussions, experimental analyses, figures, and data preparation. We also used it to generate research code for implementation and experiments. We take full responsibility for the accuracy and integrity of all submitted content.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 4D 重建采样率不够？OffBeat 用「错峰触发」的多相机把时间分辨率提上去，还顺手解掉深度-运动的混淆 ｜ OffBeat: Multicoset Sampling for 4D Capture Beyond the Camera Frame Rate
item.description:
一句话：同步多相机在同一批时间戳取帧，中间的运动就永远丢了。

要点：

  • 物理限制：4D 重建用的同步多相机阵列**在同一批时间戳取帧**，因此错过了帧与帧之间的运动
  • 已有对策是**错峰触发**：把同样多的帧分散到更多时间戳上。但如果一排相机依次触发（如 4DSloMo 在 N3DV 上的排程），**整排会被当成一台移动相机**，从而把深度与运动混在一起
  • OffBeat 因此把错峰阵列建模成一个**空间分布的多集（multicoset）采样器**，从采样理论出发解掉这个混淆，把有效时间分辨率推到相机帧率之上

为什么值得看：「采集端提采样率」是拿到高质量 4D 数据的另一条路——不靠生成模型补帧，而靠触发时序。这对需要做真实动作参考、或者训练世界模型的团队，是从源头改善数据的手段。

中文摘要：用于 4D 重建的同步多相机阵列会在同一批时间戳上取帧，因此帧与帧之间的运动信息被永久丢失。一种对策是错峰触发——把相同数量的帧分散到更多的时间戳上；但当一排相机依次触发时（如 4DSloMo 在 Neural 3D Video 阵列上的排程），整排相机看起来就像一台移动的相机，从而把深度与运动混为一谈。OffBeat 把错峰阵列建模为一个在空间上分布的多集（multicoset）采样器，从采样理论出发消解这种混淆，使有效时间分辨率超过相机自身的帧率。对需要高质量真实动作参考、或要训练世界模型的团队，这是从采集环节改善数据的手段。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-20

本期推送：2026-11-22

OffBeat: Multicoset Sampling for 4D Capture
Beyond the Camera Frame Rate

Abstract

For 4D reconstruction, a synchronized multi-camera rig records all views at the same timestamps and misses the motion between them. Staggered triggers spread the same frames over more timestamps. However, when the cameras along each row fire one after another, as in 4DSloMo’s schedule on the Neural 3D Video (N3DV) rig, the row acts as one moving camera that confounds depth with motion. We introduce OffBeat, which models a staggered rig as a spatially distributed multicoset sampler: shifted copies of one sampling grid. From the calibration alone, OffBeat derives camera groups that fire together and their firing order. Since one group records each timestamp, a short-lived primitive can fit an error its cameras share, such as a color offset, and flicker in novel views. We show that a primitive’s opacity over time weights all groups equally, for every number of groups, only if it lasts at least one camera frame interval. On Spacetime Gaussians, a minimum lifetime approximates this bound, and a closed-form smoothed box of that length satisfies it exactly, with less flicker than a Gaussian in its place at nearly equal PSNR. In simulated staggered capture on N3DV, OffBeat outperforms the full 4DSloMo pipeline with video diffusion on every test frame, by 3.04 dB in mean dynamic-region PSNR. Between the first and last synchronized frame, it outperforms the best synchronized method of each scene, with or without frame interpolation, by 1.98 dB in mean dynamic-region PSNR, while synchronized capture is better at its own frames. On PanopticSports, in this frame range, OffBeat is comparable in PSNR to synchronized capture with interpolation. On every N3DV scene, replacing 4DSloMo’s schedule with ours raises the dynamic-region PSNR of Spacetime Gaussians, 4DSloMo without diffusion, and our reconstruction. Multi-camera rigs could follow faster motion at the same frame count by changing only when each camera fires.

††footnotetext: Emails: {levi74108520963, kylechen.ankai, faidavid7, changg587}@gmail.com, kuopc@cs.nthu.edu.tw

1 Introduction

4D reconstruction from multi-view video [20, 22, 47] still fails on fast non-rigid motion, such as a flame, a hand turning food, or a ball leaving a hand. One cause is temporal sampling: in a synchronized rig, all N cameras record at the same timestamps, once every camera frame interval T. Adding cameras adds views of these timestamps and leaves the temporal bandwidth at 1/(2T). A higher frame rate costs resolution, exposure, storage and link bandwidth.

Staggered triggers fire the cameras in K groups spaced T/K apart, which spreads the same number of frames over K times as many timestamps (Fig. OffBeat: Multicoset Sampling for 4D Capture
Beyond the Camera Frame Rate). For nearly co-located cameras this is the classic high-speed array [46, 37, 1], and in a dense array staggered triggers sampled the video light field better than synchronized ones [46]. 4DSloMo [9] staggers a multi-view rig to raise its effective frame rate and repairs sparse-view artifacts at each timestamp with a 14B-parameter video diffusion model.

On the Neural 3D Video rig (N3DV) [20], the modular schedule of 4DSloMo, which gives camera k the offset (k\bmodK) T/K, fires each of the two camera rows in position order. Within a camera frame interval, such a row acts as one camera moving at constant speed: regardless of row size, a static point is indistinguishable from a moving point at another depth (Sec. 3.2, Fig. 2a).

We model a staggered rig as a spatially distributed multicoset sampler [28, 41]: cameras that fire together form a trigger group and sample at the camera frame rate on a shifted copy of one grid. As in multichannel sampling, a point whose motion is band-limited to half the effective frame rate K/T is identifiable if every group triangulates it (Sec. 3.1). Single-camera groups, as on N3DV, cannot triangulate; a motion model over one camera frame interval pools them. From the calibration alone, we choose the groups by how well the others triangulate, and their order by the predictive variance of novel views (Sec. 3.2).

The reconstruction faces a second problem: as each timestamp is recorded by a single group, an error its cameras share, such as a color or calibration offset, is fit exactly by spurious content present only at those timestamps, which a novel view sees as flicker at the camera frame rate (Sec. 3.3). A primitive can supply such content in every period only if its temporal opacity window, summed over copies one period apart, weights the groups unequally. We show that the windows weighting all groups equally for any number of groups and at any center are exactly the convolutions of a box of length T (Prop. 1). Hence a primitive’s lifetime (its window’s duration) is at least T rather than the trigger spacing T/K, while its motion is sampled at the effective frame rate. On Spacetime Gaussians (STG) [22], a lifetime floor approximates this bound, and a closed-form period window, a smoothed box, satisfies it exactly (Sec. 3.4).

In summary, we make the following contributions:

  • •

    We introduce OffBeat, which models a staggered rig as a spatially distributed multicoset sampler, and show that a position-ordered row confounds depth with motion.

  • •

    From the calibration alone, we derive which cameras fire together and in which order.

  • •

    We show that temporal windows weighting all groups equally for every K must last at least T, and derive a closed-form period window that satisfies this bound.

  • •

    In simulated staggered capture on N3DV, OffBeat outperforms the full 4DSloMo pipeline and follows motion between synchronized frames better on average than a synchronized rig of equal camera frame rate, which is better at its own frames. On PanopticSports, up to the last synchronized frame, OffBeat is comparable in PSNR to synchronized capture with interpolation.

    • 2 Related Work

    Staggered and unsynchronized capture.
