    In high-speed arrays of nearly co-located cameras [46, 37, 1], the firing order is a design parameter [46]. Color-coded illumination yields high-speed 3D under controlled light [27]. Methods for unsynchronized video treat the time offsets as nuisances under smoothness priors [3, 29, 42, 52], estimate them [8, 2, 15, 48, 19, 53], or recover structure and motion from asynchronous tracks [11, 39]. 4DSloMo [9] staggers a rig with a modular schedule.

    Multichannel sampling.

    In multichannel sampling, K channels at 1/K of the Nyquist rate recover a band-limited signal [28, 41]. Parallel MRI shares this structure [30, 40], and CAIPIRINHA [7] shifts the sampling pattern such that aliases fall where the coil sensitivities differ. Our ordering criterion plays this role for cameras by decorrelating the trigger offsets from the camera positions.

    4D Gaussians and sampling-aware representations.

    Dynamic extensions of Gaussian splatting [13] use deformation fields [47], native 4D primitives [49], per-Gaussian trajectories with temporal opacity [22, 18, 45], or tracked Gaussians [24]. RetimeGS [44] and SPIN-4DGS [16] target temporal aliasing and large displacements between synchronized frames. Mip-Splatting [50] bounds the 3D frequency of a primitive by the sampling rate of the training views, and our lifetime bound is its temporal counterpart. SharpTimeGS [23] learns a flat-top lifespan for each primitive to balance static and dynamic content, whereas our window’s box has the derived length T.

    3 Method

    3.1 Staggered rigs as multicoset samplers

    Each of the N training cameras records a frame once every camera frame interval T. Camera k fires at its trigger offset φₖ, and a synchronized rig has all offsets zero. A K-group stagger fires the cameras Sₚ of group p at the offset pT/K. All triggers form the joint grid of spacing T/K, whose rate K/T is the effective frame rate of the rig [9]. Each instant of this grid is recorded by one group alone.

    Camera k observes a scene point x through its 2×3 projection Jacobian Dₖ, with Fisher information Gₖ=Dₖ^⊤Dₖ/σ² for pixel noise σ. Gₖ has rank two, and its null space is the viewing ray ℓₖ. Group p has the information Hₚ=∑_k∈SₚGₖ. A single group cannot separate frequencies that differ by a multiple of the camera frame rate. The K such frequencies inside the band of the joint grid form an alias set, and the Fourier coefficients of x(t) there are its alias components; each group observes its own phase-weighted sum of them. For a trajectory band-limited to the Nyquist frequency of the joint grid, the Fisher information of its Fourier coefficients is block-diagonal over alias sets, with blocks built from the Hₚ, as in multichannel sampling [28, 30].

    We prove two properties of this structure in Sec. S1 of the supplementary material. First, in a synchronized rig the data depend on the trajectory only through alias sums, for any number of cameras, so adding synchronized cameras leaves the temporal bandwidth at 1/(2T). Second, in a K-group stagger, a trajectory with K alias components per set is identifiable if and only if every group triangulates, Hₚ\succ0, i.e. has two cameras with non-parallel rays to the point. When every group triangulates, staggering thus raises the temporal bandwidth K-fold. With N<2K, some groups have one camera and cannot triangulate.

    A motion model over one camera frame interval pools all groups. Let a point’s position over this period T be a degree-J polynomial in time d with coefficients θ∈ℝ^3(J+1), and let camera k see it at dₖ. The Fisher information of θ is then ∑ₖb(dₖ)b(dₖ)^⊤⊗Gₖ with b(d)=(1,d,…,d^J). For J≥1, it is singular in a synchronized rig and nonsingular once J+1 groups triangulate (Sec. S1). A polynomial per period replaces the K alias components by J+1 shared coefficients, as in trajectory triangulation [3, 29] and spatiotemporal bundle adjustment [42].

    3.2 Trigger schedule

    Position-ordered triggers.

    The trigger order leaves the identifiability condition of Sec. 3.1 unchanged but can undo the gain of staggering. Let cameras with centers oₖ=o₀+sₖe on a line each fire once, at tₖ=t₀+αsₖ with α≠0, and let a point move as X(t)=X₀+v(t-t₀). For every λ>0, the point with X₀^′=o₀+λ(X₀-o₀) and v^′=λv+(1-λ)e/α has the same image in every camera. The Fisher information of (X₀,v) from one such sweep is singular for any number of cameras (proof in Sec. S3). The sweep thus confounds depth with motion, turning parallax into apparent motion (Fig. 2a). This is the ambiguity of a camera and a point both moving at constant velocity [26, 3, 29], and of a slowly moving camera [10]; in a rig, the schedule decides whether it arises. Repeated sweeps resolve it only for points keeping their velocity over several periods, unlike fast non-rigid motion. On N3DV, where the modular schedule sweeps both rows (Sec. S3), only their vertical offset keeps the information nonsingular.

    Grouping.

    The partition into groups sets the information Hₚ of each instant, on which identifiability depends. With N3DV’s 17 to 20 training cameras in 12 groups, at least four groups have a single camera under any partition, and the motion model pools them. Over the other groups, we maximize meanₚλₚ+1/2\minₚλₚ, where λₚ is the working-volume average of the smallest eigenvalue of Hₚ (Sec. S3).

    Ordering.

    For a point moving at constant velocity v over one period centered at μ and seen once per camera, pooling with J=1 gives the information of (x, vT/2),

    I(μ)=∑ₖ\beginbmatrix1&dₖ dₖ&dₖ²\endbmatrix⊗Gₖ, dₖ=(\wrap(φₖ-μ))/(T/2),

    		(1)

    where dₖ∈[-1,1) is the wrapped trigger offset from μ in half periods. For novel views, we minimize \max_u,tV+1/2 mean_u,tV with the predictive variance

    V(u,t)=𝔼_μ,x\tr(Qᵤ A I(μ)⁻¹A^⊤), A=[I, τI],

    		(2)

    where τ is the wrapped offset of a trigger instant t from μ in half periods, Qᵤ is the information of a virtual view u midway between neighboring training cameras, and the expectation is over centers μ in one period and working-volume points x. Grouping and ordering follow the E- and G-optimality criteria of optimal design [14, 31], respectively. A local search optimizes them in seconds on a CPU (Alg. S1). Both need only the calibration; their weights 1/2 hardly affect \maxV (Sec. S3). The modular schedule’s \maxV per N3DV scene is 2.2–2.4 times ours.

    3.3 Lifetime bound

    Camera–time confound.

    Any error common to a group’s views, such as a calibration or exposure error of a single-camera group, can be explained exactly by content present only when that group fires. If each group has its own error at a pixel, such as a color offset, the periodic signal h that equals the firing group’s error reproduces it in every training image. In a synchronized rig, h is constant. A test camera belongs to no group and sees h as flicker at the camera frame rate and its harmonics (Fig. 4, Sec. 4.4). On N3DV, one or two cameras see each instant, so this explanation is always available.

    Window condition.

    Primitive i with temporal center μᵢ and window w(t-μᵢ), such as STG’s temporal opacity [22], gives group p the total weight

    Ωₚ(μᵢ)=∑ₘw(\tfracpTK+mT-μᵢ)=(Π_Tw)(\tfracpTK-μᵢ),

    		(3)

    where Π_Tw sums the copies of w shifted by whole periods (Fig. 2b). If Π_Tw varies, primitives can, for some K, weight the groups unequally and supply h. Prop. 1 (proof in Sec. S1) characterizes the windows that prevent this.

    Proposition 1.

    For a compactly supported window w, the following are equivalent: (a) Ωₚ(μ) is independent of p for every center μ and every K. (b) ŵ(j/T)=0 for every integer j≠0, with ŵ the Fourier transform of w. (c) For any centers μᵢ and amplitudes bᵢ, Π_T∑ᵢbᵢw(·-μᵢ) is constant, so no set of primitives weights the groups unequally. (d) w=box_T*g for a compactly supported distribution g, with box_T=1_[-T/2,T/2). No such window is shorter than T, and the shortest ones are shifted multiples of box_T.

    Prop. 1 thus bounds a primitive’s lifetime below by T but leaves its motion sampled at K/T. Condition (b) is the partition-of-unity or Strang–Fix condition [38] at scale T, and (d) is the order-one case of the B-spline factorization [4]. The condition constrains the weights summed over all periods, over which a persistent single-camera error recurs, and leaves those within one period free.

    3.4 Reconstruction on STG

    We build on STG [22] and keep its loss and renderer. Each STG primitive i has a temporal center μᵢ and scale aᵢ with temporal opacity \exp(-(d/aᵢ)²) at d=t-μᵢ, polynomial motion and rotation, and time-dependent features.

    Lifetime floor.

    Gaussian windows violate Prop. 1(b). Wide ones have little power at the harmonics j/T (Sec. S1), but narrow ones can favor one group. Rendering with the temporal scale √aᵢ²+a_\min² in place of aᵢ, with a_\min=T/4, passes at most 29% of the power at the camera frame rate and under 1% at higher harmonics.

    Period window.

    Since Π_Tbox_T=1, Prop. 1(d)⇒(c) holds for any integrable g, and a Gaussian g gives

    wᵢ(t)=(\erf((d+T/2)/aᵢ)-\erf((d-T/2)/aᵢ))/(2 \erf(T/(2aᵢ))).

    		(4)

    For every center and scale, the period window meets the condition with no added parameter, gradients flow through the closed form, and it tends to the box window as aᵢ→0. We keep the floor on aᵢ because the window’s gradient with respect to its center concentrates at the edges, and the floor spreads it from one to most of the 12 groups (Sec. S1).

    Polynomial motion inside a window can reintroduce group-dependent components of h that Prop. 1(c) excludes for constant amplitudes, so we rescale STG’s velocity to the displacement over half a window (Sec. S2).

    Training.

    Two settings keep any update from depending on one group alone. With per-image timestamps, the timestamp is drawn per image, not per batch as in STG. With no opacity reset, the few cameras of one timestamp never have to re-estimate all opacities alone. We call STG with the floor and these two settings the floor variant.

    Densification.

    Every training camera fires once in the period centered at t₀. For a small opaque primitive moving along x+v(t-t₀) with a period window centered at t₀, let rₖ be the residual at the pixel it covers in camera k when this camera fires. For a locally constant render, the primitive’s best color lowers the squared error by Γ(x,v,t₀)=|∑ₖrₖ|²/N. This is the shift-and-stack statistic of track-before-detect [33] and, to first order in the opacity, the dual certificate of conditional gradient on measures [6, 5]. A residual r shared by m cameras scores m²|r|²/N, so errors common to one group (Sec. 3.3) rank low (Fig. 2c). Instead of STG’s guided sampling along high-error rays, we add primitives at the maxima of Γ over depth and lateral velocity (Alg. S2), keeping STG’s cloning and splitting. Other methods densify by gradients or errors [13, 35, 43, 25], temporal visibility [36], or appearance change [34].

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Setup

    Data and protocol.

    N3DV [20] contains six dynamic scenes. We hold out camera 0 for testing and train on the other 17–20 cameras. Following 4DSloMo [9], we subsample each 30 fps video to every 12th frame (2.5 fps), with a separate offset per camera for staggered capture and a common one for synchronized capture. We report test frames 100–159 unless stated otherwise and validate on frames 40–99 of Flame Steak and Cook Spinach. PanopticSports [12, 24] has 27 training and 4 test cameras, and we use six sequences with test frames 0–59 and K=12, validating on frames 90–149 of Softball and Basketball. Each method is trained once per scene, and Sec. S6 reports three seeds.

    Compared methods.

    For synchronized capture, we train STG and STG + interpolation, STG trained on videos in which AMT [21] fills the 11 frames between synchronized frames. RetimeGS [44], for which we found no public code, reports this recipe with FILM [32] as its strongest N3DV baseline, 0.05 dB below its own result. For staggered capture, we compare OffBeat with STG, also trained with twice the iterations, and with 4DSloMo [9], using its official code and settings. We run its reconstruction stage, a native 4D Gaussian model [49], on both schedules and on the synchronized frames of N3DV (where it is weaker than STG); we run its full pipeline with video diffusion on all six N3DV scenes (Sec. S5). All STG-based methods share the initialization, renderer and clock alignment (Sec. S8) and are trained for 10k iterations unless stated otherwise. OffBeat trains in 423–481 s per scene on one RTX 4090.

    Metrics.

    At the test view, we report PSNR, AlexNet LPIPS [51] and dynamic-region PSNR (Dyn. PSNR, as in FreeTimeGS [45]); Sec. S6 reports SSIM. Dynamic pixels are those whose ground-truth luma has a temporal standard deviation above 0.05 over the 60 test frames, dilated by 5 px. Per scene and metric, the best synchronized method is the strongest of STG, STG + interpolation, the floor variant and, on N3DV, our reconstruction, all from synchronized capture. Sec. S6 gives per-scene results with paired bootstrap intervals [17]. Over 20 pairs of mask threshold and dilation, OffBeat’s Dyn. PSNR difference keeps its sign against synchronized STG, STG + interpolation, STG on our schedule (except on PanopticSports) and the floor variant (negative on PanopticSports; Sec. S6).

    4.2 N3DV

    Staggered against synchronized capture.

    Between the first and last synchronized frame, OffBeat outperforms the best synchronized method by 1.98 dB in mean Dyn. PSNR (Table 1, Fig. 3) and on five of six scenes (Sec. S6). At the five synchronized frames, the better of STG and STG + interpolation in each scene is 1.23 dB above OffBeat in Dyn. PSNR but 2.20 dB below on the 44 frames in between (Sec. S6). In Fig. 5, interpolation flattens the traces, the modular schedule fragments them, and STG on our schedule adds single-frame streaks. 4DSloMo’s reconstruction stage is sharp but jitters, and its slice PSNR on Flame Steak is higher than ours. OffBeat follows the trajectories.

    Training length and camera frame rate.

    Synchronized STG trained twice as long remains 3.66 dB below OffBeat in Dyn. PSNR (Sec. S6). With the official 30k iterations for both, OffBeat outperforms STG + interpolation between the first and last synchronized frame by 2.29 dB in Dyn. PSNR on N3DV and by 0.99 dB on PanopticSports (Sec. S8). With twice the camera frame rate (5 fps), synchronized STG is still 1.02 dB below OffBeat at 2.5 fps between its first and last synchronized frame. At 10 fps it is 0.36 dB better there, and at 30 fps it is 0.60 dB better over all test frames, or 1.20 dB if it alone gets 30k iterations (Sec. S6).

    Schedule.

    With our reconstruction, replacing our schedule by the modular one lowers Dyn. PSNR by 1.29 dB and PSNR by 0.46 dB. It also lowers the Dyn. PSNR of STG and of the 4DSloMo reconstruction stage by 1.02 and 2.42 dB. On N3DV, 48 stratified random schedules with our group sizes are 0.39 dB below ours on average, recovering 69% of the modular schedule’s loss. Our two criteria rank them only weakly, and three of them outperform ours (Sec. S3).

    4DSloMo.

    The full 4DSloMo pipeline, with its own schedule, is 3.04 dB below OffBeat in Dyn. PSNR and 4.35 dB in PSNR over all six scenes (Table 1, Fig. 6). Its diffusion stage (about a day per scene) raises the Dyn. PSNR of its own reconstruction stage by 2.03 dB; our run of that stage matches it within 0.09 dB on average. Sec. S5 relates 4DSloMo’s published 33.48 dB to our protocol.

    4.3 PanopticSports

    On PanopticSports, the 27 training cameras form groups of two or three, each triangulating (Sec. 3.1). Between the first and last synchronized frame (frames 0–48, Sec. S6), OffBeat outperforms synchronized STG by 1.30 dB in Dyn. PSNR and is on par in Dyn. PSNR and PSNR with STG + interpolation. In this range, synchronized STG is slightly better in LPIPS, and STG + interpolation is better in full-frame and dynamic-region SSIM on every sequence. In Table 2, 4DSloMo’s reconstruction stage is 0.68 dB lower in Dyn. PSNR and 3.69 dB in PSNR (Fig. 7), but better in Dyn. PSNR on Softball and Tennis, where OffBeat blurs the arms, bat and racket. At camera 0, the gain comes from staggering: unlike on N3DV, OffBeat is on par with STG on our schedule and its floor variant (Sec. S6). At the other three test cameras, OffBeat outperforms STG on our schedule on 13 of the 18 sequence–camera pairs in Dyn. PSNR. In frames 0–48, against the best synchronized method, it is on par or better in Dyn. PSNR and PSNR on 15 and 13 pairs but worse in LPIPS on 7 (Sec. S6).

    4.4 Analysis

    Ablation study.

    In Table 3, staggering raises the Dyn. PSNR of STG from 24.33 to 26.07 dB on the modular schedule and to 27.09 dB on ours. Most of the further gain comes from the lifetime floor (Prop. 1, 0.29 dB) and from per-image timestamps with no opacity reset (0.34 dB). The period window with our densification adds 0.17 dB, which comes from Flame Steak and Cook Spinach, whose frames 40–99 we used for validation. On the other four scenes, OffBeat is 0.07 dB below the floor variant in Dyn. PSNR but still outperforms the best synchronized method by 2.66 dB and STG on our schedule by 0.66 dB (Sec. S6). Under the same floor, Gaussian windows are on par in Dyn. PSNR and better in PSNR (0.05 dB) and LPIPS, whereas STG’s guided sampling in place of our densification lowers Dyn. PSNR by 0.27 dB. In Dyn. PSNR, no component helps synchronized capture: the floor variant and our reconstruction differ from STG by -0.17 and -0.54 dB (Sec. S6).

    Flicker at the camera frame rate.

    On static pixels (Fig. 4, bottom), STG on our schedule has 3.0–3.7× the residual power of synchronized STG at the first five harmonics. The lifetime floor alone lowers this to 1.01–1.05× at harmonics 3–5 and to 2.7× at the fundamental, which the training settings raise to 5.7× while improving Dyn. PSNR. OffBeat is at 3.4× at the fundamental, within STG’s range, but 1.1× at the fifth harmonic, and on Flame Salmon lacks STG’s single-frame stripes (Fig. 4, top). Gaussian windows in place of the period window raise the fundamental power on all six scenes, to 1.58× OffBeat’s (Sec. S7).

    5 Conclusion

    We presented OffBeat, a 4D capture method that models a staggered rig as a multicoset sampler to follow motion a synchronized rig misses. Under this model, a position-ordered row confounds depth with motion, the calibration alone yields a schedule, and temporal windows weighting all groups equally for every K last at least T, a bound our closed-form period window satisfies. On N3DV, OffBeat outperforms the full 4DSloMo pipeline in dynamic-region and full-frame PSNR on every test frame. Between the first and last synchronized frame, it follows motion better on average than a synchronized rig of equal camera frame rate, which is better at its own frames. On PanopticSports, in the same range, OffBeat is comparable in PSNR to synchronized capture with interpolation.

    Limitations and Future Work.

    We simulate staggered capture by subsampling 30 fps video, and the schedule needs calibration before capture. On 4DSloMo’s real staggered recording, we test only the lifetime floor, in its reconstruction stage, and find no reliable gain. In that stage, the period window as used on STG lowers dynamic-region PSNR on an N3DV validation scene (Sec. S5). OffBeat is more sensitive than synchronized STG to simulated trigger-time and photometric errors, which a real rig adds (Secs. S7 and S8). Estimating trigger times and gains during reconstruction could lower this sensitivity. Content shorter than T cannot be represented, and the fastest motion between a group’s firings stays blurred. OffBeat fails on Juggle at one PanopticSports camera (Sec. S6).

    LLM Usage Statement

    The authors chose the research problem and the core method and directed the use of Claude (Anthropic) through the Claude Code agent. Claude wrote and reviewed the experiment code, ran and monitored the experiments, computed the statistics, kept an append-only experiment log, and drafted the text and figures, including this statement. The simulated views of the velocity test in Sec. S4 were generated with code written by Claude. The authors approved each experiment plan before it was run, read every result, and edited the text. Gemini (Google) was used only to critique drafts. The authors are fully responsible for the content.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：同步多相机在同一批时间戳取帧，中间的运动就永远丢了。

要点：

  • 物理限制：4D 重建用的同步多相机阵列**在同一批时间戳取帧**，因此错过了帧与帧之间的运动
  • 已有对策是**错峰触发**：把同样多的帧分散到更多时间戳上。但如果一排相机依次触发（如 4DSloMo 在 N3DV 上的排程），**整排会被当成一台移动相机**，从而把深度与运动混在一起
  • OffBeat 因此把错峰阵列建模成一个**空间分布的多集（multicoset）采样器**，从采样理论出发解掉这个混淆，把有效时间分辨率推到相机帧率之上

为什么值得看：「采集端提采样率」是拿到高质量 4D 数据的另一条路——不靠生成模型补帧，而靠触发时序。这对需要做真实动作参考、或者训练世界模型的团队，是从源头改善数据的手段。

中文摘要：用于 4D 重建的同步多相机阵列会在同一批时间戳上取帧，因此帧与帧之间的运动信息被永久丢失。一种对策是错峰触发——把相同数量的帧分散到更多的时间戳上；但当一排相机依次触发时（如 4DSloMo 在 Neural 3D Video 阵列上的排程），整排相机看起来就像一台移动的相机，从而把深度与运动混为一谈。OffBeat 把错峰阵列建模为一个在空间上分布的多集（multicoset）采样器，从采样理论出发消解这种混淆，使有效时间分辨率超过相机自身的帧率。对需要高质量真实动作参考、或要训练世界模型的团队，这是从采集环节改善数据的手段。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-20

本期推送：2026-11-22

OffBeat: Multicoset Sampling for 4D Capture
Beyond the Camera Frame Rate

Abstract

For 4D reconstruction, a synchronized multi-camera rig records all views at the same timestamps and misses the motion between them. Staggered triggers spread the same frames over more timestamps. However, when the cameras along each row fire one after another, as in 4DSloMo’s schedule on the Neural 3D Video (N3DV) rig, the row acts as one moving camera that confounds depth with motion. We introduce OffBeat, which models a staggered rig as a spatially distributed multicoset sampler: shifted copies of one sampling grid. From the calibration alone, OffBeat derives camera groups that fire together and their firing order. Since one group records each timestamp, a short-lived primitive can fit an error its cameras share, such as a color offset, and flicker in novel views. We show that a primitive’s opacity over time weights all groups equally, for every number of groups, only if it lasts at least one camera frame interval. On Spacetime Gaussians, a minimum lifetime approximates this bound, and a closed-form smoothed box of that length satisfies it exactly, with less flicker than a Gaussian in its place at nearly equal PSNR. In simulated staggered capture on N3DV, OffBeat outperforms the full 4DSloMo pipeline with video diffusion on every test frame, by 3.04 dB in mean dynamic-region PSNR. Between the first and last synchronized frame, it outperforms the best synchronized method of each scene, with or without frame interpolation, by 1.98 dB in mean dynamic-region PSNR, while synchronized capture is better at its own frames. On PanopticSports, in this frame range, OffBeat is comparable in PSNR to synchronized capture with interpolation. On every N3DV scene, replacing 4DSloMo’s schedule with ours raises the dynamic-region PSNR of Spacetime Gaussians, 4DSloMo without diffusion, and our reconstruction. Multi-camera rigs could follow faster motion at the same frame count by changing only when each camera fires.

††footnotetext: Emails: {levi74108520963, kylechen.ankai, faidavid7, changg587}@gmail.com, kuopc@cs.nthu.edu.tw

1 Introduction

4D reconstruction from multi-view video [20, 22, 47] still fails on fast non-rigid motion, such as a flame, a hand turning food, or a ball leaving a hand. One cause is temporal sampling: in a synchronized rig, all N cameras record at the same timestamps, once every camera frame interval T. Adding cameras adds views of these timestamps and leaves the temporal bandwidth at 1/(2T). A higher frame rate costs resolution, exposure, storage and link bandwidth.

Staggered triggers fire the cameras in K groups spaced T/K apart, which spreads the same number of frames over K times as many timestamps (Fig. OffBeat: Multicoset Sampling for 4D Capture
Beyond the Camera Frame Rate). For nearly co-located cameras this is the classic high-speed array [46, 37, 1], and in a dense array staggered triggers sampled the video light field better than synchronized ones [46]. 4DSloMo [9] staggers a multi-view rig to raise its effective frame rate and repairs sparse-view artifacts at each timestamp with a 14B-parameter video diffusion model.

On the Neural 3D Video rig (N3DV) [20], the modular schedule of 4DSloMo, which gives camera k the offset (k\bmodK) T/K, fires each of the two camera rows in position order. Within a camera frame interval, such a row acts as one camera moving at constant speed: regardless of row size, a static point is indistinguishable from a moving point at another depth (Sec. 3.2, Fig. 2a).

We model a staggered rig as a spatially distributed multicoset sampler [28, 41]: cameras that fire together form a trigger group and sample at the camera frame rate on a shifted copy of one grid. As in multichannel sampling, a point whose motion is band-limited to half the effective frame rate K/T is identifiable if every group triangulates it (Sec. 3.1). Single-camera groups, as on N3DV, cannot triangulate; a motion model over one camera frame interval pools them. From the calibration alone, we choose the groups by how well the others triangulate, and their order by the predictive variance of novel views (Sec. 3.2).

The reconstruction faces a second problem: as each timestamp is recorded by a single group, an error its cameras share, such as a color or calibration offset, is fit exactly by spurious content present only at those timestamps, which a novel view sees as flicker at the camera frame rate (Sec. 3.3). A primitive can supply such content in every period only if its temporal opacity window, summed over copies one period apart, weights the groups unequally. We show that the windows weighting all groups equally for any number of groups and at any center are exactly the convolutions of a box of length T (Prop. 1). Hence a primitive’s lifetime (its window’s duration) is at least T rather than the trigger spacing T/K, while its motion is sampled at the effective frame rate. On Spacetime Gaussians (STG) [22], a lifetime floor approximates this bound, and a closed-form period window, a smoothed box, satisfies it exactly (Sec. 3.4).

In summary, we make the following contributions:

  • •

    We introduce OffBeat, which models a staggered rig as a spatially distributed multicoset sampler, and show that a position-ordered row confounds depth with motion.

  • •

    From the calibration alone, we derive which cameras fire together and in which order.

  • •

    We show that temporal windows weighting all groups equally for every K must last at least T, and derive a closed-form period window that satisfies this bound.

  • •

    In simulated staggered capture on N3DV, OffBeat outperforms the full 4DSloMo pipeline and follows motion between synchronized frames better on average than a synchronized rig of equal camera frame rate, which is better at its own frames. On PanopticSports, up to the last synchronized frame, OffBeat is comparable in PSNR to synchronized capture with interpolation.

    • 2 Related Work

    Staggered and unsynchronized capture.

    In high-speed arrays of nearly co-located cameras [46, 37, 1], the firing order is a design parameter [46]. Color-coded illumination yields high-speed 3D under controlled light [27]. Methods for unsynchronized video treat the time offsets as nuisances under smoothness priors [3, 29, 42, 52], estimate them [8, 2, 15, 48, 19, 53], or recover structure and motion from asynchronous tracks [11, 39]. 4DSloMo [9] staggers a rig with a modular schedule.

    Multichannel sampling.

    In multichannel sampling, K channels at 1/K of the Nyquist rate recover a band-limited signal [28, 41]. Parallel MRI shares this structure [30, 40], and CAIPIRINHA [7] shifts the sampling pattern such that aliases fall where the coil sensitivities differ. Our ordering criterion plays this role for cameras by decorrelating the trigger offsets from the camera positions.

    4D Gaussians and sampling-aware representations.

    Dynamic extensions of Gaussian splatting [13] use deformation fields [47], native 4D primitives [49], per-Gaussian trajectories with temporal opacity [22, 18, 45], or tracked Gaussians [24]. RetimeGS [44] and SPIN-4DGS [16] target temporal aliasing and large displacements between synchronized frames. Mip-Splatting [50] bounds the 3D frequency of a primitive by the sampling rate of the training views, and our lifetime bound is its temporal counterpart. SharpTimeGS [23] learns a flat-top lifespan for each primitive to balance static and dynamic content, whereas our window’s box has the derived length T.

    3 Method

    3.1 Staggered rigs as multicoset samplers

    Each of the N training cameras records a frame once every camera frame interval T. Camera k fires at its trigger offset φₖ, and a synchronized rig has all offsets zero. A K-group stagger fires the cameras Sₚ of group p at the offset pT/K. All triggers form the joint grid of spacing T/K, whose rate K/T is the effective frame rate of the rig [9]. Each instant of this grid is recorded by one group alone.

    Camera k observes a scene point x through its 2×3 projection Jacobian Dₖ, with Fisher information Gₖ=Dₖ^⊤Dₖ/σ² for pixel noise σ. Gₖ has rank two, and its null space is the viewing ray ℓₖ. Group p has the information Hₚ=∑_k∈SₚGₖ. A single group cannot separate frequencies that differ by a multiple of the camera frame rate. The K such frequencies inside the band of the joint grid form an alias set, and the Fourier coefficients of x(t) there are its alias components; each group observes its own phase-weighted sum of them. For a trajectory band-limited to the Nyquist frequency of the joint grid, the Fisher information of its Fourier coefficients is block-diagonal over alias sets, with blocks built from the Hₚ, as in multichannel sampling [28, 30].

    We prove two properties of this structure in Sec. S1 of the supplementary material. First, in a synchronized rig the data depend on the trajectory only through alias sums, for any number of cameras, so adding synchronized cameras leaves the temporal bandwidth at 1/(2T). Second, in a K-group stagger, a trajectory with K alias components per set is identifiable if and only if every group triangulates, Hₚ\succ0, i.e. has two cameras with non-parallel rays to the point. When every group triangulates, staggering thus raises the temporal bandwidth K-fold. With N<2K, some groups have one camera and cannot triangulate.

    A motion model over one camera frame interval pools all groups. Let a point’s position over this period T be a degree-J polynomial in time d with coefficients θ∈ℝ^3(J+1), and let camera k see it at dₖ. The Fisher information of θ is then ∑ₖb(dₖ)b(dₖ)^⊤⊗Gₖ with b(d)=(1,d,…,d^J). For J≥1, it is singular in a synchronized rig and nonsingular once J+1 groups triangulate (Sec. S1). A polynomial per period replaces the K alias components by J+1 shared coefficients, as in trajectory triangulation [3, 29] and spatiotemporal bundle adjustment [42].

    3.2 Trigger schedule

    Position-ordered triggers.

    The trigger order leaves the identifiability condition of Sec. 3.1 unchanged but can undo the gain of staggering. Let cameras with centers oₖ=o₀+sₖe on a line each fire once, at tₖ=t₀+αsₖ with α≠0, and let a point move as X(t)=X₀+v(t-t₀). For every λ>0, the point with X₀^′=o₀+λ(X₀-o₀) and v^′=λv+(1-λ)e/α has the same image in every camera. The Fisher information of (X₀,v) from one such sweep is singular for any number of cameras (proof in Sec. S3). The sweep thus confounds depth with motion, turning parallax into apparent motion (Fig. 2a). This is the ambiguity of a camera and a point both moving at constant velocity [26, 3, 29], and of a slowly moving camera [10]; in a rig, the schedule decides whether it arises. Repeated sweeps resolve it only for points keeping their velocity over several periods, unlike fast non-rigid motion. On N3DV, where the modular schedule sweeps both rows (Sec. S3), only their vertical offset keeps the information nonsingular.

    Grouping.

    The partition into groups sets the information Hₚ of each instant, on which identifiability depends. With N3DV’s 17 to 20 training cameras in 12 groups, at least four groups have a single camera under any partition, and the motion model pools them. Over the other groups, we maximize meanₚλₚ+1/2\minₚλₚ, where λₚ is the working-volume average of the smallest eigenvalue of Hₚ (Sec. S3).

    Ordering.

    For a point moving at constant velocity v over one period centered at μ and seen once per camera, pooling with J=1 gives the information of (x, vT/2),

    I(μ)=∑ₖ\beginbmatrix1&dₖ dₖ&dₖ²\endbmatrix⊗Gₖ, dₖ=(\wrap(φₖ-μ))/(T/2),

    		(1)

    where dₖ∈[-1,1) is the wrapped trigger offset from μ in half periods. For novel views, we minimize \max_u,tV+1/2 mean_u,tV with the predictive variance

    V(u,t)=𝔼_μ,x\tr(Qᵤ A I(μ)⁻¹A^⊤), A=[I, τI],

    		(2)

    where τ is the wrapped offset of a trigger instant t from μ in half periods, Qᵤ is the information of a virtual view u midway between neighboring training cameras, and the expectation is over centers μ in one period and working-volume points x. Grouping and ordering follow the E- and G-optimality criteria of optimal design [14, 31], respectively. A local search optimizes them in seconds on a CPU (Alg. S1). Both need only the calibration; their weights 1/2 hardly affect \maxV (Sec. S3). The modular schedule’s \maxV per N3DV scene is 2.2–2.4 times ours.

    3.3 Lifetime bound

    Camera–time confound.

    Any error common to a group’s views, such as a calibration or exposure error of a single-camera group, can be explained exactly by content present only when that group fires. If each group has its own error at a pixel, such as a color offset, the periodic signal h that equals the firing group’s error reproduces it in every training image. In a synchronized rig, h is constant. A test camera belongs to no group and sees h as flicker at the camera frame rate and its harmonics (Fig. 4, Sec. 4.4). On N3DV, one or two cameras see each instant, so this explanation is always available.

    Window condition.

    Primitive i with temporal center μᵢ and window w(t-μᵢ), such as STG’s temporal opacity [22], gives group p the total weight

    Ωₚ(μᵢ)=∑ₘw(\tfracpTK+mT-μᵢ)=(Π_Tw)(\tfracpTK-μᵢ),

    		(3)

    where Π_Tw sums the copies of w shifted by whole periods (Fig. 2b). If Π_Tw varies, primitives can, for some K, weight the groups unequally and supply h. Prop. 1 (proof in Sec. S1) characterizes the windows that prevent this.

    Proposition 1.

    For a compactly supported window w, the following are equivalent: (a) Ωₚ(μ) is independent of p for every center μ and every K. (b) ŵ(j/T)=0 for every integer j≠0, with ŵ the Fourier transform of w. (c) For any centers μᵢ and amplitudes bᵢ, Π_T∑ᵢbᵢw(·-μᵢ) is constant, so no set of primitives weights the groups unequally. (d) w=box_T*g for a compactly supported distribution g, with box_T=1_[-T/2,T/2). No such window is shorter than T, and the shortest ones are shifted multiples of box_T.

    Prop. 1 thus bounds a primitive’s lifetime below by T but leaves its motion sampled at K/T. Condition (b) is the partition-of-unity or Strang–Fix condition [38] at scale T, and (d) is the order-one case of the B-spline factorization [4]. The condition constrains the weights summed over all periods, over which a persistent single-camera error recurs, and leaves those within one period free.

    3.4 Reconstruction on STG

    We build on STG [22] and keep its loss and renderer. Each STG primitive i has a temporal center μᵢ and scale aᵢ with temporal opacity \exp(-(d/aᵢ)²) at d=t-μᵢ, polynomial motion and rotation, and time-dependent features.

    Lifetime floor.

    Gaussian windows violate Prop. 1(b). Wide ones have little power at the harmonics j/T (Sec. S1), but narrow ones can favor one group. Rendering with the temporal scale √aᵢ²+a_\min² in place of aᵢ, with a_\min=T/4, passes at most 29% of the power at the camera frame rate and under 1% at higher harmonics.

    Period window.

    Since Π_Tbox_T=1, Prop. 1(d)⇒(c) holds for any integrable g, and a Gaussian g gives

    wᵢ(t)=(\erf((d+T/2)/aᵢ)-\erf((d-T/2)/aᵢ))/(2 \erf(T/(2aᵢ))).

    		(4)

    For every center and scale, the period window meets the condition with no added parameter, gradients flow through the closed form, and it tends to the box window as aᵢ→0. We keep the floor on aᵢ because the window’s gradient with respect to its center concentrates at the edges, and the floor spreads it from one to most of the 12 groups (Sec. S1).

    Polynomial motion inside a window can reintroduce group-dependent components of h that Prop. 1(c) excludes for constant amplitudes, so we rescale STG’s velocity to the displacement over half a window (Sec. S2).

    Training.

    Two settings keep any update from depending on one group alone. With per-image timestamps, the timestamp is drawn per image, not per batch as in STG. With no opacity reset, the few cameras of one timestamp never have to re-estimate all opacities alone. We call STG with the floor and these two settings the floor variant.

    Densification.

    Every training camera fires once in the period centered at t₀. For a small opaque primitive moving along x+v(t-t₀) with a period window centered at t₀, let rₖ be the residual at the pixel it covers in camera k when this camera fires. For a locally constant render, the primitive’s best color lowers the squared error by Γ(x,v,t₀)=|∑ₖrₖ|²/N. This is the shift-and-stack statistic of track-before-detect [33] and, to first order in the opacity, the dual certificate of conditional gradient on measures [6, 5]. A residual r shared by m cameras scores m²|r|²/N, so errors common to one group (Sec. 3.3) rank low (Fig. 2c). Instead of STG’s guided sampling along high-error rays, we add primitives at the maxima of Γ over depth and lateral velocity (Alg. S2), keeping STG’s cloning and splitting. Other methods densify by gradients or errors [13, 35, 43, 25], temporal visibility [36], or appearance change [34].

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Setup

    Data and protocol.

    N3DV [20] contains six dynamic scenes. We hold out camera 0 for testing and train on the other 17–20 cameras. Following 4DSloMo [9], we subsample each 30 fps video to every 12th frame (2.5 fps), with a separate offset per camera for staggered capture and a common one for synchronized capture. We report test frames 100–159 unless stated otherwise and validate on frames 40–99 of Flame Steak and Cook Spinach. PanopticSports [12, 24] has 27 training and 4 test cameras, and we use six sequences with test frames 0–59 and K=12, validating on frames 90–149 of Softball and Basketball. Each method is trained once per scene, and Sec. S6 reports three seeds.

    Compared methods.

    For synchronized capture, we train STG and STG + interpolation, STG trained on videos in which AMT [21] fills the 11 frames between synchronized frames. RetimeGS [44], for which we found no public code, reports this recipe with FILM [32] as its strongest N3DV baseline, 0.05 dB below its own result. For staggered capture, we compare OffBeat with STG, also trained with twice the iterations, and with 4DSloMo [9], using its official code and settings. We run its reconstruction stage, a native 4D Gaussian model [49], on both schedules and on the synchronized frames of N3DV (where it is weaker than STG); we run its full pipeline with video diffusion on all six N3DV scenes (Sec. S5). All STG-based methods share the initialization, renderer and clock alignment (Sec. S8) and are trained for 10k iterations unless stated otherwise. OffBeat trains in 423–481 s per scene on one RTX 4090.

    Metrics.

    At the test view, we report PSNR, AlexNet LPIPS [51] and dynamic-region PSNR (Dyn. PSNR, as in FreeTimeGS [45]); Sec. S6 reports SSIM. Dynamic pixels are those whose ground-truth luma has a temporal standard deviation above 0.05 over the 60 test frames, dilated by 5 px. Per scene and metric, the best synchronized method is the strongest of STG, STG + interpolation, the floor variant and, on N3DV, our reconstruction, all from synchronized capture. Sec. S6 gives per-scene results with paired bootstrap intervals [17]. Over 20 pairs of mask threshold and dilation, OffBeat’s Dyn. PSNR difference keeps its sign against synchronized STG, STG + interpolation, STG on our schedule (except on PanopticSports) and the floor variant (negative on PanopticSports; Sec. S6).

    4.2 N3DV

    Staggered against synchronized capture.

    Between the first and last synchronized frame, OffBeat outperforms the best synchronized method by 1.98 dB in mean Dyn. PSNR (Table 1, Fig. 3) and on five of six scenes (Sec. S6). At the five synchronized frames, the better of STG and STG + interpolation in each scene is 1.23 dB above OffBeat in Dyn. PSNR but 2.20 dB below on the 44 frames in between (Sec. S6). In Fig. 5, interpolation flattens the traces, the modular schedule fragments them, and STG on our schedule adds single-frame streaks. 4DSloMo’s reconstruction stage is sharp but jitters, and its slice PSNR on Flame Steak is higher than ours. OffBeat follows the trajectories.

    Training length and camera frame rate.

    Synchronized STG trained twice as long remains 3.66 dB below OffBeat in Dyn. PSNR (Sec. S6). With the official 30k iterations for both, OffBeat outperforms STG + interpolation between the first and last synchronized frame by 2.29 dB in Dyn. PSNR on N3DV and by 0.99 dB on PanopticSports (Sec. S8). With twice the camera frame rate (5 fps), synchronized STG is still 1.02 dB below OffBeat at 2.5 fps between its first and last synchronized frame. At 10 fps it is 0.36 dB better there, and at 30 fps it is 0.60 dB better over all test frames, or 1.20 dB if it alone gets 30k iterations (Sec. S6).

    Schedule.

    With our reconstruction, replacing our schedule by the modular one lowers Dyn. PSNR by 1.29 dB and PSNR by 0.46 dB. It also lowers the Dyn. PSNR of STG and of the 4DSloMo reconstruction stage by 1.02 and 2.42 dB. On N3DV, 48 stratified random schedules with our group sizes are 0.39 dB below ours on average, recovering 69% of the modular schedule’s loss. Our two criteria rank them only weakly, and three of them outperform ours (Sec. S3).

    4DSloMo.

    The full 4DSloMo pipeline, with its own schedule, is 3.04 dB below OffBeat in Dyn. PSNR and 4.35 dB in PSNR over all six scenes (Table 1, Fig. 6). Its diffusion stage (about a day per scene) raises the Dyn. PSNR of its own reconstruction stage by 2.03 dB; our run of that stage matches it within 0.09 dB on average. Sec. S5 relates 4DSloMo’s published 33.48 dB to our protocol.

    4.3 PanopticSports

    On PanopticSports, the 27 training cameras form groups of two or three, each triangulating (Sec. 3.1). Between the first and last synchronized frame (frames 0–48, Sec. S6), OffBeat outperforms synchronized STG by 1.30 dB in Dyn. PSNR and is on par in Dyn. PSNR and PSNR with STG + interpolation. In this range, synchronized STG is slightly better in LPIPS, and STG + interpolation is better in full-frame and dynamic-region SSIM on every sequence. In Table 2, 4DSloMo’s reconstruction stage is 0.68 dB lower in Dyn. PSNR and 3.69 dB in PSNR (Fig. 7), but better in Dyn. PSNR on Softball and Tennis, where OffBeat blurs the arms, bat and racket. At camera 0, the gain comes from staggering: unlike on N3DV, OffBeat is on par with STG on our schedule and its floor variant (Sec. S6). At the other three test cameras, OffBeat outperforms STG on our schedule on 13 of the 18 sequence–camera pairs in Dyn. PSNR. In frames 0–48, against the best synchronized method, it is on par or better in Dyn. PSNR and PSNR on 15 and 13 pairs but worse in LPIPS on 7 (Sec. S6).

    4.4 Analysis

    Ablation study.

    In Table 3, staggering raises the Dyn. PSNR of STG from 24.33 to 26.07 dB on the modular schedule and to 27.09 dB on ours. Most of the further gain comes from the lifetime floor (Prop. 1, 0.29 dB) and from per-image timestamps with no opacity reset (0.34 dB). The period window with our densification adds 0.17 dB, which comes from Flame Steak and Cook Spinach, whose frames 40–99 we used for validation. On the other four scenes, OffBeat is 0.07 dB below the floor variant in Dyn. PSNR but still outperforms the best synchronized method by 2.66 dB and STG on our schedule by 0.66 dB (Sec. S6). Under the same floor, Gaussian windows are on par in Dyn. PSNR and better in PSNR (0.05 dB) and LPIPS, whereas STG’s guided sampling in place of our densification lowers Dyn. PSNR by 0.27 dB. In Dyn. PSNR, no component helps synchronized capture: the floor variant and our reconstruction differ from STG by -0.17 and -0.54 dB (Sec. S6).

    Flicker at the camera frame rate.

    On static pixels (Fig. 4, bottom), STG on our schedule has 3.0–3.7× the residual power of synchronized STG at the first five harmonics. The lifetime floor alone lowers this to 1.01–1.05× at harmonics 3–5 and to 2.7× at the fundamental, which the training settings raise to 5.7× while improving Dyn. PSNR. OffBeat is at 3.4× at the fundamental, within STG’s range, but 1.1× at the fifth harmonic, and on Flame Salmon lacks STG’s single-frame stripes (Fig. 4, top). Gaussian windows in place of the period window raise the fundamental power on all six scenes, to 1.58× OffBeat’s (Sec. S7).

    5 Conclusion

    We presented OffBeat, a 4D capture method that models a staggered rig as a multicoset sampler to follow motion a synchronized rig misses. Under this model, a position-ordered row confounds depth with motion, the calibration alone yields a schedule, and temporal windows weighting all groups equally for every K last at least T, a bound our closed-form period window satisfies. On N3DV, OffBeat outperforms the full 4DSloMo pipeline in dynamic-region and full-frame PSNR on every test frame. Between the first and last synchronized frame, it follows motion better on average than a synchronized rig of equal camera frame rate, which is better at its own frames. On PanopticSports, in the same range, OffBeat is comparable in PSNR to synchronized capture with interpolation.

    Limitations and Future Work.

    We simulate staggered capture by subsampling 30 fps video, and the schedule needs calibration before capture. On 4DSloMo’s real staggered recording, we test only the lifetime floor, in its reconstruction stage, and find no reliable gain. In that stage, the period window as used on STG lowers dynamic-region PSNR on an N3DV validation scene (Sec. S5). OffBeat is more sensitive than synchronized STG to simulated trigger-time and photometric errors, which a real rig adds (Secs. S7 and S8). Estimating trigger times and gains during reconstruction could lower this sensitivity. Content shorter than T cannot be represented, and the fastest motion between a group’s firings stays blurred. OffBeat fails on Juggle at one PanopticSports camera (Sec. S6).

    LLM Usage Statement

    The authors chose the research problem and the core method and directed the use of Claude (Anthropic) through the Claude Code agent. Claude wrote and reviewed the experiment code, ran and monitored the experiments, computed the statistics, kept an append-only experiment log, and drafted the text and figures, including this statement. The simulated views of the velocity test in Sec. S4 were generated with code written by Claude. The authors approved each experiment plan before it was run, read every result, and edited the text. Gemini (Google) was used only to critique drafts. The authors are fully responsible for the content.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 要「潜空间省算力」又要「像素级无损」：这篇不去改扩散模型，而是找一个无损变换 ｜ Lossless Latent Diffusion Models
item.description:
一句话：以往做法是直接在像素空间建模，代价是要改训练目标或架构。

要点：

  • 要解决的矛盾：既要训练扩散模型，又要**保持像素级精确重建**（lossless）
  • 以往的做法是直接在像素空间建模，但这需要**修改扩散训练目标或模型架构**
  • 这篇换了范式：不去改扩散模型，而是构造一个**无损变换**，把像素映射到「更适合扩散建模」的表示上再训练

为什么值得看：潜空间的算力优势与像素空间的保真优势长期二选一。用「无损变换」替代「有损 VAE」，等于把这道选择题拆开——它与 11-21 Direct3D-V3（直接放弃潜空间）、11-19 DWD（去掉解码器）是同一问题的第三种答案。

中文摘要：这篇研究如何在训练图像扩散模型的同时保持像素级精确重建。以往的做法通常是在像素空间直接建模，代价是需要修改扩散的训练目标或模型架构。作者换了一个范式：不去修改扩散模型本身，而是构造一个无损变换，把像素映射到一种更适合扩散建模的表示上，再在该表示上训练。这样既保留了潜在表示的建模效率，又避免了有损压缩带来的重建误差。与直接放弃潜空间、或去掉解码器的做法相比，这是「潜空间无损化」的第三条路。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-20

本期推送：2026-11-22

Lossless Latent Diffusion Models

Abstract

We study the problem of training image diffusion models while preserving pixel-exact reconstruction. Prior works typically address this problem by directly modeling images in pixel space, requiring modifications to the diffusion training objective or model architecture. In this work, we introduce a different paradigm: rather than modifying diffusion models, we construct a lossless transformation that maps pixels into a representation more amenable to diffusion modeling. We term our approach the Lossless Latent Diffusion Model (LLDM). We construct LLDM using residual latent transformation and uneven latent scaling, and explain its effectiveness through a proposed metric, semantic rank priority (SRP). Empirically, LLDM substantially outperforms prior pixel-space diffusion models in generation quality and even surpasses several widely used lossy VAEs. Furthermore, we show that SRP is strongly correlated with downstream generative performance.

1 Introduction

Training diffusion models directly in pixel space is appealing because it avoids the reconstruction errors introduced by variational autoencoders (VAEs). However, pixel-space diffusion is shown to be challenging for high-quality image generation, partly due to the high intrinsic dimensionality of the pixel-space data manifold [25, 20]. Recent advances in pixel-space diffusion have primarily addressed this challenge by modifying either the training procedure or the diffusion model itself. The former introduces auxiliary objectives, such as finetuning from latent diffusion [20], x-prediction [25], perceptual losses [29], and DINO feature losses [2]. The latter develops architectures tailored to pixel-space modelling, including pixel-field parameterization [39] and hierarchical architectures [48, 36, 28].

In contrast, latent diffusion models (LDMs) [31] simplify diffusion modeling by mapping images into lower-dimensional representations using lossy VAEs. This improves modeling efficiency at the cost of reconstruction fidelity. Early LDM research therefore focused on improving VAE reconstruction quality [12]. However, recent studies have identified a “reconstruction–generation trade-off”: better reconstruction fidelity does not necessarily translate into better downstream generation quality [45]. This has motivated efforts to learn more diffusion-friendly representations through foundation-model alignment or signal-processing-based transformations [47, 50, 45].

In this paper, we propose a different paradigm for diffusion models with pixel-exact reconstruction: rather than modifying diffusion models to facilitate pixel-space generation, we construct a lossless transformation that maps pixels into a representation more amenable to diffusion modeling. Specifically, we introduce the Lossless LDM (LLDM), which reorganizes image information into a diffusion-friendly latent representation while preserving pixel-exact reconstruction. Unlike existing pixel-space diffusion approaches, LLDM requires no modifications to the diffusion model architecture, training objective, or optimization procedure, enabling direct integration into standard latent diffusion frameworks. We construct the lossless transformation through residual decomposition and uneven latent scaling, and propose semantic rank priority (SRP) as a metric to explain its effectiveness. Experiments on ImageNet [8] class-to-image and Diffusion-Bench [24] text-to-image benchmarks show that LLDM substantially outperforms prior pixel-space diffusion methods and even several lossy VAEs in generation quality. Furthermore, SRP effectively predicts downstream generative performance.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We introduce LLDM, a new paradigm for diffusion modeling with pixel-exact reconstruction. LLDM maps images into diffusion-friendly representations through a lossless transformation while preserving the standard LDM training pipeline.

  • •

    We develop a practical lossless transformation based on residual decomposition and uneven latent scaling, and propose semantic rank priority (SRP) as a metric to explain its effectiveness.

  • •

    Empirically, LLDM outperforms prior pixel-space diffusion models in generation quality while guaranteeing pixel-exact reconstruction. Furthermore, SRP effectively predicts downstream generative performance.

    • 2 Preliminaries

    2.1 Pixel Diffusion Models

    Let x∼p_data(x) denote an image sampled from the data distribution. Pixel diffusion models directly model this distribution in pixel space by progressively perturbing x with Gaussian noise over time t∈[0,T]. Given a noise schedule defined by αₜ and σₜ, the marginal forward distribution is

    q(xₜ|x)=ℕ(αₜx,σₜ²I).

    		(1)

    The reverse process is described by a reverse-time stochastic differential equation (SDE) [1]. Sampling proceeds by simulating this SDE from t=T to t=0[35], requiring an estimate of the score function ∇_xₜ\logqₜ(xₜ). Accordingly, a score network s_θ(xₜ,t) is trained to approximate this function using the denoising score matching (DSM) objective [38]:

    L_DSM=𝔼[∥s_θ(xₜ,t)-∇_xₜ\logq(xₜ|x)∥₂²].

    		(2)

    Despite its conceptual simplicity, modeling natural images directly in pixel space remains challenging. Recent methods address this through improved training objectives and regularization [25, 29, 2], or architectures tailored to pixel-space generation [48, 36, 28]. In contrast, our approach preserves both the diffusion objective and model architecture, instead mapping images into a lossless representation that is easier for diffusion models to learn.

    2.2 Latent Diffusion Models

    Latent diffusion models (LDMs) [32] address the challenge of modeling high-dimensional pixel distributions by performing diffusion in a learned latent space. Specifically, an LDM first trains a lossy variational autoencoder (VAE) [21] to map images into compact latent representations. Given an image x, an encoder f(·) maps it to a latent z, on which the diffusion model is trained. During generation, the sampled latent z is mapped back to pixel space by a decoder g(·):

    Encode: z=f(x), Decode: x̂=g(z).

    		(3)

    By performing diffusion in a compact latent space, LDMs simplify generative modeling and enable efficient, high-quality image generation. However, conventional LDMs employ lossy VAEs, where g(f(x))≠x in general. Information discarded during encoding cannot be recovered, preventing pixel-exact reconstruction. This limitation is particularly undesirable for reconstruction-sensitive applications, such as image editing and restoration, where preserving the original image information is critical.

    3 Lossless Latent Diffusion Model

    In this section, we explore how to construct a lossless representation for latent diffusion. Our goal is to transform data x into a representation that enables pixel-exact reconstruction while remaining as easy for diffusion models to learn as the latent space of a lossy VAE. We start with a simple lossless construction that yields poor generation quality, then progressively introduce designs to improve latent diffusibility.

    3.1 Lossless Transformation via Residual Decomposition

    We begin with a simple lossless transformation. Given a pretrained lossy VAE with encoder f(·) and decoder g(·), we preserve the information lost during reconstruction through a residual:

    r=x-g(z), z=f(x).

    		(4)

    We construct a new latent representation ẑ=[z,r] by concatenating the lossy latent z and residual r along the channel dimension, after spatially rearranging r to match the resolution of z. The encoding and decoding processes are:

    Encode: z=f(x), r=x-g(z), ẑ=[z,r],

    Decode: [z,r]=ẑ, x=g(z)+r.

    		(5)

    By construction, the original image can be recovered exactly from ẑ without reconstruction error. This provides a simple way to convert any pretrained lossy VAE into a lossless representation without modifying its encoder or decoder. However, losslessness does not guarantee suitability for diffusion. As shown in Table 3, modeling ẑ=[z,r] is substantially more challenging than modeling the original lossy latent z, resulting in significantly worse generation quality. This motivates us to reorganize the residual information into a more diffusion-friendly representation.

    3.2 Lossless Transformation via Uneven Latent Scaling

    A common practice in latent diffusion models is to normalize latent channels to comparable scales before diffusion training, which we refer to as even latent scaling. However, our lossless latent ẑ=[z,r] has a heterogeneous structure. For a VAE with high reconstruction quality, the lossy latent z captures most perceptually and semantically important image content, while r preserves the remaining information required for pixel-exact reconstruction. Treating these components equally during diffusion training may therefore be suboptimal.

    One solution is to assign different loss weights or training schedules to different latent components [15, 6]. However, this requires modifying the diffusion training objective or procedure. Instead, we preserve the standard LDM pipeline and modify only the latent transformation. Specifically, we propose uneven latent scaling, which scales the residual by a factor γ before diffusion training:

    Encode: z=f(x), r̄=γ(x-g(z)), ẑ=[z,r̄],

    Decode: [z,r̄]=ẑ, x=g(z)+(r̄)/(γ).

    		(6)

    Choosing γ<1 reduces the residual scale relative to the lossy latent z, encouraging the diffusion model to prioritize the dominant image representation while preserving all information required for exact reconstruction. Importantly, this scaling is invertible, as the original residual can be recovered by dividing by γ during decoding. Thus, uneven latent scaling requires no modifications to the diffusion architecture or training objective.

    Normalizing flows [10, 11] use invertible transformations to map data into simpler distributions. In principle, an invertible neural network h_θ(·) can also serve as an autoencoder:

    \textupEncode: ẑ=h_θ(x), \textupDecode: x=h⁻¹_θ(ẑ).

    		(7)

    However, as shown in Table 1, maximum-likelihood training of normalizing flows yields worse generation quality than pixel-space diffusion. Aligning flow representations with DINO features mitigates this issue but sacrifices invertibility [7]. Like normalizing flows, our lossless transformation uses basic operations such as channel splitting, concatenation, and scaling. Nevertheless, learning an invertible transformation optimized end-to-end for diffusion modeling remains an open challenge.

    3.4 Understanding LLDM Through Semantic Rank Priority

    To understand why LLDM works and how lossless transformations improve latent diffusibility, we investigate the properties that make latent representations suitable for diffusion. Prior studies have shown that latent diffusibility strongly correlates with semantic separability, measured by linear classification accuracy on ImageNet [44, 51]. However, linear classification accuracy cannot explain the effectiveness of LLDM, as it is invariant to invertible linear transformations. Consequently, it remains unchanged under uneven latent scaling.

    To address this limitation and better understand the effectiveness of LLDM, we refine the linear classification accuracy metric and propose semantic rank priority (SRP). Specifically, we consider only the top k principal components of the latent representation. We first compute the covariance matrix Σ of the latent representation ẑ and then obtain the matrix Vₖ consisting of the eigenvectors corresponding to the k largest eigenvalues of Σ:

    Σ=Cov[ẑ]=VΛVᵀ,

    Σₖ=VₖΛₖVₖᵀ,

    where Λₖ=Diag(λ₁,…,λₖ), Vₖ=(v₁,…,vₖ).

    		(8)

    Instead of evaluating linear classification accuracy on the full latent representation ẑ, we evaluate it on the latent representation projected onto the rank-k principal subspace:

    ẑₖ=Vₖᵀẑ.

    		(9)

    When all principal components are retained, linear classification accuracy on ẑₖ is equivalent to that on the original latent representation ẑ. However, when k is small, the classification accuracy becomes sensitive to linear transformations of the latent representation, such as uneven latent scaling.

    As shown in Table 2, the classification accuracy measured by SRP with k=100 aligns well with diffusion sample quality, as measured by gFID. In contrast, conventional linear classification accuracy fails to capture the effect of uneven latent scaling. Furthermore, SRP provides insights into the effectiveness of individual components of LLDM. As shown in Table 2, residual decomposition improves classification accuracy when only the top 100 principal components of the latent representation ẑ are retained. This suggests that residual decomposition increases the priority of semantically relevant information in the latent space. Uneven latent scaling further improves classification accuracy by a substantial margin by down-weighting the residual component.

    4 Experimental Results

    4.1 Experimental Setups

    Datasets and metrics. For class-to-image experiments, we use ImageNet at 256×256 resolution, training diffusion models on the training split and evaluating on the validation split. We report peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) for reconstruction fidelity and generation FID (gFID), Inception Score (IS), precision, and recall for generation quality, following [Dhariwal and Nichol [9]]. LLDM achieves pixel-exact reconstruction by construction. For text-to-image experiments, we evaluate on Diffusion-Bench at 256×256 resolution [24], using GenEval, DPG-Bench, and GenAI-Bench. To evaluate SRP as a standalone metric, we use the generation results benchmarked by [Xu et al. [42]].

    Baselines and diffusion models. We compare LLDM against three groups of baselines. First, we consider recent pixel-space diffusion methods, including pixel-space REPA [47], JiT [25], PixelGen [29], and Latent Forcing [2]. These methods enable pixel-space diffusion through modifications to model architectures, representations, or training objectives. Second, we include widely used lossy VAEs without explicit diffusion-oriented representation alignment: SD-VAE, IN-VAE, QwenImage-VAE, FLUX-VAE, and SD3-VAE [32, 45, 23, 13, 41]. Third, we compare against diffusion-optimized lossy representations, including VA-VAE, MAE-TOK, VTP-L, and FLUX2-VAE [45, 5, 3, 43]. These baselines enable comparisons with both information-preserving pixel-space diffusion and lossy representations optimized for diffusion.

    For each latent representation, we train SiT-XL [27] to evaluate downstream generation performance. Unless otherwise specified, all diffusion models are trained for 40 epochs using Adam under the same protocol. We report generation quality both with and without classifier-free guidance (CFG) [19].

一句话：以往做法是直接在像素空间建模，代价是要改训练目标或架构。

要点：

  • 要解决的矛盾：既要训练扩散模型，又要**保持像素级精确重建**（lossless）
  • 以往的做法是直接在像素空间建模，但这需要**修改扩散训练目标或模型架构**
  • 这篇换了范式：不去改扩散模型，而是构造一个**无损变换**，把像素映射到「更适合扩散建模」的表示上再训练

为什么值得看：潜空间的算力优势与像素空间的保真优势长期二选一。用「无损变换」替代「有损 VAE」，等于把这道选择题拆开——它与 11-21 Direct3D-V3（直接放弃潜空间）、11-19 DWD（去掉解码器）是同一问题的第三种答案。

中文摘要：这篇研究如何在训练图像扩散模型的同时保持像素级精确重建。以往的做法通常是在像素空间直接建模，代价是需要修改扩散的训练目标或模型架构。作者换了一个范式：不去修改扩散模型本身，而是构造一个无损变换，把像素映射到一种更适合扩散建模的表示上，再在该表示上训练。这样既保留了潜在表示的建模效率，又避免了有损压缩带来的重建误差。与直接放弃潜空间、或去掉解码器的做法相比，这是「潜空间无损化」的第三条路。

item.title: 长片不能靠逐段拼：CaT-Movie 用「全局故事规划器 + 局部窗口渲染器」压住叙事漂移与身份漂移 ｜ CaT-Movie: Balancing Global Planning and Local Rendering for Long Multi-Shot Video Generation
item.description:
一句话：现有多次生成每次只能出有限时长，长片靠拼接，叙事推进与视觉身份就会漂。

要点：

  • 现状的病灶：当前多镜头视频生成每次只能渲染有限时长，长片只能由局部片段**拼接**而成，而叙事推进与**视觉身份**会在接缝处漂移
  • CaT-Movie 因此把系统分成两层：**全局故事规划器**用大语言模型扩展用户请求，负责保留、推断与补全故事线
  • **局部窗口渲染器**负责在每个窗口内渲染，两层配合以同时拿到时间上的连贯性与局部画质

为什么值得看：「先规划、再渲染」是影视制作的常识分工，也是 AI 长内容唯一可能稳定的结构。对做预演、过场动画或宣传片的团队，这条给的是分工方式而不是又一个模型。

中文摘要：当前的多镜头视频生成器每次只能渲染有限时长，因此长片只能由局部片段拼接而成——而在这些片段之间，叙事推进与视觉身份都会发生漂移。CaT-Movie 因此提出「全局规划 + 局部渲染」的两层系统：全局故事规划器借助大语言模型扩展用户请求，负责保留、推断并补全故事线；局部窗口渲染器则在每个时间窗口内完成具体渲染。这种分工让系统同时获得跨镜头的时间连贯性与局部画面质量，本质上复用了影视制作里「先规划、再分镜渲染」的成熟结构。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-20

本期推送：2026-11-22

CaT-Movie: Balancing Global Planning and Local Rendering
for Long Multi-Shot Video Generation

Abstract

Current multi-shot video generators render only limited durations per pass, requiring long movies to be stitched from local segments across which narrative progression and visual identity drift. To synthesize long-horizon movies with Coherence across Time, we present CaT-Movie, a multi-shot generation system consisting of a global story planner and a local window renderer. The planner expands user requests via a large language model to preserve, infer, and complete story details, while deterministic code maintains the resulting storyboard across shots to compile self-contained shot prompts and index reference frames from generated history. To execute this guidance, the renderer applies reference-routed sparse self-attention and shot-wise cross-attention to route identities from the indexed frames while isolating per-shot textual conditions. Given the scarcity of high-quality open-source multi-shot data, we construct a dataset of over 350K film shots annotated with semantic state transitions, entity grounding, and multi-granularity requests. We further build CaT-MBench, a benchmark on held-out films with the same annotations. It gives every baseline its native format and counts cross-shot consistency only when a cut opens a new camera setup, preventing repeated framing from passing as consistency. On CaT-MBench, CaT-Movie attains the highest average score and the most consistent characters among all methods. The project page is available at https://jinplu.github.io/CaT-Movie/.

1 Introduction

Video diffusion transformers have enabled high-fidelity single-shot video synthesis from text [44, 45, 10, 42, 21], and joint multi-shot generators now denoise several shots in one pass [13, 34, 30, 49, 29]. Long multi-shot videos such as movies, however, unfold their narrative states, visual identities, and scenes far beyond any generation window, as events leave lasting consequences and characters return with changed attributes. Because each pass renders only a limited duration, such videos are stitched from local segments in which every new shot rebuilds its scene, and narrative progression and visual identity drift across them [37, 11, 27].

Research systems automate parts of keeping Coherence across Time in long videos, yet face a trade-off between cross-window consistency and camera transitions, which Fig.1 illustrates. Joint generators coordinate shots and cuts within a window [30, 49, 13] but lose consistency beyond it. Memory-augmented generators carry earlier frames forward, recalled by visual diversity, learned relevance, or named subjects [69, 1, 28, 50, 43]. A recalled frame, however, bundles a character’s identity with the camera setup and story state of its shot, so recall not indexed by story state copies prior framing across planned cuts or returns stale appearances [66]. Agentic workflows plan the story before rendering it shot by shot [22, 58, 17, 53, 56, 63], yet drive frozen generators not trained on the plan format [53, 77].

Existing benchmarks mostly obscure these failures by decoupling identity from camera cuts and story state [39, 5, 14, 67]. Without testing whether a planned cut opens a new place, shot size, angle, or cast, consistency checks reward dropped cuts or copied framing as in Fig.1, echoing WorldScore’s camera-control observation [8], while omitting explicit per-shot state continuity. Generation and evaluation thus miss the same record, a structured storyboard that separates who each entity is from the state and camera setup each shot requires, which a renderer can follow and a benchmark can check.

To this end, we present CaT-Movie, which balances global story planning with local window rendering through a structured storyboard. Our planner uses a public language model to expand a request into registered entities and per-shot states and actions, preserving stated facts, inferring event consequences, and completing open details. Deterministic code maintains attire and held items across shots and compiles a self-contained prompt per shot. For each window, code queries the storyboard to recall generated anchor views of recurring characters and objects, preferring views after their latest planned attire or state change. Within each window, our renderer applies shot-wise cross-attention to isolate per-shot prompts and reference-routed sparse self-attention, so each shot reads only itself, the first latent frames of co-generated shots [30], and recalled frames sharing its entities. Trained on storyboard-compiled prompts and same-scene shots often captured from another camera setup, it learns to borrow identity without copying framing.

Training and evaluating this system require films annotated in the same storyboard schema. Our shot-first pipeline processes over 350K film shots [5, 36, 41]. Each scene block pairs multi-granularity requests with an entity registry, per-shot states, within-shot transitions, and entity grounding from boxes, masks, and depth [4, 48]. From held-out films in the same schema, we build CaT-MBench to test what the storyboard plans. Its questions ask whether each planned cut opens a new camera setup, whether returning entities and scenes keep their identity, and whether state changes are established and persist. Consistency across a planned cut counts only when the video opens the new setup, denying copied framing any credit. On CaT-MBench, CaT-Movie executes 0.974 of planned cuts and attains the highest average score and the most consistent characters, at 0.651.

In summary, our contributions are fourfold.

  • •

    Global story planner. A training-free planner pairing language-model expansion with code maintenance to compile shot prompts and index anchor views.

  • •

    Local window renderer. A multi-shot renderer with shot-wise cross-attention, reference-routed sparse self-attention, and cross-setup scene training that preserves identity across windows without copying framing.

  • •

    Film storyboard dataset. Over 350K film shots annotated in a shot-first pipeline with entity registries, state transitions, entity grounding, and multi-granularity requests.

  • •

    Cut-gated story benchmark CaT-MBench. Held-out film stories with native-format baseline adapters and gated checks of consistency and state continuity.

    • 2 Related Work

    Multi-shot video generation and visual memory.

    Joint generators denoise several shots in one window through masked attention, boundary or planning tokens, shot-aware rotary phases, or spatial grids [13, 34, 60, 20, 12, 47, 49, 29]. Wide cross-shot access leaks content and weakens transitions [59], motivating sparse designs that exchange only through per-shot summary tokens such as first latent frames [30]. To reach beyond a single window, keyframe pipelines animate consistent images [73, 16, 62], memory methods recall earlier generated frames [69, 1, 55, 61, 28, 63, 54, 43, 50], and reference models inject given images [64] or bind them to target shots [49, 18, 15]. Yet similarity- or recency-based recall drifts over multiple windows or copies prior framing [28, 43]. Our renderer routes storyboard-indexed anchor views by shared entities with explicit identity lines and trains on same-scene shots from different camera setups to preserve identity without copying framing.

    Story planning and prompt enhancement.

    Because a recalled frame may show an outdated appearance [66, 6, 27], both recalled views and shot prompts must track story progression. Agentic pipelines plan multi-shot stories [22, 58, 17], tracking planned world states [53], keying assets to costume states [77], writing back states parsed from generated video [66, 31], or, in concurrent work, selecting generated references [56, 63], yet their plans drive frozen generators not trained on the plan format. Prompt enhancers write structured captions matched to generator training but only for a single pass [74, 7]. Our planner bridges both: a language model expands requests into our renderer’s storyboard schema, and code maintains cross-shot state to compile per-shot prompts and index post-change anchor views.

    Multi-shot datasets and story evaluation.

    Multi-shot datasets caption clips shot by shot [30, 49, 5, 68], and concurrent datasets add entity states [72, 70] or 3D person geometry [76], yet none combines a cross-shot entity registry, typed per-shot states, within-shot transitions, and entity grounding, as App. D details. Benchmarks score video quality, events, story images, editing, audio, or consistency [19, 71, 52, 9, 75, 67, 26, 39, 14], and those tying consistency to cuts do so only at adjacent boundaries [61] or per video [65]. Our dataset provides all four annotations with multi-granularity requests, and CaT-MBench gates consistency between any two shots on opening a new camera setup whenever the storyboard plans one.

    3 Method

    3.1 Problem Formulation and Overview

    Given a story request, written as a one-sentence synopsis, a scene paragraph, or a numbered shot list, and a target duration, we generate a multi-shot video. A diffusion pass renders a limited duration, 30 s even for the commercial Seedance 2.5 [3]. A long story is therefore generated in windows of consecutive shots, which we cap at 8 s in training under our compute budget and at 7 s on the test stories. As Fig.2 shows, a planner writes one storyboard S before video generation, code derives from S the self-contained prompt cₖ of every shot k and the frames Rₖ it recalls from earlier windows, and a window renderer denoises each window jointly in story order.

    3.2 Storyboard Planner

    Single-pass prompt enhancers [74] do not coordinate prompts across windows. Our planner instead uses Qwen3.8-27B [35] without fine-tuning to write one structured storyboard that deterministic code maintains and queries across shots.

    Structured storyboard.

    A storyboard S pairs an entity registry with a plan for every shot. The registry assigns each recurring character, object, and location a fixed identifier and identity description, plus a default attire per character. The plan of shot k records the location, the camera’s shot size, angle, and movement, an optional opening composition, the action, and a suggested shot duration. It lists the present entities 𝔼ₖ with their opening visible state and each character’s posture, held items, and attire, and writes within-shot changes with initial and visible final values, such as held items ending empty-handed.

    Input adaptation.

    Requests, evaluated in Sec.5.3, range from shot lists fixing per-shot details to synopses leaving most open. Since generation fidelity scales with structured visual information [7], one unified prompt (App. B) instructs the model across all granularities to preserve stated facts, infer implied presence and event outcomes, and complete open details such as postures. Avoiding invented staging, it writes a composition only when the request implies an opening layout, keeps stated action positions, and leaves the remaining layout to the renderer. Constrained decoding guarantees valid JSON, and a plan that misses a shot list’s shot count or has too few shots for the duration is sent back once.

    Maintenance and compilation.

    Code, the prompt compiler in Fig.2, copies back the entity descriptions and camera settings a shot list states and propagates deterministic state across S: it carries each character’s attire from its latest recorded change into later shots and fills unstated held items from the end of that character’s previous shot. Recording when changes occur stays with the model, along with posture and visible state, which mix lasting marks with fleeting expressions. Code scales shot durations to match the target duration and packs consecutive shots greedily into windows under the cap, a longer shot filling a window alone. The plan of each shot k compiles into a self-contained prompt cₖ restating present entity descriptions, current character attire, and change outcomes. Because our renderer trains on prompts from the same compiler and S also indexes the recalled frames Rₖ of Sec.3.3, every shot’s text and visual references stem from one state record.

    3.3 Window Renderer

    Without visual history, per-shot generation loses character identity across shots, as Sec.5.1 shows, yet recalled frames bundle persistent identity with potentially outdated states and framing that should not be copied [6]. Our renderer, Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [45] fine-tuned without new parameters, borrows identity from recalled frames while taking state and framing from each shot’s prompt.

    Recalling generated frames.

    Unlike similarity-based retrieval [69, 1], recall is a deterministic query on S. Because recalling an entity’s latest appearance chains errors across windows, each entity keeps its clearest view as an anchor view while its planned appearance holds (App. A). Consider a target shot k in a window starting at shot k₀ and an earlier shot j

    compared lexicographically. Each target shot also selects the shot before its window at its location with the fewest characters, then the widest shot size, then the earliest index. Keeping up to ten unique source shots per window, we extract each shot’s last frame if it records any attire or visible-state change and its middle frame otherwise. Within the window, Rₖ holds the recalled frames whose source shot shares a present entity with shot k, preventing shots from borrowing framing from frames that show only other characters. Frames sharing no entity with the window, such as empty location views, enter every Rₖ.

    Window attention.

    Each shot is VAE-encoded separately so no latent frame spans a cut. Let Zₖ denote the latent tokens of shot k in window W, Zₖ^f its first latent frame, and Z^refᵣ the clean latents of recalled frame r. Under shot-wise cross-attention, Zₖ attends only to cₖ[30]. Under reference-routed sparse self-attention, it computes

Recalled frames keep the height–width RoPE grid of the shots and, for each reading shot k, take temporal positions five apart ending at pₖ-5, where pₖ is the position of Zₖ^f, rather than acting as adjacent preceding frames [69, 64]. Each attends only to itself and cross-attends to an identity line c^refᵣ marking it as another shot and naming, in the identifiers of cₖ, the cast and setting of its source shot, from frame labels in training and from S at inference.
